subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT DELIVERED BY SIR HENRY DRAYTON, MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speechtext:
Hon. iSir HENRY DRAYTON (Minister of Finance) moved:
That the Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that on the present occasion I shall have to ask the indulgence of the House as I shall have to address the House at considerable length. The fault is not mine; the financial position of the country at the present requires, I think, to be dealt with in considerable detail.
The conditions not only in Canada to-day, but the world conditions obtaining, are very different from the conditions which did obtain while the war was in progress. During this period the compelling necessity of the moment, the winning of the war, required raising large sums of money in the easiest possible way and with the least infMr. Fielding.]
terference with the public or with business methods. It was absolutely imperative that there should be no check in production, no questions raised which might hinder that production or hinder the war effort. It was no time for the consideration of domestic politics, which in any way might distract the nation from a united effort towards the supreme end.
These conditions to-day are changed; the war is won; expenses are great; the cost of Government operations as well as the carrying on of every business of every character in the country has increased enormously, and over and above this the country, with other countries which took their part in the titanic struggle, is faced with a pyramid of debt. The task to-day is to aid the return to ordinary economic conditions to the extent that such return is at this time possible.
The duty to-day is not only to carry on the Government of the country without any additions to the debt, but on the other hand to promote measures which will reduce the nation's obligations. The task while heavy is nevertheless not as severe and difficult as the obstacles and difficulties wh'ch the country has gloriously overcome in the five years of war and stress. Indeed, were it possible for the country to again become as united and earnest as it was during the war period, if it were possible for each and all of us to sink all differences, class and sectional interests and jealousies into an effort towards re-establishing Canada las united and co-ordinated as that which won the war, the task would indeed be easy and simple.
Canada's soldiers during that period won .for themselves and our country imperishable fame. " Their name liveth for evermore." But the productive efforts of Canada during that period were second only to their glorious record. For the five fiscal years ended on March 31, 1915, the excess of the country's imports over exports amounted to $825,521,490. For the next succeeding five years, ended on .March 31 last, this excess of imports was not only overtaken, but our exports exceeded our imports by a sum of $1,803,442,233. It is plain in view of such a tremendous productive and industrial exploit, that if anything like the same effort is made to overcome debts, and by overcoming debts to bring .about a proper deflation of prices, credits, and circulation, the task will prove well within our powers. Inflation.
There undoubtedly is in Canada as everywhere else inflation in the price of commodities, inflation in currency, and inflation in credits. Our total issue of Dominion notes on March 31, 1914, was $117,795,718. It reached a peak of $337,319,309 in November 1918 and on the 31st March last it amounted to $311,932,791. Of this amount $128,366,066 is issued against gold. The amount of gold required under the Dominion Notes Act, as amended, to secure an issue of this amount is $90,866,066. Gold to the extent of $100,286,280 is available. $26,000,000 of the remainder of the currency was issued for national purposes under the authority of the Dominion Notes Act 1915, and secured as therein provided. $50,000,000 was issued for the purpose of making advances to the Imperial Treasury and is secured by the pledge of approved securities, and $107,566,725 was issued to the banks secured by approved securities largely consisting of
Imperial Treasury Bills and our own Treasury Bills. As a result there has been an increase since March 31, 1914, in the circulation issued by the Dominion of $194,137,073.
The banks' circulation on 31st March, 1914, was $96,848,384. In November of the preceding year a high point of $126,839,620 was reached. On the 31st March last it amounted to $225,769,628. As against this increase, in the same period the holdings of the banks in cash reserves (gold and subsidiary coin) rose from $45,661,913 to $79,990,836, and the deposit of Dominion notes and gold in the Central Gold Reserves, earmarked for the redemption of the bank note circulation, rose from $3,500,000 to $108,-
200,000.	In addition, the bank holdings in Dominion notes for general reserve purposes rose from $96,227,321 to $184,152,673.

As the statement shows, the combined circulation of the country amounted on March 31st last to $440,002,420 as against $211,144,102 on March 31st, 1-914, a percentage increase of 108 per cent.
Comparing these increases with those of other countries, the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna recently stated that the circulation of Great Britain had increased 207 per cent between 1914 and the end of 1919, while the circulation of the United States, as given in the report of the Secretary of the Treasury, shows an increase of 70 per cent from June 30, 1914, to the -corresponding date in 1919. The circulation of other countries taking a prominent part in the war has increased to far greater percentages.
Unquestionably, the currency in light of former gold reserves is inflated. The fact, however, is that the world over currency to
an ever-increasing degree is related to movement of commodities, secured by a national guarantee supported by approved securities. This trend was apparent before the war. The best illustration is perhaps afforded by the Federal Reserve legislation of the United States. Under that legislation, currency issued by Federal Reserve Banks requires a gold reserve of 40 per cent and no currency stands higher.
Under all the circumstances, bearing in mind that Canada before the war had to borrow abroad to finance her own requirements, hearing in mind that during the war and since the Armistice she has not only financed herself but has- also extended credits to other nations, the situation of the country's currency is very remarkably good. The percentage of the gold reserves to the Dominion and bank note circulation is 43 per cent. The percentage of gold to

the total circulation of Great Britain based on 1919 figures is 26 per cent and of the United States approximately 55 per cent.
; The circulation, large as it is, is all required. The greatest demand that actual circulation has to meet is the pay-envelope. In view of to-day's conditions the world over on a greatly increased wage scale, much more circulation is now required for this purpose. The increased prices of commodities mean that more money must be kept in the tens of thousands of shop-tills all over the country. The constantly increasing demands on the Mint tell their own story. In 1914, 11,770,108 pieces of coinage were turned' out; in 1919, 35,906,003 pieces, and for last march,, 2,677,874 pieces were coined, as against 806,646 pieces in March, 1914.
Increased credits have contributed and contributed largely in the first instance to the abnormal increase in the cost of commodities, and to a lesser extent increased circulation contributed to the same result. The cost of commodities under new high standards once having been arrived at, however, if business is to continue in Canada under existing world conditions, both the inflated currencies and inflated credits are at the moment necessary to support it. The high prices in Canada could not be and were not made by Canadian action alone. They are the result of the general trend in the prices of commodities the world over, and to-day were it possible to suddenly deflate Canadian credits and circulation, with the general demand for commodities that to-day exists, the influence on the general situation would be negligible. Prices would continue high and the only_ result to the Canadian public consequent on the withdrawal of purchasing power would he stagnation of business, unemployment, and loss of production.
As stated, inflation of credit has more to do with increased buying power and therefore, with that increased buying power, has more to do with affecting the cost of commodities than circulation. It is true that in part these credits are increased by an inflated circulation, but the circulation deposited in banks from time to time plays but a small part of the total deposits. Every credit transaction, every advance made by a bank to a customer inevitably produces a corresponding deposit in the hanks of that customer's creditor or creditors. The net result is to increase bank deposits by the extent of the credit and to increase the liabilities of the hank granting the credit without any corresponding

increase in its cash assets. Obviously, if the money advanced is to be applied in a productive agency which would be carried on with a profit and result in a large gain of commodities to the country, there is no inflation. On the other hand, the business situation has been improved.
The credit basis which is more vicious than any other basis is that which is given for Government expenditure on non-productive objects and which does not result in any addition to the national production. Every loan for an unproductive purpose that the Government makes, no matter how successful it be, to some extent at any rate increases the credit inflation of the country. It either does it directly, as in cases where money is loaned to loan subscribers by the banks for the purpose of enabling them to take up the Government's securities, or indirectly by taking away from the productive agencies of the country savings which otherwise would be available for them, rendering it necessary for the banks to enlarge credits for essential purposes of production which otherwise would have been met by the savings of the nation. Government borrowing, in other words, has the effect of removing capital, the tool of industry, from its ordinary and legitimate purpose of industry and production. It ought to be noted that in Canada the loan situation is extremely satisfactory. Not only has the great bulk of our loans been subscribed to by our own people but in connection with all our large popular issues not one single bond has been subscribed to by the banks. Canadian banks are not loaded with governmental securities.
The increase in bank deposits which has been brought about in Canada is in a very similar ratio to that which has happened in other countries. Our total deposits on 31st March, 1914, amounted to $991,734,246, and on the 31st March last amounted to $1,855,131,598, an increase of 87 per cent. In England, according to Rt. Hon. Mr. McKenna, bank deposits increased 115 per cent from 1914 to 1919, while in the United States an increase of 80 per cent in total deposits occurred between 1914 and 1919.
In Canada it may be noted that the Government's war borrowings amounted in round numbers to $2,000,000,000 as against an increase in deposits amounting to $863,397,352. As a result, the increase in pub lie purchasing power gauged by the total currency in circulation and total hank deposits in Canada increased 91 per cent in 1919 over the figures of 1914. In England

the increase was 125 per cent and in United States 78 per cent.
The commerce of the country still requires ample credits. On the 31st March, 1914, the total of loans made by the Canadian banks amounted to $928,184,060, and on the 31st March last the loans amounted to $1,527,078,232, an increase of 65 per cent, This large sum does not include any advance to the Government. Although the business men of the country and those requiring accommodation are now enjoying this great increase in credits, the fact is that from available resources the banks in Canada as well as in all other countries ought not to meet the full requests made for further credits, apart entirely from the injurious effect credits still further increased would have on the general economic situation.
The situation is therefore one in which it is impossible by any direct Government action to bring about deflation either in circulation or in credits without great danger of economic disaster. Inflation can only safely be cured in this as in other countries, by the Government and Provincial Governments stopping further loans, and by all governmental institutions, including municipalities and indeed every individual whose circumstances permit it, reducing expenditure whenever possible and by an increased production in all our forms of productive industry.
While the trade figures of the country show advances in the value of our production and exports, and while these figures correctly show our standing and growth as compared with those of _ other nations, the fact must not be lost sight of that these figures are based on the inflated values today obtaining and that expressed in quantities the production of the country instead of increasing has actually decreased. Without wearying the House with statistics, it is sufficient to merely point to the best indicator of trade activities, that is, the amount of tonnage handled by the country's railroad system.
Those statistics show that in 1918 our railways handled 127,543,687 tons of freight. This indicates a remarkable activity particularly in view of the fact that many of the country's best workers were overseas and that relatively a very large proportion of our population was withdrawn from agriculture and industry. It is specially significant in view of the fact that in the year 1914, with our men at home, the freight handled only amounted to 101,393,989. tons. The tonnage handled last year, however, only amounted to 116,699,572 tons. Instead of decreasing our production the
imperative necessities of the country required that it should be largely increased, not only to assist in financing and carrying on the country's operations but also to assist in 'bringing about that reduction of the present high cost of living which is so much desired.
Trade.
I have already referred to the aggregate trade for the past year and the favourable balance that has developed over the past five years. The results of the past year require a greater detail. Canada's external trade in 1919-20 resulted in a favourable balance of $220,000,000. The chaotic condition of foreign exchange during the year was not without its influence on our business abroad and tended to complicate the readjustment of international trade. In the United Kingdom-our largest selling market-the Canadian dollar was at a premium ranging from 1 to 22 per cent, while in the United States, where some 75 per cent of the national purchases are made, our dollar has been at a discount of from 2f per cent to 17J per cent.
The rate of exchange thus worked against Canada in her chief selling market as well as in her chief purchasing market. An appreciated currency assists national buying in any market, in which it is at a premium, while purchases are made proportionately the more onerous when made in a market where the currency is at a discount.
Our total imports from United Kingdom amounted to $126,274,000, which is $53,000,000 greater than in 1919 and very nearly, as expressed in dollars, equalled our pre-war trade with the Mother Country. Her purchases from us totalled $489,000,000, a decrease of $51,000,000 from 1919, the balance of trade being $363,000,000 in Canada's favour. While our exports to Great Britain have fallen off, it should be noted that the 1919 figures included about $170,000,000 for munitions and war materials. To the extent of $120,000,000, therefore, this transient trade has been feplaced by trade of a more permanent character. The increase in imports from Great Britain has been very marked in recent months. They rose from a low point of $5,204,979 in April to $25,555,386 in March, the latter figure constituting not only a record but an extraordinary increase. The increase in imports from the Mother Country is very gratifying and is very significant. The greatest previous volume of her monthly exports to Canada prior to the war was $14,395,740 in March, 1913. It is to be noted that the good old Mother Country very nearly doubled March last, the greatest amount of exports she has ever sent to this country.
Exports to the United States amounted to $464,000,000, increasing by $9,000,000, while imports from that country reached the unprecedented figure of $802,000,000 exceeding 1919 imports by $55,000,000. The year's trading, therefore, resulted in an unfavour. able trade balance of $338,000,000. The volume of imports from the United States is all the more remarkable owing to the fact that for a considerable period of the year the adverse exchange rate which has
obtained has added to the extent of the depreciation of our money in New York an additional cost to the Canadian purchaser. It is apparent that the mere question of cost has not weighed very much upon the Canadian buyer. Undoubtedly, the exchange rate is against the interests of our national buying from the United States. If practicable it ought to be remedied but it cannot be properly remedied by any artificial means. It will be remedied and can only be permanently relieved when sterling advances to its normal position and Canada's interchange of commodities with United States is reduced to a more reasonable ratio.

Revenue, 1919-20.

Instead of lessened receipts, as conditions at the time the last Budget was prepared seemed to indicate, the revenue of the preceding year has been exceeded by $75,000,000, and the country's revenue for 1920 was no less than $255,000,000 greater than that of the first year of the war. Expenditure, 1919-20.
The consolidated fund ordinary expenditure will be approximately $349,000,000. This sum of $349,000,000 includes $108,500,000 interest on public debt, $26,000,000 for pensions, and $49,000,000 for Soldiers' Reestablishment.
For investment and capital outlays, beyond the ordinary current expenditure of $349,000,000, an expenditure of $187,856,991 is estimated. The resultant total is $536,741,110 and represents the outlay of Canada for all purposes apart from war during the past year.
With a total revenue of $388,000,000 and an ordinary expenditure of $349,000,000, it will be seen, that during the fiscal year 1919-20 the Government, after meeting all ordinary expenditure, including an increased amount for interest account and pensions over the previous year totalling nearly $39,000,000, has a surplus of approximately $39,000,000 over ordinary ex-158
penditure, to apply to capital expenditure.
The demobilization expenditures for 1919-20 will amount to $350,000,000, making a total outlay for the year of $886,741,110. Our total expenditure for the war, up to and including the 31st March, 1920, now amounts to $1,674,000,000, apart altogether from such expenses resulting from the war, as Pensions, Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, Soldiers' Land Settlement, and interest on war debt.
Debt.
During the year just passed the country paid off a floating debt of $247,000,000 out of the proceeds of the Victory Loan issue of 1919. The floating or short date indebtedness of the country at the close of the year amounted to only $88,956,000. The addition to the debt during the year amounted to $395,000,000 and the position of the net debt has already been referred to.

Grand Trunk Acquisition.
The current expenditure, however, will be greater this year than that already indicated. Deficits on the railway system have been reported in the Main Estimates. These deficits during the readjustment period will be materially increased by the acquisition of the Grand Trunk. The primary object of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk was to render efficient and properly complete the National system. The country had a large railway investment with proper terminal facilities in the West, but, speaking generally, lacking them in the East. The railway burden was also largely increased by the failure of the Grand Trunk Pacific promoted and owned by the Grand Trunk. The country was faced with the necessity either of providing new terminals at great cost in eastern centres, leading to a still greater railroad duplication, or of acquiring the Grand Trunk system. The traffic centres of the East had to be opened to the National system if that system was to be put upon a proper basis and enabled to properly compete in all through-traffic. Over and above this, the Grand Trunk was acquired for the purpose of reducing existing duplication and enabling extensive operating economies to be made.
Over and above these considerations, the acquisition of the Grand Trunk was highly desirable in order to prevent the insolvency of the line and the consequent breakdown of railroad facilities in the districts served by that system. Railway receiverships in some instances do not carry with them serious consequences, but in the case of the Grand Trunk a receivership would be exceedingly objectionable owing to the fact that the company's system is composed^ of many separate railway corporations having in instances separate obligations and different creditors, rendering a re-organization as of a completed system very difficult. Such re-organization would be attended with still

greater difficulty owing to the fact that part of it would take place under the direction of United States courts and part under the direction of Canadian courts. The dislocation of business would have been exceedingly great and the inconvenience and loss to Canadian shippers and consignees and to Canadian business heavy.
Some economies ought to be effected in the near future, but with the arbitration pending it is improbable that full benefit of the Grand Trunk acquisition can be expected in the current year. It will be necessary to make advances to the company to cover past due operating obligations. These advances will constitute obligations of the company and as such must be taken into account in the arbitration. In addition to this, advances of necessity will be made to provide for this year's operations, including the acquisition of necessary rolling stock.
The abstract of the company's cash book as of February 21 last shows obligations overdue or shortly payable amounting to $18,710,588, made up in large part of unpaid vouchers, bank overdrafts, drafts held for acceptance and short date notes given for supplies. As against these debts the Grand Trunk has supplies on hand and certain capital accounts as against which no capital issue has been made. They are, however, not of a character which can be relied upon for the purpose of supplying cash to meet these liabilities.
The approximate amount to cover advances for the purposes above mentioned is $28,000,000.
Railway difficulties and overdrafts ought now to be at their peak. Proper co-ordination and economies will, just as soon as the Grand Trunk arbitration is over, be practicable and will be put into effect. The balance sheet, however, inevitably depends on the cost of carrying on business, which has been very greatly increased, and the general rate schedule. The serious drain made by the railways on the country's finances ought to be materially lessened.
As a matter of common justice to Canada it should be stated that the charges of unfairness levied against Canada by different shareholders at Grand Trunk meetings, are unfounded. The simple fact remains that if the Grand Trunk had not been taken over the shareholders in all human probability would have lost their whole investment. It is entirely untrue that the Government forced the company to pay a highly increased wage scale and at the same time 158i
prevented it from raising its rates either directly or through the Board of Railway Commissioners. The chairman of the Grand Trunk is reported to have made the following statements at the special general meeting of the company:
I knew there were influential men in Canada who thought the policy the Government should pursue was to let us alone, and that the weaker we became the easier we could be dealt with - (hear, hear)-they knew we were being forced by the Government to carry on under impossible conditions-conditions over which we had absolutely no control. What were those conditions? That we should meet every order issued by the Canadian Railway War Board to increase wages by immediate compliance, notwithstanding that no increase of rates to meet the increased expenses was allowed	
In 1918 an increase of freight rates was granted on a great portion of the freight carried, something under 15 per cent in March and something under 25 per cent in August. Notwithstanding this, owing to a further serious increase of wages being ordered by the Canadian Railway War Board, without any corresponding increase in rates, there was an actual decrease in net profit for 1918. The gross traffic for 1918 amounted to £12,600,000, as compared with £9,800,050 in 1917, or a gross increase of £2,700,000, but the working expenses increased by £2,900,000, or a net loss of £200,000 for 1918.
In 1919, the accounts of which are not yet complete, the gross earnings are estimated at £14,000,000, as against £12,600,000 in 1918, or an increase of £1,400,000. Owing, however, to another large increase in wages being ordered by the Canadian Railway War Board-again without any increase in rates-it is not expected there will be any increase in net profit, and consequently the company will only be able to meet its fixed charges. Thus, in each of the three years-1917, 1918, and 1919-in consequence of being compelled, by order of the Canadian Railway War Board, to grant increased wages without sufficiently increased rates, the shareholders lost on the average at least between £1,250,000 and £1,500,000 in each of those three years, which they ought to have received in dividends.
The direct imputation conveyed to the shareholders was that the Railway Wat Board was a governmental institution to whose orders railways were subject. It was not. That board was not a statutory body but was an organization formed by the railway companies (including the operators of the Intercolonial) for the express purpose of more perfectly co-ordinating their activities and for the purpose of dealing with large railway questions. The board was organized in 1917. The Grand Trunk's representation was as follows: Mr. Howard G. Kelley, a president, and Mr. W. E. Gillen, chairman of the Administrative Committee. Mr. Gillen subsequently retired and Mr. W. D. Robb, a vice-president of the Grand Trunk, was elected a member of the Administrative Committee. In 1919 the

board was reorganized as The Railway Association of Canada with Mr. Kelley this time as sole president and with Grand Trunk representation on every committee. The 'organization was entirely a railway organization. It was not a Government organization. The organization had, however, no control over railroad rates. The Grand Trunk has American lines as well as Canadian lines. It has traffic originating at American points for Ganadian destinations, The rate for the shorter haul in Canadian territory cannot obviously be greater than the rates on the longer haul for Canadian destinations from American territory. Subject to this consideration, and just as soon as action was taken by the American Commission, every application made by the company for a general increased tariff during the whole of the war period was given effect to, and I am informed by the Board of Railway Commissioners that there is no general application for an increase of rates by the Grand Trunk Railway Company pending or refused, nor was any application of that character pending at the time the meeting was held. The highest dividend distribution of the Grand Trunk amounted to $4,736,241.22. The average dividend payments are much lower without deductions being made for deficits of the Grand Trunk Pacific (the subsidiary of the Grand Trunk and organized by it) which were met by advances made by the Parliament of Canada to an amount in excess of $50,000,000.
Luxury Taxes.
Not only is more revenue necessary but extravagant and luxurious expenditure ought to be checked. Just so long as expenditure on non-essentials and extravagant expenditure continues, just so much longer will the drop in the value of essentials be postponed. On those having income more than necessary for properly maintaining themselves and families, there rests a special duty of saving whenever possible and in this manner adding to the available financial resources for development and for industrial undertakings. Extravagant buying should stop. With this end in view, as well as for necessary revenue, it is proposed to levy on certain specified articles excise taxes which are to be paid by the purchaser to the vendor at the time of sale for consumption or use, or on importation for consumption or use other than resale. Upon certain articles of wearing apparel, such as boots, shoes, etc., in excess of $9 a pair, men's and boys' suite in excess of $45 each, fur coats and

robes in excess of $100 each, women's dresses in excess of $45 each, women's suits in excess of |60 each, men's and women's overcoats in excess of $50 each; hats, hose, neckwear, shirts, purses, and gloves bought above specified prices, and on fans and opera cloaks, it is proposed to levy a tax of 10 per cent of the total purchase price. The women are given a little preference over the men because men's suits in excess of $45 will 'be taxed, whereas women's suits up to $60 will be exempt from taxation.

In view of the necessities of increased revenues, a tax of one per cent on the sales of all manufacturers, wholesale dealers, jobbers and importers is proposed. The tax will not include retailers as such but w'ill include the goods manufactured or imported by any retailer although manufactured or imported by such retailer for r tail sale by himself. Consideration must also be given to the cost of essentials and on this account it has been determined that the tax

The sales tax ought not to be used as a basis of further profits and must not, therefore, be included in the manufacturer's or wholesaler's costs on which profit is calculated. The tax when not absorbed by the vendor must then be included in his invoice as a separate item.
Stamp Taxes.
The existing tax on cheques will be continued, but the rate increased on bills of exchange and promissory notes so as to provide a 2 cent tax on all bills or notes of $100 or less and for every additional $100 ot fractional part thereof 2 cents more. A tax of 2 cents for each share of stock transferred is also proposed.
The method of collecting stamp duties on patent and proprietary medicines and perfumery will be changed by having the stamps affixed by the manufacturer or importer instead of the retailer at the time of sale. The stamps are not to be included in the costs of the manufacturer or importer but if not absorbed by the seller are to be added in the invoice as a separate item.
Removal of Tax on Moving Picture Films.
Under existing legislation a special tax is collected on films used in moving picture theatres. The tax provided is a charge of 15 cents per film for each day upon which such film is used. It has been found that this duty has worked a hardship on small movie theatres. Many complaints nave been received and it has become apparent that the tax in the case of the small theatres sometimes represents a charge of as high a-s 6 or 7 per cent of its total receipts, already subject to municipal and provincial taxation, while in the case of large theatres the tax amounts to less than 1 per cent of receipts. Undoubtedly the present tax is unfair in its incidence and it has been decided to remove it. Movie

As a means of raising revenue, the tariff should be so adjusted as to place the chief burden upon those best able to bear it. Articles of luxury should be heavily taxed through the imposition of customs and excise rates. Food commodities and other necessaries of life, not produced or manufactured in Canada, should, if taxed at all, bear only such imposts as are necessary for revenue purposes. Those produced in Canada should be subjected to such customs duties only as may be necessary in the general national interest to be determined after strict investigation from time to time.
Apart from the question of revenue, the tariff should have regard to the maintenance, stability and prosperity of Canadian enterprise in the development of all our natural resources in lands, forests, mines, fisheries, as well as our agricultural and manufacturing industries. Consideration must also be given to the importance of creating and maintaining conditions that will afford to Canadian industrial workers
opportunities for steady and remunerative employment. It is undoubtedly in the true interests of Canada as a whole that Canadian workers should not be forced to seek in foreign countries employment and opportunity denied them at home by reason of the export of the natural resources, primary products, and raw materials with which the Dominion is so amply endowed.
For the purpose of encouraging the fullest development of our natural resources the tariff should be so adjusted as to permit machinery and the implements of production to be purchased at prices that will compare equitably with those paid in other countries for similar articles. The revised tariff law should be so framed and administered as to effectively prevent any customs duty being used to facilitate the formation or maintenance of any combine, trust, association or agreement among manufacturers, dealers, or producers for the purpose, at the expense of the general public, of restraining trade, preventing competition, or unduly enhancing the selling price of any article of commerce. The principle of trade preference between the different members of the Britannic Commonwealth should be maintained and extended from time to time to such degree as may be found practicable and consistent with Canadian interests.
While a general revision of the Canadian tariff based upon the foregoing considerations is due, it must be recognized that, owing to the war, economic and commercial conditions the world round have been profoundly disturbed and that, as a consequence it is neither practicable nor possible in the national or public interest to undertake such revision until a thorough inquiry is made to ascertain the essential facts upon which tariff provisions must necessarily be based.
All the financial difficulties of the moment can be, and I have no doubt will be, readily met. I am confident that every hon. gentleman has the firmest belief and confidence in Canada-and that belief is well justified. Immigration and a reasonable investment of outside capital rendering our illimitable national resources available, but above all the national characteristics and strength of character of the citizens of Canada, will easily surmount the past. And Canada's situation to-day is indeed an enviable one. There is no country in the world that can offer greater inducements to the immigrant and greater inducements to foreign capital than Canada can. Prosperity is entirely relative. Our position relatively has

enhanced. We have finished borrowing, and notwithstanding the great increase in our debt, Canada's securities to-day stand as high, or higher, than those of any foreign country in what is to-day the great market for foreign securities-New York. Canada's world status is far greater to-day notwithstanding her losses and war debts than it was in 1914.
I crave the indulgence of the House, Mr. Speaker, for the length of time I have spoken before introducing these resolutions. I wonder if before reading them I might not say just one or two words more. You know, some people to-day think, and apparently believe, that the country is in a bad state; I do not. Some people to-day think, and apparently believe, that the job ahead oi Canada is a bigger job than Canada can look after; I do not. I wonder if we are not altogether too prone to forget what Canada has done; I wonder if we are not entirely too prone to forget the amount of hard work, of sacrifice and of devotion that the Canadian people showed themselves capable of sustaining during the war period.
Are we not a little too apt to forget that it was the soldiers of Canada who formed just a few short monlths ago the spearhead of the forces of righteousness? Are we not a little too apt to forget that we have got the same spirit and the same blood in Canada yet? Are we not a little too apt to forget that their magnificent achievements never could have been and never would have been possible had not the men behind and, indeed, the women, too, seen to it that the soldiers were supported, that reinforcements were sent? Yes, the war record is a glorious record; but there were other war activities. Why, there is no better record than the record of the Canadian Medical Staff; no better record than the record of Canada's production; no better record than the record of Canada's transportation facilities, which remained at a higher point than did those of any other country engaged in the war.
Does it not seem rather ridiculous for any one to seriously think that a nation that has done so much will not now be able to look after its own business; that a nation that has done so much for Europe and the world is not going to do something for Canada- something for that Canada which is so dear to every Canadian, something for that Canada which is to-day so infinitely more precious and glorious by reason of the sacrifices made by her fighting men than she ever was before, something for that cohintry which the very best of us in consecrating his services to her is compensated

by the thought that it is impossible for any Canadian to do too much for Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
speechtext:
'Mr. 'Speaker, while we can
hardly be expected to agree with all that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) has said, I am sure that I can speak for my friends ori this
side of the House as well as for myself when I offer him my very sincere congratulations upon the manner in which he has performed, coming to him as it does for the first time, the duty of presenting that annual statement of our financial affairs which we call the Budget Speech.
At all times the preparation of the Budget is a matter calling for painstaking labour. It is a matter of large responsibility which any Minister of Finance must necessarily take very seriously, and that responsibility has fallen on my hon. friend at this time under circumstances of more than usual difficulty. There is a notion in some minds that the Government during the war had a hard time, and I am not sure but that my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), may have had the idea that he particularly had a hard time. That is

all a mistake. The Government did not have a hard time during the war. The burden of carrying a load is not to be measured merely by the weight of the load, one has to have regard to the condition of the highway over which it has to be carried. A light load may be heavy where the road is rough and the grade hard. In the case of a heavy load, if the road is smooth and the grade not steep, the yoke is easy and the burden light. So it was with the Government during war time. There was a condition of the country unusual, it is true. My hon. friends opposite had to deal with some new and unusual problems, hut if they had to deal with new problems they found a new spirit abroad in the land to meet those problems. The patriotic spirit of the country, stirred as it should have been, and was, by the war, stood behind the Government during the whole period of the war. The Government had the support of Parliament to an extraordinary degree. Did they want appropriations? Tens and hundreds of millions of dollars were voted to them promptly, unanimously, and with less inquiry than will be made to-day on a $1,000 appropriation. Did they want men? Until a little unpleasantness occurred towards the end of the war, they had the men almost tumbling over each other in their desire to volunteer and participate in the war. Did they want loans?- The hon. Minister of Finance had only to issue his proclamation, and the people responded with an enormous sum of the public money. In all these things the way was easy. The Prime Minister and his colleagues had only to ride on the crest oi the wave. But now is the time of trouble. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance of to-day has the heavy end of the load. The difficulties are coming to-day and there have been no such difficulties in the past, as some persons have too hurriedly imagined.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has taken hold of the Government's enterprise at the present time under certain circumstances of difficulty, but in one respect he has been highly favoured, and he is to be congratulated. The hon. gentleman came into office just about the time it became necessary to float another loan, and the response that was made to his demand in that respect, I am sure, must have been gratifying to him, as it was to the country generally. It is very gratifying to know that the Canadian people responded so liberally to that demand, and I think that perhaps my hon. friend the ex-Minister of 
Finance (Sir Thomas White) may look on the situation with a little of envy, because the present Minister of Finance received his $670,030,000 without offering the bait of tax exemption. So I am inclined to think my hon. friend the ex-Minister ot Finance may look on the Finance Minister of to-day with a little of envy, and perhaps feel that if he had had more courage he might have had a similar experience. It is, of course, gratifying to know that this money has been obtained, and yet there is a thought which we cannot put aside when we are reminded that of about two billions of dollars of these loans floated, $1,3Q0,000,-
000	are exempt from taxation. A bargain is a bargain. The Government of the day agreed that these should be exempt, but I have never concealed from myself the fact that that exemption is going to be a continuous source of trouble.
1	am afraid it will be one of the things which will tend to increase the disrontenl which unhappily prevails. But the contract was made, and there is no use complaining of it. I know there were some reasons which tempted my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) of that day to offer the loan in that ,vav, and I am not saying that he was wrong. But looking back over it, I think he will agree that it is a pity he did not have more courage and ask the people of Canada to present this money to the Treasury without offering the bait of tax exemption.
I remember meeting a distinguished visitor to Canada several years ago who had been here in former years, had gone away and returned. He was noting the many things in which Canada had made progress and when somebody said, "Yes, Canada has become known to the world," "Ah, yes," he replied, "not only has the world discovered Canada, but Canada has discovered herself," and that he thought was a good thing. Well, in the matter of finance, surely we will all say that Canada has discovered herself to a surprising and a gratifying degree.
I think I am right in saying that the largest loan ever offered by the Dominion of Canada before the war was a loan of $30,000,000, or six million pounds sterling. It was offered in England, and I remember it was with fear and trembling that we asked so large a sum; and when it was suggested to the financiers of London that perhaps it might be expedient to increase the amount to $50,000,000 instead of $30,000,000 they gravely shook their heads and said, "Oh dear, no; that is too much." So that

$30,000,000 was all we dared then ask from the financiers of London. Yet, here in this country, our own Canadian people were prepared to put their hands into their own pockets and in so brief a time to bring out $2,000,000,000 to meet the demands made upon them. And at one fell swoop the Minister of Finance found them offering him $670,000,000, the amount of the last loan. All that is very gratifying in some respects; but there is no rose without its thorn, and there are some things in connection with that loan which we may as well frankly recognize.
There is one feature which, while well known to the inside circle of finance, has not been made known in any marked way to the Canadian public at large, and I think it is time that the Canadian people knew something about it. If you take up the last volume of the public accounts, for the year ending March 31, 1919, you will find a couple of interesting items. There is a later volume than that but we have not got it. For that period, however, any hon. member will discover in the statement of receipts and expenditures an item called "Bank of Montreal Loan Trading Account,"-a very interesting account. Hon. members will read the item therein contained and will discover that the Government paid out on that account the sum of $7,450,000 and got back $5,177,904, so that on that account, whatever it means, the Government of Canada-in other words, the people of Canada-lost $2,272,000. Now, what does that mean? It means, to put the matter plainly, that the Government have been trading on the stock exchange with the money of the people of Canada. That is the plain way to put it. I know what will be said by hon. gentlemen opposite; I anticipate the explanation and will give it voluntarily myself. We have no returns for the year just closed. But I venture to say that in all human probability the loss on that trading account during the last twelve months was even much greater than it was in the previous year. Now, it will be said on behalf of the Government that this has been done to stabilize the loan. The Government will say-reasonably and with some force-that they were looking forward to putting other loans on the market, and were concerned with keeping up the price, and therefore made this arrangement with the banks for them to buy bonds in order to prevent depreciation. That, I think, was the object in view.
You are all wrong.

If my hon. friend will pardon an interruption, I should like to
point out that he is entirely wrong on the so-called trading account. In the year 1918 the Government not only did not lose money but made money. The stabilization did not cost the Dominion Government one cent.
I am exceedingly glad to hear that statement from my hon. friend, but the public accounts show
You are wrong.
Order.

I give the items as they appear in the public accounts:	"Bank of
Montreal Loan Trading account." This item shows that the bank received $7,450,000 and that there was paid back into the Treasury, credited on the other side, $5,177,904, so that there is apparently, between the receipts and the expenditures, a difference, roughly, of $2,272,000.
Represented in bonds which were taken in-cancelled.

The item is charged
up on one side as expenditure and on the other side as receipt, and I cannot see any other explanation than that I have given. I recognize, of course, that the object of the Government was to stabilize the loan in order to prevent depreciation, and there is this to be said, that war time conditions must necessitate war time methods, during and even after war. I am not saying that there was absolutely no justification for the ground which the Government took; on the contrary, I admit the force of the argument that may be advanced. I can understand that the minister, anxious to have the support of the financial houses, would offer them a guarantee and assurance that if they would invest their money in the bonds they would be protected against loss. I can understand that there would be a temptation to do that, and I think I am stating fairly the reason which the Government had in view. All I desire to say, however, is that if you want to understand that transaction completely you must apply to a private corporation the principle which it involves. An individual owner of shares, -a director owning shares,-would be justified in spending his own money to support stock in the market; but if a corporation had issued a block of securities at a certain price and sold them to the public, and if, with a view to keeping up the price, they then took the money of the company and went out to buy the shares in order to keep up the market, that would not be considered a very sound financial trans-

action. Indeed, I think that would be a transaction which, if it occurred in connection with a private corporation, would be very severely criticised. Well, what is sound business in the case of a private corporation may, to say the very least, be usefully applied to the operations of a government. I quite appreciate the object which the Government have had in view, and I am not sure that any other Minister of Finance would not have been tempted to do the same thing. At the same time, however, I regard this as a financial measure which is open to grave question, and at all events it would be wise on our part to advise the Minister of Finance not to do the same thing again if he can help it. If he has given assurances to the financial houses he must keep faith with them, but it would be well that he should avoid in the future a method such as this. I find that the same question has arisen in the United States. Various efforts are being made there to give an artificial and fictitious value to United States bonds, and a measure was introduced in the United States Congress for the purpose of attaining this end by exchanging one form of bond into another, issuing a new bond which was of a more attractive character, the probable result being that prices would be kept up. The matter came before the Secretary of the United States Treasury who was asked to give his opinion thereon, and Secretary Houston wrote a letter, of which I shall read only a part:
As the Treasury views it, the present depreciation is due chiefly to the fact that of the 2 0,0'O O', 000 Americans who patriotically subscribed during: the war large numbers have not been willing or able to exercise such control over their personal expenditures as would enable them to retain their bonds after the cessation of hostilities.
Many patriotic people who bought Liberty bonds under the impulse of patriotism have been unwilling since the war was over to continue to lend their money to the Government and have forced their holdings on the market more rapidly than others could save funds to invest, with consequent depreciation in market prices. The remedy is for the people to work and save, to keep their holdings of Liberty bonds as investments and to purchase additional Government securities with their savings.
The present prices of Liberty bonds are causing no loss to real investors, who are holding their bonds as permanent investment; they are not suffering because others see fit to sell their bonds now for less than they are worth, and neither these investors nor those who wish to sell their bonds have any ground for expecting a donation from the United States in the form of additional tax exemptions or othet; privileges.
I think that opinion of the United States Secretary of the Treasury might usefully be

applied in Canada. If it has been necessary to do these things in order to stabilize bonds and to give them an artificial value it is a policy that we should get rid of at the earliest possible moment consistent with the obligations that have already been assumed.
There is another feature in relation to the loans which we must present, not by way of complaining, but merely that the public may see all sides of the question. It is, a3 I have said, a very gratifying thing to find that the people of Canada are able to subscribe so handsomely to these loans It is a grand thing to know that we have ihis immense sum of money in Canada, and I warmly congratulate the Minister of Finance on his success in obtaining it; but at the same time there is an old, homely proverb that you cannot eat your cake and have it. This vast sum of money which has been absorbed for the purposes of the Government has been withdrawn from the ordinary fields of industrial and other activities in Canada. It is money which, if the Government had not taken it, would have remained in the pockets of the people until they could find a convenient investment for it in some of the forms of industrial or commercial activitiy. If you take that vast sum away from the people you diminish to that extent their ability to carry on the ordinary business of the country-that is clear enough.
There was no immediate effect and for the reason that at the first stage of these operations no actual money passed. The man who subscribed for bonds gave a cheque on his account in the bank and handed it over to the credit of the Minister of Finance. It went to the credit of the Minister of Finance and there was really no actual passing of money. It was only as time passed ana when the Government began to absorb this money that we began to feel the effect of it. What is the effect of it? We are beginning to see to-day that in consequence of the withdrawal of these large sums of money the banks are finding themselves a little harder up. The usual story put forward in the public and financial press is that the banks are contracting their credits. They will have to contract their credits because as fast as money is paid or used for the purposes of these loans it passes away and the banks do not have it any longer. It will be seen that we are beginning to feel now some of the effects of the withdrawal of this vast sum of money from the ordinary fields of activity.

We feel it too in another way. There is the housing problem all over Canada to-day. Certainly, housing is one of the chief needs in all big cities and towns. It is partly because during the war there was less activity than usual in mortgage and building operations, partly because building materials are high in price, but it is largely because there is no longer money available to lend to people who want to buy property and build houses. When the Government are offering 54 per cent on a gilt edged security, the finest security that exists in the world perhaps except British consols-when the Government are offering 7 per cent for money in New York, when they are borrowing money to-day under the guise of the National railway in New York at 7 per cent; when the Government are offering these large rates of interest to the public, what is more natural than that the funds of the people shall flow into the treasury of the Government and that they shall not be available for various other purposes? I believe that the housing difficulty to-day is to some extent-to a considerable extent-the result of that policy. Mind, I am not complaining; the Government had to have money and they got the money which it was absolutely necessary they should get, but we should remember that in getting it for the purposes of the Government it is not available for other purposes.
The lesson that I would draw is this: It is a great thing to be able to get our capital in Canada when you have to get it. It was a great thing to be able to get money in Canada when the money markets of London and New York were closed against us. It was a great thing that in a condition of emergency we could get the money. But it is just as well to remember that Canada is a comparatively young and a com-partively undeveloped country. Canada is a country which will need capital and therefore it is exceedingly desirable that the Government should gradually get its finances into a condition which will enable it to go when new loans are needed-let us hope they will not be needed right away- to the money markets of the world. If they need new loans it is most desirable that the Government, if possible in the financing of Canada, should appeal for those loans to the ordinary money markets of the world. In order that local capital may be made available for the development of local interests, housing enterprises and other activities I trust that when the moment comes
for another loan the conditions will be such that the Minister of Finance will not have to raise it at home but will get it somewhere abroad.
The Minister of Finance certainly has, as I have said, an exceedingly difficult task. I wonder if the public really understand it. I do not think they do. If you strike a man a little blow he knows what hit him and he perhaps measures the pain. Hit him a little harder blow and you simply knock him speechless and he does not know what happened. I think that the man in the street has had such a hard blow in regard to these big questions of debt that we talk so much about, that he is knocked out. The figures are so large that they are rather beyond his comprehension.
I wonder if the public really understand the financial position of Canada to-day. The Minister of Finance has very fairly put it before the public and I am anxious only to help him in the matter. I am anxious that the people should appreciate the situation to-day, I do not speak of this matter in any complaining spirit, or in any party spirit,' but I am anxious that they should actually understand the tremendous burden that they are taking upon themselves and the share of the burden that they must carry in order that the finances of Canada may be made sound and that the credit of Canada may be upheld. I want to offer a few comparisons, not as between the administration of on Government and another, not as between the period of one party and another, but as between a year before the war and a year after the war. I cannot expect to offer anything that is new but I will merely to put one or two things in striking contrast-
If my hon. friend does not wish to commence a new subject at this time we might call it six o'clock.

Very good; thank you.
At Six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

The Minister of Finance, in his speech which we had the pleasure of listening to this afternoon, very properly gave us a mass of statistics on the business of the country which we shall have the pleasure of seeing in Hansard. The figures can be better



examined then, and I presume they will be found useful for the purposes of reference.
My hon. friend in very general terms expressed a note of hope and wholesome optimism, and desired it to be understood that he had great faith, great hope and great confidence in Canada. I sympathize with all those sentiments and I am glad to be able to say that I also have not less confidence than has my hon. friend in the ultimate judgment, success and prosperity of the Canadian people. I think they aie about the sanest people on earth; I know of the people of no other nation who are more sane and very few that I would say to-day are as sane as the Canadian people. I feel confident that when they fully understand things they will appreciate the difficulties which the Government, and every man in public life, has to face; that they will make all due allowances for those difficulties and that they will be actuated by the desire to assist the minister and the Government to -bring about satisfactory results. That will be accomplished -all the quicker, and all the more certainly, if we endeavour to give them a clear appreciation of what the situation is.
I mentioned before you left the Chair at six o'clock, Sir, that I was afraid the ordinary individual-as we say, the man in the street: the man who makes no special study of public affairs and yet is an interested and patriotic citizen-I expressed the fear that be has failed to appreciate the seriousness of the position. I do not say that in any pa-rty sense. No matter what Government might be in power it would be a very serious position, and I am anxious that 'the people generally shall come to understand it fairly and well.
When a Minister of Railways, a few years ago, -came into this House with a deficit on the operation of the Government railways of perhaps six, or seven, or eight hundred -thousand dollars, there was -a keen appreciation of what that -meant. There was keen- ^questioning, there wa-s sharp criticism, there was wide inquiry; the people understood, and could appreciate' -a deficit of such an amount in the Government railway operations. But this year the Minister of Railways comes in and frankly acknowledges that the deficit on the operation of the Government railways during the last year was $47,000,0000. Well, that is an illustration of what I described before as the "knock-out" argument; the thing is really iso big as to be beyond the comprehension of the ordinary m-an.

I was about to make -a few -comparisons, not as between party and party, or as between government an-d government, but merely between a year before the war and a year afterwards, in order that by some simple and sharp contrasts I -might help the Minister of Finance to h-ave the public clearly understand the great -change th-at has taken place. Now, let us take the year 1914. The year ended 31st of March, 1914, was a year before the (war, and the year 1920, ended a few days ago, was a year after the war. With respect to the first period the public accounts, of course, are available. With respect to the second -period the volume of public -accounts is -not out- the year only closed a few days ago. But the minister has, both in his -speech and elsewhere, furnished us wit-h information which gives us a general idea of the operations of the year 1920. Noiw -the revenue for the year 1914 was $163,174,394.56. I come now, for the purpo-ses of comparison, to the estimate for the year 1920, -and here I find -a little difficulty. The -minister today, I -think, stated that his estimate o-f the revenue for the year 1920 was $388,000,000. Weil, there have no doubt been reasons for a very recent revision of my hon. friend's figures, because only a few days ago, before the end of the year, in answer to a motion for returns, my hon. friend's department issued -a statement -showing that in Itheir judgment the revenue for 1920 would be $325,000,000. If, in -the few days that have elapsed, my hon. friend has h-ad reason to enlarge his estimate of the revenue I am very glad o-f it; but I shall have to -make the comparison which I -am about to make on the hasi-s of the figures which he supplied a short time ago. According -to those figures, in 1914 we received a -revenue of $163,174,394.56 and for the year 1920, $325,000,000-which -the Minister of Finance has now enlarged to $388,000,000. Well, if there were nothing but the revenue statement to look at, that would be a very gratifying situation. According to my hon. friend's latest figures the revenue.'has more than doubled. Let us convert it into revenue per head of population for convenience of comprehension. In 1914 the revenue per head was $21.12; in 1920, according to the first figures given to me by -my hon. friend-which would have to be enlarged a little now-the revenue per head was $36.11.
As I said, if we had only the revenue side to look at, that would indicate great progress and flourishing finance; but when we turn to the expenditure side we find a

pretty serious state of affairs. The total expenditure in 1914 was $186,241,047.63. When I speak of total expenditure, I am disregarding the question of the consolidated fund or capital expenditure or anything of that sort. It is what Mr. Mantalini calls the "demnition" total, and that is what we have to provide for. So I am merely presenting the total. As I say, the total expenditure in 1914 was $186,241,047.63. When I come to the total expenditure for 1920 I have another difficulty. My hon. friend to-day said, I think, that his estimate of the total expenditure for 1920 was $556,000,000. Could my hon. friend tell me from memory whether that is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot.

I took the figures down at the time. But I am now confronted with this difficulty, that the previous statement which my hon. friend was kind enough to furnish me, in connection with a return I asked for, placed the total expenditure for 1920 at $675,125,000. That is the amount contained in a return presented by the hon. minister, and which he gave as the estimated total expenditure for 1920. My hon. friend's statement to-day shows a large reduction in this amount. While I was glad to find from 'his figures that there has been a great increase of revenue, I should be equally glad to find that he has a diminished expenditure, but again I have had to make a few calculations based on the figures he gave before. So $675,125,000 I take as the total expenditure for 1920. Converting that into expenditure per head for simplicity of understanding, we have this result, that in 1914 the total expenditure per head was $24.11; in 1920 the total expenditure per head, according to the figures previously given to me, would be $75.01.
Now, that is a contrast which should make our people think for a moment. If we had in 1914 before the war what we thought a large expenditure of $24A1 per head, and to-day we are expending $75 per head, that is a very striking comparison which should suggest to every Canadian the gravity of the situation.
Let us turn now to the extent of the debt.
I take the gross debt of 1914 as stated, at $554,391,368.86. The population, as estimated at that time, was 7,725,000. So that works out the gross debt of 1914 at $71.75 per head. We have no absolute close estimate of the population to-day, but I under-159i
stand for all practical purposes the officials of the Government are treating it as around 9,000,000; and we shall all be delighted to find that is correct. Taking that as correct, the gross debt of 1920, the year just closed, according to the figures supplied to me in the return I have referred to, was $3,014,483,774.12, which works out per head at $334.90. Again I ask the House, but still more I ask the country, to note those figures,-that in the year before the war our gross debt per head was $71.75, while it is now $334.90. That is an immense debt, and surely reflection on these figures will make us all realize the gravity of the .situation.
I come now to the net debt. In 1914, with a population of 7,725,000, our net debt stood at $335,996,850.14, or $43.49 per head; turning now to 1920, and taking our population at 9,000,000, we find that the net debt is placed at a little less than two billion dollars-$1,935,946,312.85, or $215 per head.
Let us reflect a moment on those figures. In the year 1914 we had a net debt of $43.49 per head. What did that represent? How did it come about? We had the accumulations of debt from the older provinces before Confederation; we had all of the various public works that were carried on through the fifty odd years of Confederation; we had built three transcontinental railways; we had immense outlays in connection with our canals and other public works; we had built extensive terminal facilities, for we had been carrying on down to 1914 what was regarded as a big progressive policy; and as the total of it all we found that we had rolled up what was considered the large net debt of $43.49 per head. But if we make a comparison of it with the net debt now, we find it has advanced to $215 per head.
Again, I say my only purpose in making these comparisons is merely to awaken, if I can, in the public mind a keen sense of the real seriousness of the situation. I do not use these comparisons for any party purpose or for any alarmist purpose; I use them simply to help my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to bring the country to realize the seriousness of our financial position.
When we talked of our debt in days gone by and up to a recent period we usually spoke of our net debt as the real measure of the obligations of Canada. We ascertained that net debt by taking the gross debt-all obligations of every sort, deducting what we called our "assets," and striking a balance, which balance

was called our net debt, and that term has been generally used by all our public men to represent the real debt of Canada. I was glad to hear my hon. friend the Minister of Finance frankly point out to-day that we cannot rely on that statement of net debt as telling the whole story. Our assets have at all times contained some items to which, on careful examination, exception may be taken; but while our assets did not bulk very largely that perhaps was not of so much importance. However, our assets, according to the latest returns, have gone from about $77,000,000 in 1899, or about twenty years ago, to the immense total of over a billion dollars to-day, and when they run into such big figures it becomes necessary to give them a more critical examination.
I am glad the Minister of Finance looked at the matter frankly to-day. I had a statement made as to the earning power of those assets for a series of years, and the interesting fact was disclosed that the earning power last year was higher than before. That struck me as rather remarkable, and naturally I made some further inquiries. The explanation is that at present there is a large item in the shape of the debt due from the British Government, which is actually a sound asset, and on which the interest is computed. But that is an entirely temporary affair and will be closed out iv a short time, when we shall have before us what may be called our statement of assets. But that ordinary statement of assets is becoming weaker now by certain factors *to which attention was ealled to-day by the Minister of Finance. These assets, so called, include the obligations of railway companies which have paid no interest, and from which we can expect no interest. Indeed, here is a specimen. When my hon. friend dealt with the same point to-day I think he quoted from different data. I find among interesting specimens of our valuable assets what are described as Grand Trunk Pacific loan account, $51,000,000; and my hon. friend gave as of a later date a larger sum; then there is another item, the Canadian Northern railway, $108,000,000, and I think again my hon. friend gave the figures as of a later date and a larger sum. These are not assets that we can count upon getting much from. I have heard of a man who gave a note of hand and when he had signed it, he said: "Thank -God, that debt is paid." We are doing a little better than that in this statement. We are giving our note of hand, for that is what the Canadian Northern Rail-[Mr. Fielding.!
way Company is doing and we are the Canadian Northern Railway, and we are not only saying "Thank God, that debt is paid," but we are putting this amount in a statement of assets and saying that it goes to reduce our obligations. I am glad to know there is no difference between the Minister of Finance and us in that regard. One of these days there will have to be a revision of that balance sheet and we shall probably not differ as to what will have to be done. I mention these things merely to show by sharp contrast the tremendous change that has -taken place in the short period between 1914 and 1920.
With all the economy that the minister can manifest, with all that he has manifested in his present estimate, and with all -that he is likely to manifest in -the future, a very serious financial situation will still confront us, and it is well that we should understand it, face it, grapple with it courageously, with a conviction that the mass of the people in some shape or form have to provide the vast sums of money necessary for the carrying on of this increased burden.
My hon. friend has presented estimates for the comin-g year, which estimates are certainly very large. As he has pointed out to-day, they show a considerable reduction from the estimates of the previous year, and I am sure that if he makes a comparison between the sum which he is asking for and the sum which he was asked for by the various departments, he would be able to show a very much larger diminution, but, he has made an effort in the right direction. I think there is one thing we could do to help the minister in this matter. We ought to stand between -the minister and our constituencies in these demands that are made u-pon him. Economy is a fine word to apply to your neighbour's constituency; it is not a very pleasant word to apply to your province or district. I read in a newspaper the other day a long article which was piously calling on the Minister of Finance to exercise the widest, the most careful economy, and in another part of that paper I found an article which demanded the immediate construction in that community of public works which would cost many millions of dollars. We are all prone to do that sort of thing; we are all apt to be advocates of expenditure with respect to the -district from which we come, and I want to say frankly that every membeT of the House, in face of this situation should help the minister by telling his constituents plainly that -many of the things they ask for, good,

useful though they may be, are not of the most urgent character and ought not to be pressed upon the attention of the Government at this time. We all owe that to the minister and we should give him that help. But we must ask him to be fair; if modest applications in one region are refused and those who are interested, in them and who are refused, discover that very lavish expenditures are going on in some other direction, there will naturally be discontent. The minister, his colleagues, supporters and friends should be willing to adopt what I may call a self-denying ordnance in these matters and see that we practice a real policy of economy, so far as such is possible.
Canada cannot stand still, we are living in a progressive age; there are urgent things which will come before the Government; there are public services which must be rendered ; but I want to ask the minister to see that in the various demands that are made upon him only those that are necessary and that are not only meritorious in themselves, but of the most urgent character, shall receive the benefit of his approval. There is no other way by which we can better the unhappy condition which exists; there is no royal road out of this present trouble. The solution is national economy and individual economy and only by those means can we hope to meet the difficulty, and I trust my hon. friend will be supported in every legitimate effort he makes to that end.
The minister stated to-day-and I was glad to hear him state it-that his hope and expectation is that during the coming year he will be able from his revenue not only to provide for the ordinary expenditures, but to take a substantial step towards paying off the public debt. We should make such an effort even though that involves heavy taxation; we should endeavour to grapple with the question as it was grappled with the other day by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in England who said that they were preparing immediately to make a long step towards paying off the public debt.
The tariff question is always with us; it figured in the discussion to-day, being mentioned by the minister towards the close of his address. While it is true that at all times for many years all our tariff discussions have been more or less tinged with the question of free trade, there has of late been a revival of what I may call the free trade movement, and the free trade question is now thrust to the front of our
tariff discussions in a larger way than it has been in recent years. That, I take it for granted, is because our farmer friends attach so much importance to the matter and have pushed it into their platform. With all due respect to them, I take the-view that free trade is not a practical question in our tariff discussions of to-day. There are some things that we should dowell to remember. In the first place, it may be well simply to remember that there never has been in the Dominion of Canada such a thing as free trade. There is not anything of the kind now, and with all due respect to those who may be described as extreme free traders, I think it is no wild guess to assert that there will be no absolute free trade in Canada within the lifetime of any man who sits in this House to-day. It is not practicable, and that is not to say that free trade principles are not sound.
If I had to engage in an academic discussion on the question of free trade versus protection, I would hold up my hands for free trade. I think free trade-I say this reverently-is part of the divine order of things; at all events, it is part of the law of nature. I say this reverently. In all parts of the universe, an all-wise Creator has given the capacity to produce something which, properly understood and developed and handled, will minister to the comfort of the rest of the world. The icebound region of the North has its mission no less than the warmer lands of the sunny south. In every section of this world, there is some wealth; it may be hidden, but it is there. No land was ever created by an allwise Providence without having some purpose. I believe it is part of nature's intention that man shall discover, develop and utilize this wealth in every section of the country for the carrying out of the great work of civilizing the world. That is free trade. But it is quite possible that the best of principles may be carried too far; it is quite possible that men who believe in the general principle of free trade must recognize that there are conditions under which it cannot be applied. There is great merit in that statement, hackneyed, you may call it if you will, which is often credited to Grover Cleveland: "It is a condition and not a theory which confronts us." If we were the men of the Mayflower just landing at Plymouth, or the men of the grand army of Champlain pitching their tents at Annapolis Royal and Quebec, we might be able to have free trade. But three cen-

turies have passed since then and many things have occurred which restrict the freedom of those days, which make it difficult if not impossible for us to-day to carry out to the full extent the principles which we may cherish.
I am going to ask my farmer friends and my free trade friends-because I know I have been criticised sometimes during my tenure of office as a minister for not following out as rigidly as they would desire the principles of free trade-to let me take a couple of cases by way of illustration of what I may call exceptions to the free trade rule. I am going to take a couple of cases within the experience of the Government of which d was a member, cases for which I am largely individually responsible, cases for which I know I have from time to time been criticised by many friends who pressed the doctrine of free trade further than I would. Let me take first the question of the anti-dumping law, which is a radical departure from free trade principles. What is the anti-dumping law? It is a special duty to be applied in certain circumstances with a view of keeping goods out of the country, and that is certainly not free trade.
