Manufacturers would come to the Government asking for an increase in the tariff, and we would ask them to show us reasons, and very often they would say: "Well, we could do very well under the tariff, you know, but our American neighbours have a dumping system; they will at certain times send over their surplus goods and sell them here at .any sacrifice price and destroy our business." The thorough going free trader, the man who is more thorough going than I am on that question, would say: "All right, send the goods along; the more the merrier; if they are willing to send in goods for less than cost, thank them for that and tell them to send along some more; cheapness is everything." That is the view of many of my free trade friends. I pointed out to the manufacturers that this dumping condition w.as after all not a continuing condition but one which, according to their statement, would arise from time to time. I pointed out to one of them: " Don't you see that when, you ask us to give a large increase in duty you are creating a machine which is to be of a permanent character in order to deal with an evil- if it be an evil-which is of but a temporary nature? From our point of view, you are going to penalize the people of Canada twelve months of the year to meet a difficulty that may arise once or twice, or perhaps thrice,

in the course of a year." I thought that that was a fair stand to take in objecting to the manufacturer's attitude. I had a call one day from a manufacturer who informed me that he had no complaint in regard to the tariff. He said he was satisfied with it and as a matter of fact was doing fairly well in- his business. Indeed, he said, he was contemplating an expansion of his business, -and he felt that in view of the large trade he was then doing and the larger business he was planning to do in the future he could afford to sell to the ulti mate consumer at a little lower price, and so he had scaled down the price of one article of importance in which he was dealing. I remarked that that was gratifying, but he said:	"Wait a moment, I
want to show you a letter I have;" and thereupon he placed on my desk a letter written by an agent of an American manufacturing concern which engaged in making in the United States a similar commodity to his and shipping it into Canada. This agent wrote to the man of whom I am speaking:	"Why do you cut the price?
You can just as well get the larger price and there is no reason why you should not. If you reduce your price we will have to reduce too. We will meet your reduction and we will do more than that; if you .are going to start reducing prices we will meet you and keep on reducing, and no matter what price you name we will cut below you." Ah! that was a new light upon the question of dumping. Again, I suppose my free trade friends would say, " All right, let him send his goods in; let them come in; so much the better." Well, if we could have got a bond from those manufacturers in the United States that would compel them to send their goods forever at sacrifice prices it would have been an excellent thing to have adopted the course suggested in this hypothetical quotation. We could afford to close our Canadian factories and buy American goods if we could have got a bond from across the border guaranteeing us their goods for all time at a sacrifice price. But who imagines that the American had any intention of doing that indefinitely? His avowed intention was to cut prices and sell at a sacrifice just long enough to close the other man's business. That was the clearest thing in the world. My manufacturing friend visiting me asked me what he was to do. I said to him: "'What do you think of the situation yourself?" He replied: "Well, I suppose I have to go back to the old price or shut

up shop;" and I told him that I could not blame him; I said we would have to think the matter over. We did consider the matter and the conclusion we came to was embodied in the dumping duty. We came to the conclusion that if big manufacturing concerns in the United States could come here and close up Canadian manufactring interests it was right that there should be a special duty to meet that condition. It was considered by some as a piece of freak legislation, but I am glad to know that it has been copied in other countries, and the present Government have paid us the compliment of continuing it on the statute book. It is the law today.
And if my extreme free trade friends ever came into power I think on due reflection, they would make up their minds that it was the part of wisdom to keep the dumping duty to apply to special circumstances whenever the evil was found that called for its application. Now, I do not believe that my free trade friends will be persuaded even now that I am entirely in the right, but it is only fair that we should ask them to consider some exceptional circumstances, in which men who believe in the general principle of free trade may very possibly agree that some departure is. necessary from the broad doctrine they hold. Take another case in which I know our Government have been criticised-a case in which I know I have been criticised. I am going to consider the question of iron and steel bounties, and I shall do so without the slightest reference to any present question which may be in contemplation. If any one has any bounty claim afloat now I know nothing about it and I have no desire whatever that anything I say now shall be construed as being intended to bear upon any question of bounty, current now, or hereafter to be raised. Bounties on iron and steel originated with the Conservative Government in the days of Sir Charles Tupper. The operations under them were not large. There was a small operation in the province of Quebec and another in the province of Nova Scotia. I have not' the figures but I think no very large sum was paid out until after our Government took up the question. When I was Premier of Nova Scotia a question arose regarding the' operation of the coal mines of the province; there was a feeling that the coal mines, which were natural resources, should contribute largely to the revenue. The Government informed the-managers of the
companies that the royalties would be increased, and the managers complained, alleging that business would not stand it and that mining could not be carried on. They said we would ruin their business. No doubt they were sincere. We were able to come in contact with an American gentleman of great business enterprise, Mr. Henry M. Whitney, of Boston, whom I regard as a benefactor of Nova Scotia, and we were able to induce him to take up the enterprise of consolidating a number of these companies. That is a merger, I imagine some one to say; and mergers, I know, are not popular. But there may be good, and there may be bad, mergers. In this case we were able to induce that enterprising American gentleman to arrange to consolidate a number of mines. We made some changes in the mining law, costing the Government nothing, and gave that gentleman facilities to carry on his work; and in consideration of those facilities we required that he should pay not only the royalty then imposed, which the other men could not pay, but even a higher rate. The other men complained of a royalty raised from cents per ton to 10 cents. VVe required Mr. Whitney to pay cents. That arrangement was the means of starting the development of the coal business down there. Soon after that business got established it was my lot to come to Ottawa, and shortly aftrward, Mr. Whitney came to Ottawa to interview our Government. He made representations as to what he had done to organize the coal industry of Nova Scotia, and he said that he could build up a steel industry on top of that if he had assistance. He stated that he had great faith in that enterprise, but he represented that if he had to obtain capital he must have inducements to bring in other men. In short, he wanted some help from the Government; he wanted a bounty. At that time-and even before and since-there was a good deal of talk about assisting infant industries. Now, I would be always willing to help an infant industry if I were sure that when the infant grew up it would accept the full responsibility of manhood; but when it grows up and begins to knock the old man around the house and feels that it controls the whole thing I think the case is different. I repeat, I would willingly help an infant industry, and as between protection and bounties, I think I would prefer the bounties. Why? When you give a bounty you know what you are giving; every one sees it, and if you don't like it you can stop it.

But if you increase a duty there is often great dispute as to what is its effect. At all events, we were willing to aid Mr. Whitney, with this proviso: We said that we would not help him if he insisted on bounties as a permanent thing, but if he was prepared to accept them for a short or a moderate period, with a distinct understanding that they should be gradually reduced, and wipe themselves out, there would be reasonable ground for considering his proposition. He acquiesced in this view, thereupon the bounty scheme was adopted on a sliding scale for a period of years. After several years we checked the slide and gave them a year or so longer. At all events the time came when the bounties automatically ceased, and to-day no bounties are paid. What was the result of that? Was there anything in the result which wouild justify that departure from free trade principles? I am afraid my farmeT friends will not agree, but I believe it is susceptible of proof that every dollar that was paid out by way of bounties on iron and steel, and millions were paid out, came back to the Dominion treasury in the form of excise and customs duties on the new business created as the outcome of that policy. I think that can be established as a pure financial question, but there is more than that. There has been the making over of Eastern Nova Scotia. What happened? Let me take first the statistics of the coal trade. In the twenty years up to 1893, 'before these transactions to which I refer began, the increase of the coal output in Nova Scotia-not the total output-was 604,000 tons. That was before the days of Mr. Whitney's operation in coal, iron and steel. In the twenty years which followed, from 1893 to 1913, the increase was not 604,000 tons, but within a few tons of 5,000,000 tons. That was the increase in the coal trade under the operation of the scheme to which I have referred. If there were nothing more, surely that is some vindication of what I considered an exceptional circumstance. But there was more than that. Small villages down there developed into towns, and towns developed, shall I say, into 'cities. Nova Scotia is no longer a province of one city. Where the little town of Sydney of 2,000 or 3,000 population existed, there is to-day the splendid city of Sydney with 25,000 people, and in the neighbouring towns and villages the same story is told. There is the town of Glace Bay, big enough to be a city. On the other side of Sydney harbour, you have the towns of North Sydney and Sydney 
Mines, both flourishing towns. The whole eastern part of Nova Scotia was virtually made over under these new conditions. And not Nova Scotia only. The benefits of that transaction extended to the neighbouring province of Prince Edward Island, to New Brunswick, and even to some parts of the province of Quebec, and possibly to some parts even farther away. I do not want to insist that these departures from free trade are absolutely right, but I put them before my friends who are extreme free traders, as facts which I believe can be sustained. I believe they justify a departure from free trade principles under certain conditions. If those conditions can be limited, if we can get anybody to start any new industry under the circumstances under which these were Started, then I think myself that would justify a departure from the abstract principle of free trade.
The tariff question continues to be a large one. It is going to be the biggest question, I suppose, in the next campaign. What, then, is a sound and sane and sensible and safe tariff policy for Canada? To what quarter shall we look for such a policy? Not, I am afraid, to the Conservative party, even when they state their case in a camouflaged way, as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance did at the conclusion of his speech 'to-day. He gave, if I may say so without offence, what seemed 'to me to he a fine example of steering north by south. At all events, we know that the historic policy of the Conservative party is a policy of protection, and protection for protection's sake-a policy of high tariff for the sake of the tariff. Without arguing on .the merits, though I know that a great many of our best citizens believe that that is a sound policy, I am going to be content with saying that the trend of public opinion is not that way, and I do not believe it is any use to look to my Conservative friends for a sound tatriff policy. Where, then, shall we find it? Not from my Conservative friends, not even from that .section which my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) represents. (He has on several occasions lately spoken of a moderate tariff. Moderation is always a good thing. In nearly all things it is wise to be moderate, but the meaning of the word "moderate" depends largely on the viewpoint of the man using it, and I am afraid that if my hon. friend were permitted to frame a tariff which he would call moderate, it would be deemed very immoderate by some of my hon. friends

who sit further down the House. So I do not expect we can get a sound and safe tariff from him.
Where, then, are we going to get it? Shall we get it from the platform of our farmer friends? Sir, I do not think their platform if carried out would give us the sound policy which I desire, and I hope to be able to show them-at all events I hope they will find that it is wise to modify some of their views. Much in their platform is entirely in harmony with the views I am prepared to support, but I rather think they press the doctrine a little, too far. I am less alarmed than many are about a farmer government. I do not think the country would suffer dreadfully if my farmer friends were to come in and form a government in this country. I know that if some of their views were pressed, they would make some trouble, but the farmer is not a dangerous man. His associations with the soil, whether it be as owner or as land-worker, create, shall I call it, a natural conservatism-with a small " c." He is naturally a conservative in all business matters. He is going to stand for law and order. Now, responsibility generally sobers men, and I think if our farmer friends came into power in all probability they would modify their views a good deal and would probably be able to carry on government with fair satisfaction. But is there any likelihood of that? My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) made a speech the other day at one of the outlying towns, I forget where, in which he said that the farmers had no expectation that they would come into power at the next election, but they did think they would have an increased body in the House. I think that is a fair guess; I think he was right. If we had a general election right now, some things are not clear, but I am afraid if there is anything clear, it is that my hon. friends on the Treasury benches would be soundly beaten, and I rather think they believe it themselves. But it is not quite so clear to me, as to some of my hon, friends around me, that the Liberals would be in a position to control the House. There will be a large farmer party. I think the Liberals would be the largest group in the House. They might even have a majority, but I am troubled by the thought that they would not have a large enough majority to carry on the Government. Our farmer friends say they do not expect to win, but that they do expect to come here in increasing numbers. What for? Two years ago in a discussion in the House of Commons I ventured to suggest-I do not presume to offer advice-to my farmer friends, that so long as they pursued a policy of isolation they could not expect to accomplish much. Well, much water has gone under the bridge in two years. The Farmers' party is larger and stronger than ever, and it naturally feels less willing, I suppose, to look at things outside of its own political platform. Nevertheless, I am going to suggest to my hon. friend's that if they want to do any constructive work they cannot do it by a policy of isolation. They can be a strong party, a critical party. They can make an opposition, but there will be no need of their opposition. If I am mistaken in my view and hon. gentlemen opposite come back to power there will be a strong opposition over here, you can make up your mind about that; and if hon. gentlemen on this side of the House move across, I am willing to admit that there will also be a strong opposition in the House by my hon. friends opposite. Therefore, it will not be necessary for the farmers to create an opposition; there will undoubtedly be one. The farmers want to be constructive. I do not believe the farmers of this country, earnest and sincere as I know they are, want men in the House merely for the purposes of faction. They have ideas and they want to do things, but so long as they stand alone they cannot accomplish their aims. I therefore hope that events will so shape themselves that these gentlemen will find it their duty to associate themselves with some other men in the House who, though they may not go all the way with them, will go quite a long way with them.
While I would not fear dangers from a Farmer Government, I do not think myself, as things are going now, that we can look to that party for a sound tariff policy so long as they stand alone. What then? I do not even think we can expect to get a sound and safe tariff policy by a too rigid adherence to every line and every letter of the Liberal tariff platform. I think myself that we will find that we are all prone in framing platforms to put things perhaps a little more strongly than is wise and we all find when we come to the responsibilities of office that we may have to modify our views. If we are to get a sound and sane tariff policy where shall we look for it? Where shall we find the guide posts which shall direct the people into right lines at this time of trial?
Turn back to the policy of 1911, the policy of the Liberal party, the tariff as it stood

at that day, with the amendments that weie contemplated when they went out of power, and in this you will find the elements of a sound and sane tariff policy; not the finished edifice but the ground work and the frame work of a sound tariff policy. Some conditions have been changed since and we will have to meet them, but I believe that if men will look back to the policy of 1911 as it stood at that time, and to the tariff of that day plus the proposals that were then being put forward, they will see that they can accept it as a basis, as the ground work, the frame work, of a fair tariff, although not the finished edifice.
But some people will say: " That is the National Policy." My Conservative friends are much given to the practice of saying that the Liberal policy isthe National policy, and once in a while an unthinking Liberal is found who will listen in silence to that retort. The Liberal policy of 1897 was not the old National Policy, If you want evidence of it turn to the records and you will find that the Conservative leaders and the Conservative press denounced the Liberal policy of 1897. It was not the old National Policy. They said it was going to tear down and destroy the old National Policy. But as the years rolled on and as they found that policy was winning success and the country was prospering, they swung around and said: " That is our policy."
Let nie picture the situation as seen on a race course, say, at the hospitable city of Toronto, when the Ontario Jockey Club is preparing for one of the great events such as the King's plate on the 24th May. There are two horses entered, a Liberal and a Conservative. The bell rings and the horses eome to the stand. The owner of the Conservative horse says: "Judge, you are not going to make my horse run against that animal; he is not in our class; take him out; I will not permit my horse to run a race against a poor, miserable, spavined, knocked up thing like that." But the judge says: " This horse is entered for the race and you have to run against him." They start the horses and in twenty seconds time there is a considerable space between them. The Liberal horse pulls out in front and as they speed down the back of the course is seen to be far ahead. He increases the lead and as they come around the track he is found to have left the other far behind. Finally the Liberal horse crosses the line a winner and the other is left away back in the distance. What does the owner of the Conservative horse do? He rushes out and says: " Do not give the prize to that 
fellow; that is my horse that he is riding; that is a splendid horse!"
That is about the attitude of our Conservative friends when they talk about the Liberal policy of 1897 being the old Conservative National Policy. You can prove that it was not the old National Policy by taking the facts and figures during the period of the Liberal Government. Taking into account the actual savings in customs duties and comparing the duties paid then with what would have been paid if the old tariff had been in force, and taking into consideration the savings that were made by the reduction in the prices of home manufactures, you will find that the change made represented hundreds of millions oi dollars in the pockets of the people of Canada. It was not the old National Policy. It- was the policy which made this country grow and prosper. For many years we were able to look back with pride and satisfaction to the results which followed the adoption of that policy. What were those results? I do not want to dwell too long upon this point because I want to hasten to a conclusion, but I am going to call a witness to testify as to the fruits of that 9 p.m. policy, and as to the situation that we turned over to the Minister of Finance of that day, now the hon. the member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White). We left him in the happy position that he could bring down to Parliament the last volume of .the Public Accounts that were not ready when we went out of power, showing a surplus for 1911 of $30,000,000. We left him an overflowing treasury and a fiscal system which, being allowed to continue for another year, placed him in the happy position of coming down to Parliament with a surplus of $38,000,000. We left him, I repeat, with an overflowing treasury. What was his testimony as to the condition of the country generally? ;I am going to ask you to listen for a moment to a statement made by my hon. friend which appeared in his Budget Speech of May, 1912. My hon. friend had the pleasant duty of describing the condition of the country then as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance of to-day (Sir Henry Drayton) has had the duty of describing to-day. He was talking not merely of incidents of Government but he was describing the condition of the country as it was at that time when the Liberal Government had just gone out of power. What was the condition of Canada? I quote from the Budget Speech of Sir Thomas White in 1912:

It will, as I have said before, be gratifying to all that the material prosperity with which we have been so highly favoured still continues to be our portion. Despite the serious vicissitudes through which the western wheat crops has passed and the unusual heat experienced in the province of Ontario during the past summer, the field crops of Canada show a bountiful yield and with the high prices prevailing for practically all its products the great basic industry of agriculture continues in a flourishing condition. Almost every department of trade and commerce shows expansion. Our mines are wonderfully productive. Our *coast fisheries, notably the Atlantic, have enjoyed a good catch and high prices. Our manufacturers are thriving and new industries are springing up throughout the whole Dominion. Railway construction, especially in the west, proceeds apace, preparing a way for settlement in districts not yet opened up and for trade with other markets than we now enjoy. Our increased bank deposits, clearings and circulation, the amount of public and private building evidenced in municipal and business structures, extensions to manufacturing plants and residences in almost every part of the country, all attest that the general prosperity of Canada at the present time is very great.
Our Dominion continues to be the land ol hope and promise to the home seeker. During the last year, as before shown, our immigration from Europe and the United States reached an average of nearly a thousand a day, bringing their capital, their intelligence and their energy to assist in the great task of developing the resources of Canada and building up her nationality. Much has been said in the past with which I am in accord as to the selection of immigration as far as possible with an eye to the quality and character of our future citizenship. Notwithstanding the large stream of immigration, labour conditions are good and extreme poverty, from any reason other than incapacity or direct misfortune, is hardly known.
Under the favourable conditions which 1 have described, and with every prospect for their continuance, the future of Canada looks bright indeed. In the enjoyment of peace, plenty and prosperity her energetic, loyal and patriotic people look forward with hope and expectation to an ever great and greater future.
That, Sir, is the story of fifteen years of Liberal fiscal policy as described by my hon. friend: fifteen years of peace and plenty, fifteen years of blessed peace, fifteen years of joyous plenty, fifteen years of splendid progress, fifteen years of wonderful prosperity! Let us frame and glaze this statement; let us post, it on the walls of the country; let us frame and glaze it and put it into every household, and office and factory, so that men may look upon it and say, "Ah, yes, that is the story of the good old days. Pray Heaven that it may come back again."
And come back pretty soon.

The Minister of Finance to-day gave us some tariff changes which we shall be better able to understand when we read them in detail in Hansard. Let me
say, however, that I am sure there must be deep disappointment on the part of a great many members of the House who were, or are, supporters of the Government, to find that the tariff reform which they are getting-if you call it tariff reform-is of such a moderate character. We must not forget that the Government have for the last two years been, shall I say, coquetting with this tariff question, jollying their friends along and promising that something was going to be done. If I might use a quotation :
" They promise, prepare, propose, postpone,
And end by letting things alone."
Last year the Minister of Finance gave us a very positive assurance that there would be a tariff inquiry in the interim, and a tariff reform measure at the present session-a measure of general tariff revision. If the Minister of Finance is not able to make that tariff revision he is, of course, disappointing his friends; but I think there is another reason why we should have a larger measure of tariff reform than we are getting. There is unrest in this country to a degree which must be disturbing to us all. There are various causes for that. Part of it is world-wide; some of it probably might be dealt with in a better manner. There is a widespread opinion in the country-with that portion of the community which is easily susceptible to, shall I say, the movement of unrest-that the Government and Parliament-we may as well count ourselves in-are not doing much to meet the situation. The high cost of living is pressing upon people severely. It presses on all classes. Those whom we for convenience call the working class-although we are all members of the working class in Canada-those whom we speak of sometimes as the working class have been able to protect themselves in some degree 'by the increase in wages which they have obtained, although I think there are few cases in which the increase in wages has been equal to the increase in the cost of living. But there is a very large class of unorganized working people in Canada who are feeling this pressure very keenly. The clergymen, the public school teacher, the college professor, the clerk in an oflace -who is paid a fixed yearly salary and not wages by the day-a large class of people- and the Civil Service may be included in the number, although they have received some little aid-but there is a large unorganized class of people in Canada who feel the situation to-day regarding the cost of living very, very keenly, and they do

not say much about it. They are the class of people who bear their burdens and say nothing about it. For the sake of these people, and for the sake of others, I think it is a pity that we do not make some effort to show them that we are doing something -or at all events trying to do something- to meet the difficulty. What have we done? We have appointed a Board of Commerce. We had a committee last session to inquire into the high cost of living. That committee worked hard, and I am quite sme had every intention of doing something; and in the end the committee, in part, and certainly the Government, got to be panicky, and suddenly they resolved that they would pass this Board of Commence Act. They were warned that a measure of such importance, rushed through in that way, would probably get them into trouble. However, they felt 'that something must be done and so they rushed the legislation -through. What has happened? They appointed three able men to the board, and I have no doubt these gentlemen sincerely desired to do the best they could. But what has happened? The board has been paralyzed almost from the beginning. I think at the start the fact that such a board was in existence had a tendency to check profiteering,-if there ever was a tendency of that character-but before the board got very far it found itself paralyzed. Doubts arose as to whether it had the power to do anything. In the most important step it ever took it was immediately vetoed by the Supreme Court of Canada; and today a case is before that court asking the court to tell the board what their powers are. The chairman of the board resigned some time ago, and the members of the Government are permitting the paralysis to continue. They are afraid to appoint another chairman, and the board is doing next thing to nothing. I am sure the members of the board desire to help all they can, but whatever the cause may be the public at large do not feel that relief has come. Now we think that something should be done-some effort should be made even though it be not very successful. I think that something should now be done in the way of reducing the tariff upon the necessaries and the comforts of life-some of the things which the average man requires from day to day. I do not overestimate the value of tariff reductions in affording relief from the high cost of living, and the people may expect too much therefrom. There is a curious thing about tariff taxes. Increased taxes always reach the consumer the next morning. If my hon. friend were 
to-day to add five cents a pound to the taxation on sugar every shop-keeper in Canada who gets a newspaper would tomorrow morning add not five but six cents to the price. That would reach the consumer instantly. But when tariff reductions are made it is a slower process. Then the shop-keeper says, "You see I had to buy these goods under the old tariff, and I cannot reduce the price." The process of reduction is slow; the process of increase is rapid. Therefore I grant if you make tariff reductions now you may not get as much relief from them as perhaps is desirable. I do not overestimate their value, but I think it would be desirable that an effort should be made; and in doing so, at all events, we must give to the country some assurance that we are trying to meet the difficulty. I think we are doing less in this direction than has been done in Great Britain, and less than has been done in the United States.
I therefore conclude my remarks by moving, seconded by Mr. King:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be omitted, and the following inserted instead thereof:
"the Minister of Finance, in the Budget Speech, in the session of 1919, gave assurance to the House that during the ensuing parliamentary recess there would be a public inquiry by the minister and one or more of his colleagues into the operation of the customs tariff, with a view to a general revision of the tariff at the following session.
"That the promised public inquiry has not taken place, and the expected proposals for tariff revision at this session have not been submitted to the House.
"That in view of the continued increase in the high cost of living, of the greatly increased burden of taxation, of the hardship which many of the people suffer from these causes, and the unrest naturally arising therefrom; and in view of the desirability of adopting measures to increase production and effect such relief to consumers and producers as may be within the power of Parliament, the House is of opinion that, pending a wider revision of the tariff, substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation should be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance; first, diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country."

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before going into the subject matter of the remarks which have been made by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) who has just taken his seat, I may be allowed a personal allusion. It gave to me personally, and I

am sure to- hon. members on this side of the House, a peculiar and particular pleasure when on the rising of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's he was received with such evident marks of goodwill and approbation by the hon. gentlemen who sit behind him. I allude to this because personally I feel something of the same pleasure which I imagine my hon. friend felt when he received that -acclamation from his own side of the House and evidence of goodwill from this side as well. It is a pleasing thing to the elder brethren in political life who are at a stage a little before their hair completely whitens and the westering skies have closed over their journey that the younger and more vigorous and ambitious elements on both sides of the House seem to have a feeling of fairly deep respect and-shall I say-of friendship towards those who have long borne the burden and heat of the day. And I reciprocate and join in the kindly demonstrations that were made to my hon. friend by both sides of the House when he rose to speak.
I am also greatly pleased with the speech which my hon. friend has made. But before saying very much with reference to that I wish to add to the note which was struck by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) in one portion of his speech this afternoon, and which I would like to emphasize, and if possible, to prolong. It was that note in which he vindicated the fine effort made by -Canada during the five years of the war we waged and upheld in unity and co-operation on both sides of the House in defence of justice, and of -right-principles which have long animated- the British Empire. He called upon that same spirit of co-operation and sacrificial effort to prolong its action and so to unite us in the common duty-not simply the duty of one party or another of the various parties which have their being at this time in Canada-of healing the w-ounds and repairing the waste of war.
The work which is upon us to-day is preeminently the work of Parliament and of the country and not of party or faction. It is the extension and consequential entailment of a war which was our common war and which wa-s upheld by this country in co-operati-on and with a large spirit of unity in -all its parts. The very same spirit, the very same qualities, the very same efforts, ought to be projected into the co-operation necessary, as I have said, to repair the wastage and heal the
wounds of war. What my hon. friend has done in this Budget presentation to-day ought not, I think, to be lost sight of in its general -and broad lines.
Before we get into the discussion of details and travel off into individual paths where we may lose sight of the principles which have been the ground bases, so t-o speak, of the presentment, it will be well to tabulate them for a moment so as to keep them clearly in -mind during the subsequent discussion. And may I say that if we can maintain throughout the debate the spirit which has animated the speeches which have been already made, if we can forget the individual in the general, and forget a portion of the partisan in the patriotic, we will make this discussion memorable in itself in this Parliament and of very great benefit to the cause which weighs so heavily upon u-s for a fair and speedy adjustment of conditions following the war. That spirit has been eminently well displayed to-day.
Now, what are the guiding principles or points, so to speak, in the presentment which has been made by my hon. friend in his speech this afternoon? There is first a laying bare, down to the very bone -and marrow of the truth, just what the condition of Canada is to-day, financially and economically, in its -domestic relations and its relations with other countries. I look upon it as a fine contribution to the discussion which has now . been begun-that there was no attempt on the part of the Minister of Finance to camouflage the position. He was frank, open and truthful in his presentation of our financial and economic condition, and he well merited the compliment which was paid to him by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding).
There was no concealment of the amount of -debt that this country is now bearing upon its shoulders; there was no -attempt to minimize that burden by counting in assets which were not properly to be considered as live assets; and a distinction was made with a corresponding addition to the net debt that we carry by a diminution of those assets which could not be looked upon as being live assets. We might collect our assets, say under three headings-the quick, the dead and the purgatorial. The quick assets we can very easily pick out, -and there are many of them. The dead asset wfe have picked out and laid aside; we respect it for its -memories and for the associations which it had in the past; but we have laid it away, and we

heavy, though the country has untold unexpected liabilities and obligations which have to be met,-and we intend to meet them, though those liabilities are very pressing and very onerous,-the Finance Minister has stated, what business people believe to be right, and what we around these benches believe to be right,-that foi this year, and if possible next year and the years after,-Canada shall not incur Ifurther debt. We may be obliged to carry for years the debt which we have at the present time, but that we should from this time on, so far as we can, balance our accounts and make our revenues tally with our expenditure. Taking that into account,, the other j fact must also be taken into account, that it is not possible to do everything we would like to do because of the heavy burden oi carrying the war debt of the country,-that $2,250,000,000 of net debt that we have to carry. At the same time, the promulgation of the principle that no loans are to be made at the present time, but that we must out of our own resources meet our own liabilities year after year, is a. great step forward; and if Parliament and the country will stand behind the Government in that declaration and in trying to have it fulfilled, we will come all the sooner to the time when inflation and big debt charges, and all the discomforts and disorganization resulting therefrom, will be mitigated, and gradually iwe will emerge from the mists into the sunshine of liberty and prosperity so far as economic and financial considerations are concerned. I think that is a healthy principle to instil, and a healthy determination to make, both here in Parliament and outside in the country. Let us pay our own way.
Another thing that has been done by the Finance Minister is this: He has made a courageous attempt to devise and to impose methods of taxation which shall help to square our accounts and bring us up to the position to which I have just alluded. I say that is a courageous attempt, and it deserves our support here in this House. It is not popular. As I was passing out to-night I heard a member who does not belong to this side of the House express a view which I am quite sure will be often expressed. Speaking of the taxation schemes of the Minister of Finance he said, " It is going to make the Government very unpopular. There are women voters now, and the Government is not going to gain many of their votes by taxing women's dress and women's jewellery." There, again might- I be allowed to suggest- how my hon.

friends on the other side of the House can help mightily towards the readjustment of things financial and economic? It is in this way. When you visit your constituents do not go back on your promises and principles of to-night and do not say to the electors, as you meet them: " Are you going- to keep that Gov-ernmenit in power?" Do not say to the woman voter: "What is this you have around your neck-a fur? The Government put 20 per cent on that fur. Have you a vote? Then, when the next time for voting comes around don't you vote for that Government or a representative of it.'' Be careful and not stultify yourselves by saying that you will take the duty off if you get in, though you may make that premise with impunity for tlhe prospect is far in advance. But if you do not do that you will greatly assist in bringing about the payment of those dues which are absolutely necessary if we are going to pay our way and reconstruct and readjust our economic and financial affairs. I know it is a courageous thing for the Minister of. Finance or the Government to put on new forms of taxation, but there are some blessed and good features in -the direct form of taxation; and one lesson which cannot be taught too quickly and which cannot be brought home to the people too strongly is that the burdens of the country are to be borne by the country itself and that the people must stiffen their backs and strengthen their courage and double their endeavours in order to bring the country out of the position in which it is to-day to a better economic and financial basis.
Every one must realize the fact that there is a duty to be done, and that it is not by the indirect method, only that it shall be done. We have had two systems of taxation, one almost entirely predominating up to the present time, and that is the method of indirect taxation, by which the people paid heavily and did not know when they were doing so. All sorts of assertions have been made as to the amounts they paid,-assertions which of course would partake of the particular power of imagination of the man who made them and of'his boldness of speech. All kinds of assertions have been made, many of them grotesquely exaggerated; but nevertheless one of the features of indirect taxation is that you pay out not knowing how much you do pay. I doubt if that system of taxation, altogether imposed upon a country, is a good school teacher to that country and does finally eventuate in what is best for the interests of the people. I think that a judicious mix-

ture of the two, by practice made necessary and by practice gradually worked out without too great a wTench, is a mixture that the body politic should be asked to take, and if they will do it we shall place no stamp or excise duty upon the administration of that mixture. So that now we are working up along the line of direct taxation every year a little further, and yet not by too violent advances that would produce-I was about to say a revolution, but that word does not convey my meaning-but a reaction against that principle of taxation. We have now a judicious mixture, I think, of the two kinds of taxation. In our business profits tax, in our income tax, we have examples of the direct method. We add to these now our sales tax on luxuries and other articles. By the methods of taxation adopted we bring it to the mind of the purchaser that this is a tax which is paid by the person himself or herself, and which is not added to by the profits of the middleman, the man between the manufacturer and the retail counter. By bringing this fact home to the purchaser .at the time of the purchase, we adopt, I think, a practical way of inculcating in the body politic a real interest in and solicitude for the good government and economic administration of the country.
I shall not follow that line of thought any longer. These are just some of the views I place before the House with its kind permission. Now I desire to come to the speech delivered by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and I hope he will not think, if I disagree with him in certain particulars, that I am at all detracting from my general admiration of his speech. Just on that point let me say that it has been to an eminent degree nonpartisan in character. The hon. gentleman drew a line of .comparison between 1914 and 1920, and he did that with his long experience behind him, not for the purpose of a partisan appeal, but rather to inform the country itself, as a man of his experience and length of public service could well do, to put before them the duties of the present as compared with the duties of the past, the obligations of -the present as compared with the obligations of the past, and to show the sacrifice and effort which would be necessary on their part in the future as compared with the standard of necessity in these respects that existed in the past. That is a good thing to have done, and I congratulate my hon. friend on having done it. He paid a compliment to the Minister of Finance, but it was 160
rather left-handed, in that in paying a compliment to one minister he somewhat took away from .a complimentary reference to another minister. He said that it was easy in war time for Finance Minister No. 1, but it was hard in peace time foT Finance Minister No. 2; and he thought that if Finance Minister No. 1 had had a little more foresight and a little more courage he might not have done some of the things which he did do. Ah! those afterthoughts ! How they plague us, and pursue us, and chastise us; but they never remedy the thing that was done before the second thoughts came. They have no power of salvation for an error or an act committed before they were brought out from the misty depths of thought or imagination and applied in their sober secondary condition. Now, you have to put yourselves in the position the man was in when the thing under consideration was done, and if my hon. friend will put himself in that position I think he will revise his opinion and say that during the five-year period of the war the task of the ex-Minister of Fin-nance No. 1 was a hard one.. He may well say that, in peace times finance minister No. 2 will have a hard task. I have collaborated with both and I think I have a pretty good idea of what has been done by the former Finance Minister and what so far has been done by the present Finance Minister. I do not envy them the work they had to do but I give my tribute, and I give it most willingly and unreservedly, to the able management of the finances of the country by Finance Minister No. 1 during the trying period of the war. There were difficulties which had to be surmounted. Some things were made easy because of the buoyancy of the feeling of patriotism and service which was then at its height. But there were other things that were awfully hard, tremendously grinding, and that worked into the very vital sap of the man who had to bear the responsibility of it and work out in practice and in administrative system what there was to be worked out. But let us give due credit to each.
Afterthoughts! Yes, my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's has had afterthoughts. But they did not rectify the errors of the past; his primary action which probably would not have been taken if he had taken time for the afterthoughts. There was a time when my hon. friend- lest he think too. highly of himself I just want to suggest it to him-prophesied' that the Grand 'Trunk Pacific could be bbiilt at a

cost to the country of only $15,000,000. After thoughts would have told him that it would cost $200,000,000. It would have relieved him and relieved the shoulders of the present Minister of Finance if my hon. friend had only had after thoughts before he took the action itself. It is just one sample. You can go through the list of all governments, all ministries and even all individuals, and you will find this brooding nightmare of after thoughts coming to plague and pursue them.
What was the position of my hon. friend on loans? I followed him with a great deal of interest and, really, I could not quite follow him. Although years have passed over him, as they have passed over myself, he is yet agile in body and agile in mind and in spirit. And he did skate most scientifically around that business of the loan domestic or the loan foreign. What his idea was it is difficult to say, but I analysed his position like this: Glad in a way that we received a lot of money in our own country when we could not raise it in any other because there was no other country we could go to that would give us a dollar, outside of the United States and they would give us very little. In fact, we had to loan to outside countries instead of borrowing from them. Glad, then, that Canada showed that she possessed such resources that she was able to raise a billion dollars to prosecute the war; yet finding when we come to the readjustment that the money which has been wasted in war is not available in the banks or in the pockets of the people to go into the business and industry of the country, and he moans and bemoans that fact. But there you are; the money was there, the money had to be raised. We raised it and if it was blown away on the battle.	field it is not in the banks to-
10 p.m. day nor in the pockets of the people to put info business enterprises. We must dig up other money, and the way to dig it up is to stop strikes, stop holidaying, stop doing half work, stop wasting, and set ourselves to the business of honest toil and honest production. That is the only way we can replace the money so spent. I wish my voice could penatrate to the heart of every man and woman in this country and impress upon every heart this message and keep it there like the message on a film: "Stop wasting; go to work; produce; stop grouching and grumbling; and we will soon get back to an atmosphere that i,s bright and happy and hopeful.
My hon. friend had something to say about a stock transaction. I am sure he [Sir George Foster.!
would not have said what he did if he bad had the facts before him. I propose to place just the bare facts before him, and these facts are amply proved by the documents and accounts. What did my hon. friend say?
There is one feature which, while well known to the inside circle of finance, has not been made known in any marked way to the Canadian public at large, and I think it is time that the Canadian people knew something about it.
Here we have a mystery. The hon. gentleman's words go out to-morrow morning in the papers and the public will scent a mystery. Something has taken place. The public ought to know it because the exMinister of Finance says it is so. What is this thing? Some more rascality of the Union Government! He goes on to say:
If you take up the last volume of the Public Accounts for the year ending March 31, 1919, you will find a couple of interesting items.
Interesting! The public cocks up its ears again ! A mystery; an interesting mystery ! The ex-Miliister of Finance says so! He had thirty years' 'experience; he had that solemn oracle, the Public Accounts, in his hand, and he backed up his statement with the Public Accounts! What is this interesting mystery?
If you take up the last volume of the Public Accounts for the year ending March 31, 1919, you will find a couple of interesting items. There is a later volume than that, but we have not got it.
More of a mystery, more interesting facts to come out in volume 2! For the time being my hon. friend contents himself with volume 1:
For that year, however, any hon. member will discover in the statement of receipts and expenditures an item called " Bank of Montreal Trading Account "

a very interesting account. Hon. members will read the items therein contained and will discover that the Government paid out on that account the sum of $7,450,000 and got back $5,177,9*04. So oh that account-whatever it means-the Government of Canada-in other words, the people of Canada-lost $2,272,000.
N*ow that is the statement. I am sorry to say, on his own account, that my hon. friend is .altogether mistaken in coining to that eonelusiono and I take the occasion to put the proof before the House so that it may, come out on the wings of the same press which takes that interesting mystery propounded by my hon. friend on its plumage to carry abroad to the reading public. Now, what are the facts of the case? In brief, they are these: That the Government expended $10,950,000 for the whole

completed transaction. It got back out of that transaction $11,074,088,, and instead of losing $2,272,000 it made a gain of $124,088 for that whole period on the bonds of the Victory Loan of 1917. This transaction was closed on September 7th, 1918.
Will my hen. friend allow me to ask from what public record he is quoting? Where does it appear in the Public Accounts?

It will be found in an Order in Council which I propose to lay on the Table.
Some hon. MEMBEES: Oh, oh.
An Order in Council!

Well, now some hon. gentleman, as I should judge, has expressed a bit of dissent-a little bit of dissent. What do my hon. friends want? Will they take the Auditor General's authority? Will they take the report of the Auditor General? My hon. friend holds up a book, and he Teads from that book two sets of figures, but he makes his own deductions. That book does not show that $2,272,000 was a loss accruing to the country; it simply gives a statement of an expenditure and an income in an unfinished account. My hon. friend's fault was that he did not state what was in that book when he told the people of Canada that this Government has been trafficking and has lost $2,272,000. The latter statement was an inference of his own and it was absolutely incorrect.
An hon. MEMBEE: Another dark secret exploded.

Now my hon.
friend went on to the tariff question, and there I sat in blissful amazement. Looking over the thirty years that have passed and the controversies that have taken place between my hon. friend and myself, and between his party. and the party on this, side of the House I felt almost like saying,, when he had finished, "Now lettest thou thy servant depart in. peace; " and the question forced itself upon me. "Has the tariff millennium come?" The whole party behind my hon. friend never voiced opposition to what he said; they could not; they dared not. They do not like to admit, what in their hearts they know to be the truth-that is repugnant to them; yet if they were all as honest as the ex-Minister of Finance they would get up and say the very same thing. Now, after these confessions-not of an 160J	.
opium eater, but of a virile, experienced public man-rafter this candid confession, let me say to hon. gentlemen opposite: "Do not let us hear anything more of camouflaged assertions ifrom that side as to free trade being the doctrine which is dear to your hearts and embodied in your ipolicies. You cannot put it into your policy now. I do not think you ever meant to put it into your policy to carry out as a reality when you got into power. That was done once before in the history of this country, and the lesson is to be read in the records of Canada. O, don't I know all about it? Didn't I go through all those campaigns preceding 1911 when from the highest authority down to the lowest there was this universal declamation against the principle off protection; that it should be eliminated from the tariff- not be allowed to lurk in corners and by-places, but to be eliminated. To-day what have we? We have the ex-Finance Minister standing for ,an anti-dumping clause-when circumstances require it; standing for a substantial aid to industries-when circumstances require it; standing for mergers-when circumstances require it; aye, and even more, standing for the protected infant industry while it was an infant industry, until it had attained years of maturity; standing for all these-when the circumstances of the case seemed to require it. Where is the free trade doctrine, and

where is-the difference in principle between myself as a moderate protectionist and my hon. friend as a now .avowed protectionist, the principle to be adapted and adopted-as circumstances require if? That was always the doctrine on this side of the House. We never worshipped protection as a fetish; can the same be said by hon. gentlemen opposite with reference to free trade? WTe have always believed that the circumstances of the time should dictate the financial and tariff policy of the time. And my hon. friend's confession to-night has amply justified the policy advocated during thirty years by Liberal-Conservatives in all parts of Canada.
Now, what is t-o be said hereafter to our friends who compose the Farmers' party? Oh, my friend from Shelburne and Queen's is a youthful w'ooer yet; was there ever such a Eomeo? Was there ever such a Juliet, looking out of a window embowered in vines and flowers, for a Eomeo that attuned so sweet a note, so persuasive a love ditty, as my hon. friend has sung to-night? It did my old heart good, and I felt almost like making love to something myself. I

know I never before could have done it as
*well, and wi'th this example before me I unay try yet again. But, alas, for the Juliet, *when it came to that prosaic allegory of the horse race! My hon. friend then forgot the party that he wooed so ardently. The only *two horses allowed on the traok are the Liberal and Conservative. The Progressives are counted out. My hon. friend says to them in effect; you may be good for some *purposes1, tout .when it comes to the real race you are out, you are scratched, there *is no Chance for you.
Then my hon. friend starts off on a quest of his own, it is like the quest of Japhet- in search of a father. Where shall we find the proper policy? IWe cannot find it in the Liberal-Unionists; we cannot' find it in Meighen's vocabulary; we cannot find it in Crerar's vocabulary; cannot find it in Clark's vocabulary. Where shall we find it? And the answer to the weary seeker comes from the member for Queen and Shelburne. " Here is the embodiment of the plan leading to proper tariff policy. I have just repudiated the errors of the past. Come with me, and I will take you to the Promised Land." Jordan and the desert may be between, it is true, but to-night he forgot Jordan and the desert, and was almost in the Promised Land, with the Farmers tagging behind him as beneficiaries of all the grapes of Escol and the other fruits of that delectable country.
I will not continue further and will now resume my seat.

I therefore .suggest that it would suit the purpose of the House better to have a discussion general in terms upon the whole question, as would be the case if the amendment were not submitted.

If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I was quite aware of the point, but I understand it has always been the practice in the case of the Budget debate that though an amendment was moved the whole question remained open. It was be-

cause of that understanding I made my motion.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words
must be those of thanks to the Prime Min-

ister for having kindly consented to adjourn this debate in order to give myself and other members of the House an opportunity to examine the very important matters contained in the speech of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) delivered yesterday.
Before considering the speech of the Minister of Finance, there is another speech *which might perhaps be dealt with. As -we listened last night to the two ex-Ministers of Finance, one who adorns the Conservative, -and the other, no less adorns the Liberal side of the House, w-e were reminded of that ancient saying, "Old books to read, old wood to burn, old wine to drink, and old politicians to listen to," because nothing could have been more agreeable -than to listen to the remarks of these two gentlemen (Hon. Mr. Fielding and Sir George Foster), whether one agreed entirely with them or not.
Now, let- me take up the remarks that, after all, were of a somewhat light nature which were ma-de by the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday. I cannot attempt to follow him into his figurative or imaginative finance. I am an unworthy member of a church, Mr. -Speaker, that does not believe in purgatory, and I have got an idea that our -claims or assets are either good or bad, and I am afraid that our bad assets do not give room for any doubt as [DOT]to their worthlessness. The minister (Sir George Foster) mentioned the trend towards economy. After all, it is delightful to know that a man who is approaching the milestone of four score can see in the Estimates of this year any trend towards economy. My eyes have not served me for so many years, but I have discovered no trend towards economy at all, and I am afraid that my bon. friend was then simply calling upon his poetic imagination, as -he did later on in the discussion.
Then there was his criticism of the Civil Service. No doubt, Mr. Speaker, the -Civil Service has many aspects in which it might be better. But does any severe criticism of it lie in the mouth of the Minister of Trade and Commerce? He has been associated with -the public life of this country for very many years. Under him for many years the Civil Service grew up, to a certain extent at any rate; and if the Civil Service is badly organized it appears to -me that a leading member of a government that has been in power for the last eight years-too long a time-and for eighteen far too long years some time -ago -has got to share to a very considerable degree the responsibility.
Then we had the Minister of Trade and Commerce acting as a sort of Greek chorus to whatever the Minister of Finance said. "We must have no more loans," says the Minister of Finance; echoes the Minister of Trade and Commerce: "No -more loans." What a splendid policy! No more loans. "We must pay our way," the Minister of Finance tells us; the refrain is taken up by his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce: "We must pay our way." Of course, we -must pay our way; of course we must have no more loans. But is not that sort of preaching rather the preaching of an apostle of the obvious? There was one point to which I listened with a certain amount of amusement, and that was the credit and praise which my hon. friend (Sir George Foster) bestowed upon the Minister of Finance for his being truthful. Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance belongs 'to the profession to which I belong-

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
And we do not have to be praised for telling the truth. We are truthful: Cela va sans dire. Then we had some talk about the methods of taxation; there was direct taxation and indirect taxation; and, if I may without impropriety attempt to do so, I may suggest that we had Dr. Fo-ster's judicious compound of taxation, both direct and indirect. We shall examine that mixture later on, but for the time being I merely direct attention to that part of the right hon. gentleman's speech. I will not attempt to follow my venerable, learned and honourable friend into the realms of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet or into the more prosaic field of horse racing at the Woodbine track, Toronto.
But I purpose now to take up what I might call -the more serious part of the mental pabulum afforded the country and the House by the Government yesterday. The Minister of Finance, at the outset of his discourse, pointed out that there were two objectives to which this country should bend its energies: first, the resumption of ordinary economic conditions-the economic conditions which prevailed, I presume, before the war;-and, second the endeavour -to reduce the debt. Now, what did he mean by ordinary economic conditions? If he meant conditions which obtained before the war, then I say that those conditions are such that we should not try to resume -them, because before the war mankind was suffering through the conglomeration of great quantities of wealth in the hands of the few, and a great deal of the hardest, the most unpleasant and the most

us some more dreadnoughts, and you will be safe. I know it was difficult when one great nation had set the pace for other great nations to refrain from keeping step -I realize that. But that nation that set the pace has suffered for the setting of the pace-it lies prostrate to-day. What reason is there, unless other nations are imbued with the same miserable, proud, arrogant, selfish, aggrandizing militarisms which cursed Germany

what right .is there for a continuation of that policy to-day? And are we to follow in its footsteps? Canada was one of the most unmilitary nations of the world. I suppose our expenditure on military and naval services before the war, compared to our size, was as small as that of any other nation in the world. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, was there a nation when it got into the struggle that did better? Did our young men who came from the farms, and the counting-house, the warehouse- did they do as well or did they do better than men who had spent three or four years of their life as conscript soldiers? I ask the House to agree with me that we can save at least $4,000,000 on our expenditure on, military services this year. Let the boys who fought for four years overseas enjoy their summer holiday this year in some other way than in camp. I am sure that often when they were overseas they thought of the happy times they had spent in Canada on lake and on river, or in the woods. If the need arises again- please God it will not-they will do their duty once more; but let us lead the way in peace-as we led the way on this continent in war-towards reasonable retrenchment and a stopping of this mad race of armament, this mad race of militarism. I say in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, that the great standing armies which were supposed to be the bulwark of the safety of the different nations which supported them were sources of danger rather than sources of protection. I say this:	That if onetenth of the expenditures which Europe devoted to military armament and military services had been expended for the purpose of trying to organize international friendship and peace the war would never have come. I say that, militarism has shown that it is a ghastly failure and a stupid mistake, and I ask the people of this, my country, to show the way to cut down that expenditure and to save the money of the people-aye, and perhaps save the future of Canada.

When I spoke like this some months ago the then Minister of Militia and Defence said: We do not fear another war hut we have internal unrest in the country. That is one reason why we propose doubling the permanent force in Canada. To that I made reply then, and I make reply now: That is not the way to keep peace in Canada. Restore free speech; restore a free press; let the people know that the destinies of this country are to be decided by votes-by ballots and not by bullets. If there is unrest in the country give the people an opportunity to select the governors that they wish to have govern them, and you will have no necessity to increase the permanent force.
Now we come to another phase of the question. I find that Railways and Canals, chargeable to capital are responsible for a very large sum of money. My advice to the Government would be that we should save on everything; we should refuse to take on any expenditures except those that are absolutely necessary. Mr. Speaker, you are connected with a large business. If you had a deficit staring you in the face of something like half your ordinary revenue, would you propose to enlarge your plant? No one would do it in private life; no one should do it in public life. I find that the Hudson Bay railway is responsible for $100,000. The Hudson Bay railway I know is dear to the hearts of some of my Western friends, but I would be recreant in my duty if I allowed that fact to weigh with what I have to say. I think that perhaps we are over-built with railways in Canada just at the present moment, and I can see no harm in postponing the expenditure of that money. We propose to expend five and a half million dollars on the Wellartd ship canal. Well, surely the present canal system can take care of the business that is offering this coming summer, with this tremendous increase in the debt of the country. The Trent canal is responsible for $400,000. Surely that can also be postponed. It has been suggested that men who represent counties in this House are always willing to suggest economies for the neighbouring counties. Well, " Let the galled jade wince, my withers are unwrung." I have not been very long a member of this House, but I have never asked for the expenditure of one dollar in my county, unnecessarily-not one dollar for a public work-and I doubt if I have asked for the expenditure of one dollar for any purpose, in the constituency. I would raise my voice

in unison with the voice of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I would ask him to go even further and see whether he cannot cut out some of these trade commissioners whose reports, when they are read, show that they must spend a good deal of their time holding down their chairs.

Well, that is what
one would gather from some of their reports. At any rate, my hon. friend can look into the matter; he can promise consideration in his usual considerate manner.
We now come to Railways and Canals, chargeable to income, $50,000,000. Surely there is something to be saved there. Oh, that I could revivify in the soul of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that passion for economy which he showed between 1896 and 19,11!
We now come to Public Works, chargeable to capital $6,400,000. We find Esquimalt dry dock, $500,000; Port Arthur and something else, $600,000; Quebec harbour, $150,000; St. John harbour, $1,250,000; Toronto harbour-and oh, it would be gratifying to have the amount of tonnage which clears from that interesing place year by year- $1,700,000; while the breakwater on the Island-that pleasant place dear to the hearts of Torontonians-calls for an expenditure of $200,000. Then we have Public Works chargeable to income; andTiere Mr. Speaker, I would draw your attention to the fact, that the Amherst drill hall calls for $25,000. Surely this expenditure on the Amherst drill hall might very well be postponed. Then there is a public building in Granby, which calls for an expenditure of $18,000.

speechtext:
I trust, Mr. Speaker,
that for this offence I shall not be called to order too often. The Toronto Postal Station calls for an expenditure of $425,000. Portage la Prairie has not been forgotten, although the Laprairie motor road may have been neglected many years, and that calls for an expenditure of $25,000.
Then comes an expenditure to which I wish to draw the attention of the House. For years past in the Northwest Territories we had a magnificent police force- a police force of great prestige and the finest in the world. To-day we find it merged into the Royal Dominion Police Force; and that merging means $500,000.
Surely the Royal Northwest Mounted Police -might well have been left in the Northwest Territories, and the administration of order in this part of the Dominion left, as hitherto, to the provincial authorities. Was Eastern Canada such a desperately dangerous place to live in prior to the bringing east of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police? Is it necessary for us to see on the streets of this city the splendid figures of those strapping young men in their red coats and spurs? When I visited Europe I never liked to see the armed gendarmerie in the streets of Paris or elsewhere, and I do not like to see -them in the streets of Ottawa or elsewhere in this country.
It is said of the late Sir Richard Cartwright, after he had examined the Estimates for wharves in Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, that he ejaculated: "Is there a cove forgot?" And when I look at the provisions made -for wharves and -breakwaters throughout Eastern Canada, I have this suggestion -to make to any hon. gentleman on the otheT side of the House who are responsible for the present administration of our affairs: That they should along with the Estimates print statistics of the number of vessels and the tonnage of those vessels which cleared from these various wharves during the last year of navigation. I cannot tell whether all these wharves are nepessary; they m-ay be; if they are, -we will have to go on paying for them,. but surely something could be saved along this line.
Now let us look at the next item to which I would draw the attention of the House: Mail subsidies and steamship subventions, $1,250,000. If there is one class of people who have been making money during the last two years, it is steamship owners. They have been making money to such an extent that even a single voyage would pay for the cost of the ship. Under -those -circumstances, surely there would be room for cutting out -these annual subventions that have to be voted year by year. I find an item of $340,666.66 for a steamship service between Canada and the West Indies or South America. But the Minister of -Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) has just placed a large number of boats in -commission, at a very heavy cost to the country. It is true that, according -to his statement, interest has been earned upon that outlay; but nevertheless the capital expenditure has been very large. Now, he cannot expect to be allowed to build ships and operate them, and at the same time to pay other people for building ships and oper-

ating them; it is not reasonable. There certainly is room for economy there. Our ' steamship subsidies should, in the light of present conditions, be very carefully scrit-inized.
I see on the other side of the House the member for Lambton East (Mr. Armstrong). I trust that I will have his support, as his eloquent voice has been raised in this Chamber on many occasions to show us the extortionate profits that the steamship companies have been making, and to be consistent he ought to support my demand in regard to these maritime subventions.

[Mr. McMasterJ
a stop to these payments; there should be a free press.
I believe that the journalists of this country are high-minded men, I believe that they want to say the right thing-whether they are always at liberty to say the right thing is another matter.
Now, I have endeavoured to show and perhaps at greater length than I should have attempted-
