-the economies, which should be practised. As a matter of fact I would like to trace out the footsteps that the Government may follow in continuing their trend towards economy.
The new tax proposals I will now deal with. And just let me say here, how delightful it was last night to listen to the Minister of Trade and Commerce talk, not about Union party-he had forgotten all about the Union party-but about the Liberal-Conservative party, about which he tallied with enthusiasm. I understand that a political club in Ottawa is now waiting to know what the Government is going to do so that it may be in a position to style itself either a Union or a Liberal-Conservative club. But, after all, it must be difficult to make these changes. One man in his time plays many parts, and my right hon. friend (Sir George Faster) used last night one of the various titles of his party -the Unionist party, the Liberal-Conservative party, the Conservative party and the Tory party-mais, pour moi, toujours la meme chose! But for me, Mr. Speaker, always the same thing.
Before attempting to consider the duties which the minister has brought down, may 1 make this preliminary observation: That these taxes should not have been brought down before the minister had informed us that he had exhausted other and more direct means of taxation. During the last five years, there has been in this country a great deal of money heaped up in a comparatively few hands. During the war there were those who called, with alt sincerity, "for the last man and the last dollar." But some others there were who crying the most loudly meant the last dollar they could get out of the situation-and they got it.
Now, in Great Britain, to which I like to go for examples in sound finance, a Committee of the Treasury has reported that a levy on war wealth is perfectly feasible and would bring into the coffers of the State a very large sum of money.

Now, I will say this for the very wealthy people in the ipart of the country from which I come: That their sons and the young men among them left their luxurious homes and went to the front as gallantly and as gladly as those in humbler circumstances. I 'believe that there are many among the rich men of Canada iwho would have no objection to giving up a very large portion of the wealth which they made during the war, provided that the tax strikes everybody equally; that all are treated alike. I think that the Minister of Finance has been somewhat negligent, if I may dare ito use the word, in not sounding to the bottom that proposal and either bringing it in or explaining to us iwhy it cannot be brought in.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Will the -hon. gentleman permit me to put a question to him, now that he lis on that very interesting subject? I would like to know 'his 'own view; [would he favour a direct levy on wealth in this country?
Mr. MoMASTER: I would certainly advocate a direct levy on [war wealth; that is to say, wealth which was accumulated because of the war. It seems to me that that is an absolutely proper subject of taxation. Whether a levy on all [wealth would be required is another matter; I would like to exhaust the possibilities of the levy on war wealth before I went into the question of a levy on all wealth. But I may point out to the hon. member that we have to find money; we have to pay back a large part of the deibt, while the level of prices is high. To-day with a bushel of wheat you can pay off, I suppose, three dollars of the national debt, but if we wait for ten years until foodstuffs resume their normal price level, we may find that it will require three bushels of wheat to pay off three dollars of the debt.
Let me make also this preliminary observation. Excise duties which have been brought down are open to the objection which pertains to all duties on consumption; that is to say, they are unequal in their .incidence. Take a man who has "his quiver full"; let us say that he has six children. The man who lives next door, with an equal income, has perhaps only one child. Any tax founded on consumption is bound to strike much more heavily the man with the six children than the man who has only one child.
4 p.m. These excise taxes are open to this Objection; a tariff, even a tariff for revenue, is open to the same objection.
I should also like to direct the attention of the House to the fact that the excise duties now proposed are superimposed on the tariff, and that they should -rather be countervailing to the tariff. Let me illustrate. Suppose I have some money which I can invest in a motor car,-a somewhat unwarranted suggestion,.but let us make it for the -purpose of argument. If I go to Detroit, buy a car for $1,000, and bring it into Canada, I will pay, under the new duty of 35 per -cent, the 7^ per cent having been taken off, $350 by way of customs duty, and then I will pay a 15 per cent excise tax or $225, -a total payment to the Government of $575. Buit suppose instead of going as far as Detroit I stop at Toronto and buy a -ear there; I will find that I can purchase a car equivalent to the ear that would cost me $1,000 in Detroit, for just about $1,500-. But how much Will the Government get out of my purchase? $225 instead of $575. What we have to do in this -country is to deflect into the treasury a great deal of the money which is going into the pockets of the -privileged classes, the manufacturers. The ex-Minister of Finance, the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), whose moderation in statement is known and appreciated by all members of this House, last year said that 'he believed that 'for every dollar that went into the treasury of the country through the operations of the tariff, ait least two dollars went into the -pockets _ of private -interests. What we have to -do is to take some portion of that two dollars and deflect it into -the treasury, not leave it in the pockets of the protected manufacturers.
Now, let us see how this would work out. Suppose instead of superimposing a tax of 15 per cent on motor cars we impose an excise tax of 10 per cent on imported motor cars and of 20 per cent on 'home produced motor -cars. What would the result be? The profits of -manufacturers of motor cars would be somewhat reduced, and I do not think that would hurt the country. The trasury would benefit by a very large amount and the consumer would not pay any more than he is paying now. Surely that should appeal to the Government, if it wants to get on the road to economy.
In all other countries-perhaps I should not say in all other countries, but certainly in Great Britain-the principle of -a countervailing excise tax has been admitted and has been operated. For instance, into India there is imported year by year a vast quantity of cotton. A tax of 10 per cent, I think, is collected by the Indian

authorities upon the cotton *which conies into the country, but a countervailing duty of 10 per cent is placed upon the cotton manufactured in India in order that no private interest in that country may enjoy the benefit of special privilege and in order that the Government may reap the full benefit of the tax. I think that that point will appeal very strongly to the people of Canada.

I am going to read it. I shall read the whole of it; I am commenting on it as I go along. I would almost think that the Minister of Finance had been reading this resolution and had been struck by its wisdom, that he had been about to indite something similar to it when his hand was stayed by the more experienced hand of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who said, "What are you going to do? Are you putting into our platform a part of the Liberal party's platform? Don't forget that you belong to the Liberal-Conservative party. You must not do anything like that." The resolution continues:

and repair parts thereof, rough and partly dressed lumber, gasolene, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, nets, net twines and fishermen's equipments, cements and fertilizers,' should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards-
You know, Mr. Speaker, the promise of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance just calls for a thorough revision, but he does not tell us in what direction that revision is to go.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
There is a specific proposal. Compare it for a moment with the vague generality of 161
my learned and hon. friend the Minister of Finance:
-to specially promote and increase trade with the Mother Country, the sister dominions and colonies and Crown dependencies.
Is there any statement made there that there is going to be so much in their favour? No, that is left for the future to disclose. If I remember aright, the old Conservative party, in the days gone by, abused in unsparing measure my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's when he introduced the British preference. But now a change has come over the spirit of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and he proposes, but not in any definite language, to foster trade relations with the Old Land:
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provisions of this resolution when returned to power.
That is the tariff plank of the Liberal party. It closely approximates, although it is not in all respects precisely similar to the tariff policy of that other great progressive force in this country, the Farmers' party.
Let us see for a moment why -we think this is the proper time to adopt this policy. I believe that protection is an evil thing, I believe it brings evil and not good to the people, the manufacturers and the Government of Canada, and that its influence throughout the world has been for harm. I believe with the hon. member for -Shelburne and Queen's, that in the beneficent wisdom of Providence He intended each part of His footstool to supply out of its surplus the other parts and that all should form one whole. I believe that by an adherence to this policy we shall find peace for the world as well as increased wealth for ourselves.
There are two great causes which have -made for international jealous)'. -Chauvinism, or Imperialism, is one, and Protection is the other. The great protectionist nations in Europe were anxious to increase the ambit of their power for what reason? That they might exploit -the peoples and the resources of the uncivilized nations that might come under the power of -their governments. I believe that few things have -made so much for international discord as the principle of protection.
We have reached a time in the -history of this country when every ounce of national energy and every dollar of national -capital have to be put into those channels which will produce the greatest economic return, not only in this country but all the world -over. In a book -written by Mr. Keynes,



am authority who is admired all over the English-speaking world, he proposes a remedy for the ills of the war, and what is that remedy? That Europe shall become a free trade territory-a free trade entity. We have a tremendous amount of wastage to make good. The world has five years of wastage to make good and that we can only do with reasonable celerity by each nation devoting its energy and capital to. those lines of activity in which it has the greatest advantage and then by a free interchange among them all. That is the policy which the Liberal party aim at in the future. That is the policy which I wish to see adopted in this country. I do not propose that it shall be adopted to-morrow. I am willing to give every reasonable opportunity for men who have developed their industries undeT a false economic system to adjust themselves to the new conditions, but we have to move forward and we have to move forward with sufficient speed not only to show in what direction we are going, but also to show that real progress has been made.
There has been in years gone by in the mouth of my protectionist friends an argument which has appealed to me as not being sound, but as being arguable. It is this:	We would be prepared in do away
with the tariff or at least accept freer trade provided we had a market to enable us to carry on production upon a large scale, because when you have production on a large scale you are as a rule able to reduce the cost of the unit. For many years the United 'States maintained a high tariff against the importation of Canadian goods. But the United States has turned from being a highly protected nation, from a nation which collected most of its revenue through a tariff, to a nation which collects 95 per cent of its revenues through direct taxation. Where as in the last fiscal year the United States, with a population fourteen times or thereabouts greater than ours, collected through its tariff about $189,000,000, we collected through our tariff $169,000,000, the United States collecting less than $20000,000 more than we collected. The United States has a free list much more extensive than the free list we have. The United States has become much freer in regard to trade than it was before. We cannot expect to exist on the northern half of this continent as an independent political power unless we are able to have a fiscal policy as economically sound as that of our neighbours to the South. We cannot expect to attract and hold people in this country unless we are prepared to give them as good

living conditions as they will find on the plains of Dakota o>r of the Argentine Republic. It is not merely a question of economic theory; it is a condition as well as a theory which confronts us, and that condition is that we have spent vast sums of public money to develop our western lands which are largely empty, and until these western lands are filled up the great capital expenditures that this country has incurred will not carry themselves. We cannot fill up these great lands of the West unless we are prepared to give to the newcomers and to give to those who are already there conditions which will enable them to .meet the competition which they have to meet when they export their products to the markets of the world.
In order that the fact of the United States has now a very large free list may be borne in on the minds of the people of this country I have arranged their free list in a series which I call "Reduction Rimes." This is very low grade poetry, and I would not have dared to place it on Hansard if I had not been encouraged by the action of the right bon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who last night made an incursion into Shakespeare and referred us to the grapes of Escol. Even if this is an inferior brand of poetry it is original. We have no assurance that Shakespeare is original; some people say that it was Bacon who wrote the works that are attributed to Shakespeare. This is a list of the things which are on the American free list:
Reduction Rimes.
Setting out the many articles now upon the TJ.S. free list.
Agricultural implements, first on our list, Next animals for breeding must not be missed.
Bread, biscuits and buckwheat are next in the line,
While flour of the latter makes pancakes so fine,	.
Cash registers, machines for setting up type, Show that for trade progress the U.S. is ripe. While sewing machines, the housewife's delight,
Keep company good with the typewriter bright.
Machinery for shoes and Portland cement Join the procession of nothing per cent.
Coal, coffee and cocoa come next in a row, Cotton and corn from where warm breezes blow;
Eggs, fish, fats and berries march next in the line,
With furs, skins and gloves to withstand a cold clime,
Grease, fats and oils which do similar work, While lard and lard compounds their duty don't shirk;
To warm up the feet they use duty free boots, While harness on horse helps get in the roots;

Free beef, veal and mutton they greatly enjoy,
While hams, lamb and bacon no duties annoy.
Nails, staples and horseshoes are on the free list,
Tacks, needles and oilcake must never be missed.
Oils for eating, for lighting, of all sorts, are found,
While rye, sago and salt are not to be bound.
Seeds to increase their production so great
Are found with the haddock, the cod and the skate.
Swine, cattle and sheep, the boundary cross,
Join wheat, tea and tallow without fiscal loss;
Barbed wire as in Canada now pays no tax,
Nor do logs, planks or clapboards to cover the cracks.
Wool of sheep, camels' hair are the last on my list;
I need not declare there are many I've missed.
Mr. Speaker, protection as a policy for this country is not only dead, but, after the next election, it will, as Disraeli said, be damned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to reply
to my poetical and free trade friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) I wish first of all to compliment him upon the very kindly manner in which he has treated the able Budget speech which was yesterday delivered by my colleague, the Minister of Finance. During the long speech to which we have just had the pleasure of listening, the hon. member (Mr. McMaster) has not uttered one word relating to a policy of a constructive character. He has reiterated once more his fealty to free trade principles; he has once more condemned the policy of protection for Canada; he has, in a general way, referred to the Budget, but he has not enlightened the House as to the ways and means of raising revenue that he would adopt if he were occupying a seat on the treasury benches. Later on I shall deal in greater detail with my hon. friend's remarks. Let me first take notice of his observations with respect to the Main Estimates. The gist of his argument amounted simply to this: he wants this fair, progressive and enterprising Canada of ours ' to fold her arms, to sit still, to put the shutters up, to let the grass grow on the steps. My hon. friend does not want any money spent on the deepening of the Welland canal, he does not want- any money spent on building ships, he does not want any money spent on maintaining the militia force of Canada. In a word, he does not want any money whatever spent; he is satisfied-and I take it from the applause of the hon. gentlemen sitting around him, that they are satisfied also-to sit still and not IGli
endeavour to take advantage of, and develop, the wonderful possibilities of Canada notwithstanding the large war debt that we have to struggle with at the present time. My hon. friend made only one suggestion this afternoon, if I followed him correctly. He said that a committee of the Imperial House had considered the advisability of levying some special form-

speechtext:
I am quite willing to accept the correction of my hon. friend, but it does not alter his argument. He informed this House that a proposal was under consideration in Great Britain at the present time to levy a special tax on what he is pleased to call, " war wealth." I wish to state that Great Britain has not adopted such a proposal. True, the proposal has been made, but it has not yet been adopted.
With reference to the Budget presented by the Minister of Finance yesterday, I am satisfied that it will be favourably received throughout the country, and that under the circumstances it is the very best that it was possible for any government to, prepare. A close study of the Budget will reveal a few salient points worthy of notice. First of all, the luxury tax is placed on those best able to pay it; it does not apply to eatables, nor to articles of wear that are of moderate price. I am sure that the country will be perfectly satisfied that the luxury tax shall apply to those people who have money to buy boots and shoes costing over $9 a pair, or a suit of clothes that will cost over $45. It is not only fair, but it is most reasonable, that they that have the money should be those to come under this special luxury tax. It is clear to everybody except the hon. member for Brome, that this tax does not apply to persons of moderate means. I heard some reference in the House last night to the possibility that our brave and courageous women might make some objection to this luxury tax. I, for one, have no such fear. During the recent war the women of Canada showed where their hearts were; they stood loyally behind the government of the day, and our soldiers at the Front, from the very beginning of the war until i.ts victorious conclusion. The heavy burden of taxation that now must necessarily fall upon the people is only an aftermath of that war, and I am satisfied

that the women of Canada are willing to bear their fair share of that burden. They will cheerfully do so because of the recollection of their beloved ones who will no lunger return to them, for the sake of the wounded and those who will be blind forever; and for the sake of the national welfare as well.
A very important point in connection with the Budget is that it will give Canada sufficient revenue not only to take care of the ordinary expenditures, but also to pay off part of our national debt.
1 wish to refer briefly to the business war profits tax. I know that there is a general feeling throughout Canada among the business men that this tax should have been dropped. I realize and appreciate the many objectionable features that pertain to it; but when we know that Great Britain is not only maintaining a similar tax, but has raised it from forty to sixty per cent, and that the United States is also retaining on her statute books a similar method of collecting money, in view of the very great necessity for Canada to obtain the necessary revenue, the Government could not see their way clear to entirely eliminate the business war profits tax.
I am sure it will be gratifying to the business men of Canada to know that there have been made certain reductions to which I need not refer in detail, as my colleague the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) dealt with them yesterday in his Budget Speech. Our Income Tax has been raised. It is not only as high as the Income Tax of our neighbour to the south, but it is still higher as a result of the five per cent added yesterday. The Government have also placed a tax on sales. It will, I think, be manifest to every one in this House and outside of it, that the burden of taxation now falls, as it properly should, on those best able to bear it.
My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) has stated that the Government have made no effort to reduce the high cost of living. I must take issue with him there, because as the Minister of Finance explained yesterday, the Government have eliminated the special war tax of 7i per cent, thereby losing a revenue of $30,000,000. I am satisfied, and so will be every reasonable man, that that reduction of 7i per cent must of necessity reduce the cost of living. The Government fully appreciate the urgent necessity of more revenue to take care of our war debt and our heavy expenditure, but in an honest endeavour to

bring down the cost of living they made that reduction.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, it might be of interest to know what our sister overseas dominion of Australia is doing in re-gar to tariff matters. I do not know whether she possesses as a member of her Parliament such an ardent free trader as my hon. friend from Brome, but judging from the article which I am about to refer to I should not think there are many free traders in the Parliament of the Australian Commonwealth. It will be seen from this article that the Government of Australia have revised their tariff, not downwards but upwards. I will read the article:
The Australian Tariff.'
An important revision of the tariff of Australia recently made imbeds more firmly the principle of protection to native industry, increases rates of duty for revenue purposes, and provides contingently for reciprocal tariffs with British countries. A cablegram from the Canadian Trade Commissioner at Melbourne runs as follows:	.
"Tariff Bill introduced Parliament, March 24, and becoming operative Maroh 25, has three schedules similar to Canadian. All embargoes and restrictions hitherto Imposed upon importations such as confectionery, motor car bodies, etc., absolutely cease on May 19. Excluding existing limited African agreement, no preference has been granted any dominion, but minister stated that bill provides for reciprocal arrangements with any dominion on the basis of British preferential tariff or intermediate schedules whole or partly and to foreign countries under intermediate only but subject to approval of Parliament. Tariff strongly protective with increased British preference. Marked increase duties iron steel products, motor car chassis, and bodies."
The consequence of this legislation can scarcely be other than the contraction of the somewhat limited market Canada has hitherto found in Australia. There is a preference given Great Britain, according to one despatch, of from ten to twenty per cent, but other advices indicate a much greater preference. The tariff on manufactures of iron, for example, is said to be:

Plates and sheets	heavier	Free	10%than 1-16, after June	1, 1922	48 s	85sAt present	Free	10%Barbed wire	68s	105sBolts and nuts	27i%	40%Wood screws	Free	10%Tacks and spikes. . . .	5 is	8swhichever is higher.	325%	45%If the foregoing schedule of duties	is retained, there will be small chance of Canadian
manufacturers obtaining a footing in the Australian market in competition with Great Britain. Of the preferential feature of the tariff no complaint can be made, and it is the business of the Australian Parliament to legislate as seems to it in the best interest of that country, but when the avowed object of the tariff is to promote British trade, Canadians may with reason contend that as a member of the Imperial family they should not be excluded from opportunity to trade on equal grounds with the United Kingdom. There is not now, nor ever has been, a reciprocal tariff between Canada and Australia. New Zealand, South Africa, and some other British countries do enjoy the preferential tariff in respect of their exports to Canada, but Australia has hitherto declined an arrangement for reciprocal commerce. The Canadian Government should without delay open negotiations for the extension of the Australian preferential tariff to this country. The time Is opportune, the need urgent. The Australian legislation opens the door, and with mutual goodwill existing, with a desire on the part of both dominions to promote Imperial trade, the hope may be entertained of more family and friendly treatment being extended to Canada than being placed on a parity with foreign nations. It has always seemed an anomaly that Canada's preferential tariff should extend to New Zealand, and not to Australia, though the fault is not that of this dominion. In any event if our trade with the Antipodes is to grow, the Government should hasten to conclude a reciprocal tariff arrangement.
That will serve to show what our sister dominion is doing. Australia evidently believes in the policy of moderate protection. Canada believes in the policy of moderate protection, I believe in that policy, and so does the Government and the party to which I have the honour to belong. I do not believe in free trade. And, Sir, there lire many hon. members on the other side of the House who do not believe in free trade any more than I do.
I was rather amused to hear the hon. member for Brome this afternoon citing the tariff policy of the Liberal party as enunciated in the resolution adopted at its convention held in this city last August. I am sure the House will bear with me if I read that resolution once more, because it is well worth while to keep it very plainly before not only the members of this House but before the people of the country. It reads as follows:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance:	First, diminishing the very high
cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing the cost of instruments of production-
That is a very vague expression, and I hope that when the hon. leader of the Opposition addresses the House he will explain what the Liberal party means when they refer to the " instruments of production." In my judgment, that would refer to everything that is made in this country.
-in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends,

And here is the important part:


wheat, wheat flour and all produots of wheat; the principal articles of food; farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net-twines and fishermen's equipments; cements and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to Implement by legislation the provision of this resolution when returned to power.
During the short time I have been in public life I have thought that when a great party, after having given serious consideration to the question of what their fiscal policy should be, published at a convention its deliberate policy in that regard, that policy would receive the unanimous approval of the members of the party and would be adhered to by them when speaking on the floor of this House and on public platforms. But, Mr. Speaker, the ink was hardly dry on this famous resolution before the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) delivered a speech at St. John, New Brunswick. The newspaper report which I have of the hon. gentleman's speech is headed in large type, " Mackenzie King for Free Trade." Then follows the hoh. gentleman's speech, which I will now quote:
The Liberal leader favoured the abolishment of all tariff duties,-
I cannot find that in the tariff resolution of the Liberal party. Let me quote the report in this newspaper:
The Liberal leader favoured the abolishment of all tariff duties, all instruments of production in industries based upon the natural resources of the Dominion, such as mines, fishing, lumbering and agriculture, the development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of the country.

Well, the leader of the Opposition had scarcely delivered that speech when one of his followers, the member for West Lamb-ton (Mr. Pardee) made a speech before the Liberal Reform Club in Montreal. He said nothing about the policy of free trade as enunciated by the leader of the Opposition in his St. John speech, and he carefully avoided any reference to the Liberal tariff policy as adopted at the Liberal Convention held in Ottawa during last August. But I must say that I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for West Lambton on that occasion. He said that he was a protectionist; aye, he even went so far as to say how he would fix the tariff. He said that in his opinion a tariff should not bear a lower ad valorem duty than 25 per cent. It seems strange to me that shortly after the adoption of this tariff policy at the convention in August the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) should make the strong protectionist speech that he did before the members of the Reform Club of my city. I will say this for the wisdom of my hon. friend: He knew the city that he was speaking in; he knew the proper policy to enunciate there.
Now, a by-election was held in St. James division in Montreal. If there is any constituency in Canada which does not want - to listen to free trade talk or any suggestion about slaughtering the tariff so as to crush our industries, it is the constituency of St. James, Montreal. My genial and astute friend the member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) who was doing all he eou(d to elect the hon. member who now represents that great division in this House (Mr. Rinfret), also made a very strong proteetionist speech. But that is not all. I have listened with a great deal of pleasure to the expressions of very strong protectionist sentiment that have come from the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie). He and I do not always agree, but when it comes to tariff matters I think we do. The hon. member holds good, strong, protectionist views, and how he could have swallowed the policy that was adopted at the Liberal convention last August, how he could have stood for that platform, is more than I am able to comprehend.
But I understand also, Mr. Speaker, that all was not milk and honey at that convention. By the little birds who chirped on that occasion and who were not in the know-that is, in the inner circle-I have been informed that many good and true Liberal protectionists strongly objected to the proposed tariff resolution when it was being considered by

a committee, and that they were absolutely opposed to it on the floor of the convention. Not only that; the Liberal Premier of British Columbia also made a speech during the course of the convention in which he expressed himself as being opposed to the Liberal policy as I have just given it. Moreover, Sir Lomer Gouin, the greatest French Canadian Liberal that we have in the province of Quebec, made a speech in the city of Quebec at a meeting which was attended also by my colleague, the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen). The Minister of the Interior and Sir Lomer Gouin both made protectionist speeches on that occasion, and notwithstanding the eloquence and convincing logic of the Minister of the Interior-and he never was in better form than he was at that banquet-the Premier of Quebec excelled him-and made a much stronger protectionist speech than did even my colleague. The papers did not publish the speech of the Premier of Quebec, but I have it here and I will read what Sir Lomer Gouin said on that occasion:
I understand that you feel anxious on a certain question of public policy with regard to the future of your industry.
Referring to the boot and shoe industry.
X mean the tariff. This was the theme of the speech I read this morning. I would not like to be excommunicated-
Listen to this:
I would not like to be excommunicated for what I will say now. but I would like to speak my mind very candidly.
I remember the day when many, too many, of our people, labourmen, farmers and merchants, had to leave the province of Quebec and emigrate to the United States. At that time I know there were very few manufacturers in the province of Quebec. X could not say why so many left Quebec, but they had to go for one reason or another.
We now have manufacturers in Montreal, Quebec, Trois Rivieres, Sherbrooke, and all our centres of a certain importance, and I cannot help but think that these manufacturers have contributed to bring back many of those who had gone and to keep with us many who would have had to go were it not for such industries.
What we want in Quebec is a tariff that will keep our industries going-
A little different from the tariff policy of my friend, the leader of the Opposition.
-our labourmen working for good wages, and the most deserving of all our citizens-our good farmers-content and prosperous.
I am not asking for a tariff of 15 per cent, 25 per cent, 30 per cent, or 40 per gent; give us a fair tariff that will keep alive honest industry on our good soil of Canada.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the wise words of one of the ablest statesmen in Canada,

a man whose utterances and policies carry far more weight in the commercial metropolis of Canada, the city of Montreal, than do any words of my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster).
Mr. Speaker, it has been my privilege to live in the province of Quebec since my boyhood days,-and it is indeed a great privilege to live in that province and to mingle with our French-Canadian friends. So far as I know their views on fiscal questions they are not free traders; they are protectionists. But I am afraid that the new Liberal party of to-day is in the hands of reactionaries and young bloods and that the old policy that was carried out for fifteen years by the late Bight Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the then Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is no longer the policy of the Liberal party. Last night that veteran statesman the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) rose in his place and made statements like this: ''I have been criticized by my party for believing in the policy of protection, but I still believe in it. I have been criticized by certain members of my party because I was willing when I was Minister of Finance to assist infant industries; I have no regrets or apologies to offer now. I thought that was the right policy then, and I think it the right policy now." Again, he said that during his term of office-and he certainly was a most excellent Minister of Finance-he gave certain bonuses to the steel industry in this country. He was criticized at the time, he said but he believed in bonuses then, and he believes in bonuses now. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and I ask hon. members of this House and I ask the people of the country how they can judge; how they can form any opinion as to the policy of hon. members opposite? True they did draw up this policy, but the leader of the Opposition, as I have said, deviated from it, because he said in the city of St. John that he was in favour of free trade.

speechtext: I was not here when my hon. friend read the particular despatch from a paper, but two or three times he has mentioned in my presence that in the speech which I made at St. John I departed from what is laid down in the platform of the Liberal party. In the speech I made at St. John I was reading from the platform of the Liberal party as laid down at the convention. I said that I stood by that platform, and I repeat that statement now.

The Liberal leader favoured the abolishment of all tariff duties.

That clearly
is a statement by a reporter in a general way. While speaking on that occasion I had in my hand a copy of the platform of the Liberal party and I read what is contained there, as I shall read it to this House again when I have the privilege of speaking in this debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

Do I understand
that the leader of the Opposition is not in favour of the abolition of duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I must accept the
hon. member's explanation that the press incorrectly reported his speech.
Inasmuch as my hon. friend has given us to understand that he is not a free trader and would be in favour I judge, of a certain form of protection, and as the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has reiterated in this House this afternoon that he is an absolute free trader, if our friends opposite should come into power it is quite likely the hon. member for Brome, who has been the financial critic of the Opposition for the last two or three years, would take the portfolio of Minister of Finance. And in that event it is clear that the leader of the Opposition would have lots of trouble trying to reconcile his Finance Minister s free trade ideas with the protectionist ideas that have been given expression to by several hon. gentlemen sitting wi'th him to the left of the Speaker.
The hon. member for Brome in his whole two hours' speech did not indicate in any way how he would raise the revenue. He dealt only in generalities, and therefore I am at a loss to know how my bon. friends opposite, if they came into power, would propose to raise the necessary revenues. I trust that the leader of the Opposition when he speaks in this debate will not only let us know whether he adheres to the tariff policy adopted at the Liberal convention in August last, but that he will also enlighten this House and the country as to how he would raise the revenue if he and his party came into power.
I notice that the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) some time ago made a

speech before the Montreal Reform Club in which he differed considerably from the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) and the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Pardee), both of whom had made protectionist speeches before the members of that club. The hon. member for Lunenburg did not do so. In his speech on that occasion he made the rather remarkable statement that there wias no difference between the underlying principles of the present Liberal policy and those of the United Farmers party. So there, again, we have a very marked difference of opinion among hon. gentlemen opposite as to what should be the tariff policy of the Liberal party.
The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) referring some time ago to the speech delivered at Quebec by the Minister of the Interior, to which I alluded a moment ago, said: "What a calamity it would be if a record of that speech was played on a gramophone at Calgary, what a commotion it would create out there." I would ask my hon. friend what kind of a commotion and impression it would create if a record of the speech of Sir Lomer Gouin to which I have referred was played in the city of Calgary.
The hon. member for Brome, who I .am sorry is not in his seat, felt very jubilant this afternoon. He challenged the Government to go to the country and was very confident that in such an event the Government would be defeated and that he and his friends would move over to the Treasury benches. I am afraid it was simply a case of the wish being father to the thought. He would indeed be a courageous man if he really wanted a general election now. Speaking for the Government-it has been said before, but I will state it again now- there is no reason why we should go tk>
the country until the full term Of this Parliament has expired. During my election campaign I never said anything about being elected only for the duration of the war, or that my service would end with the war. When the election comes, in due time, in the fall of 1922 or 1923-

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Make it 1925.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
-the issue is going to be a clear-cut one. The issue by which parties are going to stand or fall will be: Moderate protection versus free trade. I, for one, while I have no political ambitions whatever, have no fear what the verdict of the people will be on that issue when a general election comes. In all former

general elections that have been held in this country, any party that proposed to interfere seriously with the well-established fiscal policy of Canada met defeat at the polls, and if my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition, thinks he can carry the country on the tariff resolution adopted at the Liberal convention, I can only say he misjudges the intelligence of the electorate of Canada. With the necessary publicity that will be given, I am satisfied when the people from one end of this country to the other come to decide between the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite and the policy which this Government stands for, namely, a policy of moderate protection, with favour to none and justice to all, framed for the diversified interests of Canada, a policy that is equally good for the farmer, the lumberman, the workingman, the fisherman and the manufacturer, I have no doubt, and this Government- has no doubt, what the verdict of the people of Canada will be. The Minister of Finance yesterday clearly set forth the Government's policy, and I desire to have the privilege of placing it on Hansard. He said:
Our policy calls for a thorough revision of the tariff with a view to the adoption of such reasonable measures as are necessary: (a) to assist in providing adequate revenues, (b) to stabilize legitimate industries and to encourage the establishment of new industries essential to the proper economic development of the nation-to the end that a proper and ever-increasing field of useful and remunerative employment be available for the nation's workers, (c) to develop to the fullest extent our natural resources, (d) to specially promote and increase trade with the Mother Country, the sister dominions and colonies and Crown dependencies, (e) to prevent the abuse of the tariff for the exploitation of the consumer-
That is the policy of the Government, and it has my full and unstinted support both in this House and outside of it.
Just a word with reference to our friends of the Agrarian group, sitting across the way. I am sorry my good friend the leader of that party, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), is not in his seat. There is one thing on which I can compliment the Agrarian group, the U. F. O., or whatever name the party is known by, and that is the very clear way in which they have given expression to their policy on many occasions during this session of the House.
The hon. member for Marquette and those who sit behind him are out and out free traders; they make no bones about that point'and I think they deserve our thanks and appreciation for the very clear exposi-

tion which they have given us of their policy. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) when speaking in this House a few weeks ago was asked whether he believed in the policy of protection and he replied that he had never believed in protection, he did not believe in it then, and he never would believe in it. What could be clearer than that, Mr. [Speaker? We know exactly where the members of the Farmers' party stand. I find no fault with them because this is a free country and we are assembled in a free parliament. Every one in this country has a right to think as he pleases and to vote as he pleases, and it is every man's prerogative to stand by whatever policy he considers is best conducive to the welfare of the country. But I rather differ from my hon. farmer friends when they say that this free trade policy of theirs, this new progressive policy, so-called, is a sound policy for Canada. If they said it was a policy for the three Prairie Provinces and one peculiarly framed for their own interests, then I could agree with them; but when they assert that the free trade policy which they advocate is a good one for all of Canada's diversified interests, I confess I cannot follow them in their logic. How could a free trade policy maintain our great manufacturing industries that exist from one end of Canada to the other? How could it afford employment for hundreds of thousands of workmen throughout the length and breadth of this country.
And what good would a free trade policy be even to the farmers? If any policy in this country is framed to suit any one particular interest and that interest alone, it is a wrong policy and can have only one result. If the farmers are to be prosperous in this country, then the manufacturers, the business men, the workingmen and all other classes must live under a policy that grants special favours to none, and which is framed in the national interests and for the benefit of the whole people. The moderate protection policy that has prevailed in this country since 1867 has proved just such a policy. Suppose for a moment that we had a free trade policy in this country. Suppose our friends of the prairies produced vastly more grain than ever they did, but other interests in Canada were not prosperous; the people did not have money; the railways did not have freight to carry east-bound and westbound; and our grain growers found a lack of demand for the enormous amount of wheat they were growing, and found prices low-for all that would
follow a free trade policy-what would be the effect? The farmers would suffer with the rest. With all deference to my hon. friends, I am at a loss to know why, in a country like this, those gentlemen could purpose to put such a policy into effect if they had the opportunity to do so. The hon. member for Marquette, I will admit, modifies his policy very much according to the locality in which he happens to be speaking. He made a speech in this House a year ago and I have it here in Hansard. He said that the policy of protection was economically an unsound one, and he went on to say that he had recently travelled through the fair province of Ontario and had seen hundreds of farms, many of which were vacant, and this fact he attributed to the policy of protection. How he could come to such a conclusion is beyond my comprehension. Then later, when he was making a speech in the city of Toronto-a very strong protectionist city-he naturally modified his views. The leader of the Farmers' group on that occasion said, if I remember rightly: "I would not with one .fell swoop demolish the fiscal policy and all the industries of this country. I would prefer to let them die a slow lingering death. I would therefore bring about this end slowly, gradually, but surely." Well, if such a policy as that is ever to be put into practice, I for one should prefer the former manner of fiscal decease, so as to let the industries of the country be put out of existence with quick despatch.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up the time of the House any longer. 'Once more I express my pleasure, as a member of the Government, at the Budget which has been presented, and if I may be permitted to do so, I extend my heartiest congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) for the splendid, comprehensive, fair and logical statement which he submitted to the House yesterday, and which is meeting with the general approval of the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the Budget Speech which the Minister of Finance delivered yesterday afternoon I observed that it was his intention not to get all the national milk, so to speak, from the same old cow. He has taxed the unnecessary things of life, he has taxed the slaves of fashion and the molly-coddles of the country, and in that respect I have no complaint to offer. There is one particular, however, in which I would have been very much interested had the minister taken very drastic measures.

I should have liked to see an enormous tax on American automobiles or automobiles coming from any other country. The automobile, in my opinion, has been the means of more injury in this country than any other invention of civilization. It has destroyed homes, and the worries which expensive automobiles have created have sent many a man to his last resting place, because he was nagged and harassed to such an extent, and his business pride was such, that he preferred to die physically rather than face financial death. No one but an acrobat is safe in crossing the streets now. You go to any garage in the country and you will find automobiles galore; and in many of them in the small towns you will find anywhere from twenty-five to seventy-five secondhand automobiles for sale. There is a perfect craze on the part of people to-day to go riding through the streets in burnished, shining vehicles. It is an appalling fact, Sir, and I hope our Finance Minister will consider this phase of the subject and see to it that no more expensive cars are brought into the country. There is a craze among the people to go running around in these glaring, death-dealing instruments.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I see there is unanimity on that point, and there is no question about the truth of it. It is but too well known that people, even wise people, have a mania to spend their money foolishly, and the automobile is one of the chief sources of their extravagance.
I noticed that last night the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce went so far as to say that my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was inconsistent, comparing his present policy with his old time policy. Probably I am not quite as old as the two ex-Ministers of Finance but they isplayed a fellowship towards each other last evening which did my heart good. I believe that in a few years a new era will dawn on this country. But when the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce claims that my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's is inconsistent I might remind him that he himself went to Washington in the eighties and the nineties to try to effect a treaty of reciprocity with the United States. On several occasions he went down there and was unsuccessful. On the last occasion that he and his colleagues went to Washington the Canadian delegates found that* the people who were to meet them had their bags
'Xlr. Baldwin.]
packed and they offered them the excuse that they were going on 9 southern trip. I think that what I say is exacitly correct. And so, the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues came home disheartened.
The question of reciprocity was not brought up again for a considerable time because the United States ignored all overtures until the time of President Taft. Then the United States had a vast population, 'they needed free natural products and free food. Naturally they had their eye on this half of the North American continent and they wanted free raw material. They made several overtures to Canada and pay hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's ,was very properly sent to Washington to have a conference with the Americans. An agreement was prepared and the Canadian delegates came home. Instead of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the great leader of the then Government of Canada putting that treaty into force at once he delayed in order to consult Parliament and in the meantime false representations, were put before the people by the press which declared that such a policy was disloyal and unpatriotic and that reciprocity with the United States would prove a dismal failure. But the present right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, as well as all the principal members of Sir John Macdonald's Government proclaimed throughout the wide country their feeling for reciprocity after that principle had been abrogated in the early sixties following the war of the rebellion in the United States. In the county that I represent, Sir John Macdonald spoke in favour of reciprocity in natural products and the Hon. C. C. Colby, who represented that county for about a quarter of a century always had as one of the planks of his platform reciprocity in natural products. Throughout the country they proclaimed that policy. I am sorry that the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not in his seat because if he were I would point out to him how inconsistent he was in fighting the very policy which he had tried to consummate for many long years. It was the policy of the party that he followed, and which he continued to follow, except for the short interval when he was out of the House.
The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Ballantyne) says that we on this side of the House are willing to do nothing hut sit around and that we have no policy. I have never known in all the years of the Liberal party that a free trade policy was advocated. Alexander Mackenzie, Edward

Blake and Sir Wilfrid Laurier never proclaimed themselves in favour of an absolutely free trade policy. These leaders advocated a tariff for revenue. The right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce last night stated plainly that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's had championed a free trade policy. That is something new in Canada. It seems to me that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's said that no member of this House is willing to acknowledge that Canada has yet reached the stage when she could have free trade.
We must remember that Canada has a vast heritage to develop. She has great wealth in water-powers which are better than the black coal of the United States. At present tens of millions of capital are coming into the province of Quebec, towns are rapidly growing up, manufacturers are coming in large numbers and they are building plants now that will cost millions for the bricks and mofar alone without taking into consideration the working capital. We have a vast country here and as true Canadians we believe in its development. We know that under the present policy of the Government we cannot develop it without immigrants coming here to help us. This may be a suggestion to the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). He talks about a hand picked people only being allowed to come in. I disagree with him decidedly. I know, as other hon. members know, that approximately a million emigrants annually went into the United States for many years. They went forth, engaged in different spheres of activity and helped to develop the country. I believe that immigrants should be allowed to come to this country regardless of colour and that we should make such laws as would give them to understand before they come that we have no place for any who are not law abiding and do not wish to work. I have said before and I say it again that all crooks, shysters and loafers should be kept out of Canada. People who come to this country should be made to understand that they cannot loaf around, commit crimes, and play crooked games on the people. If that is made plain to all who may contemplate coming to Canada people of that class will not come and we will get a better type of settlers. We have tremendous resources. There has been no boosting in Canada. We are not boosters. Why is it that we have not a larger population? The House was yesterday reminded that the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. White) said during his first Budget that about a thousand people a day were coming into
Canada. If the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier had been continued this country would now have had eleven or twelve million people. We know that the tide had turned before the war and that tens of thousands of people were leaving Canada in 1912-13. Then there came this horrible war that has given such a staggering blow to this country. But it has brought Canada to its senses and enabled here to see herself Canada played a part in the war that at one time we never thought she was capable of; she demonstrates the ingenuity, the sagacity and the strength of other people. Canada to-day stands at the point where we should all get together and, regardless of party politics, work for the good of the country. The time has gone by when members on one side should picture those on the other as being either manikins or brass monkeys. We should get together and develop this wonderful country. Take for instance the Georgian Bay Canal. There is enough water power on that system of canals and waterways to pay for the completion of the enterprise within a period of fifty, or possibly seventy-five years. The cost of developing hydro-electric works now is enormous, but before this stage was reached there was ample time for the Government of Canada to let contracts for the development of the Georgian Bay Canal by granting for a term of years the use of the water-power that might be developed. Does any one imagine that these contracts could now be awarded at the present time for anything like a reasonable figure? The same may be said of the project for the deepening of the St. Lawrence canals. These works, in view of the present enormous debt, would be a tremendous undertaking to-day. The way to rwith our obligations, as well as to develop our great natural resources, is not by working eight hours a day; we must take off our coats and work for ten hours a day or more. I happen to be one of the unorganized labour party that takes pleasure in working fifteen hours a day. That does not kill people; it is far more healthful than indulging in nonsense and all sorts of extravagant pleasures. I repeat that our great need to-day is to develop this wonderful country. In so saying I only wish that the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Marine were in their seats.

speechtext: I am here.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am sorry, but as the minister is not occupying his own seat he escaped my notice. Let me say to the hon. gentleman that we have not a mile too many

railways in Canada, nor a steamboat too many for the development of the country, if the rates on those railways were only raised to make them self-sustaining, and thus prevent the present and coming generations from being burdened with an enormous debt to make up the deficits. .

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
If the hon. member
would address the farmers .at the other end of the Chamber and convert them to his idea it would make my task easier.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I believe in the system of bonusing as to which we heard expressions of opinion last night from the exMinister of Finance (Sir George Foster) and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding); it would doubtless bring about better results than some other policies that have heen advocated. It is ridiculous that a country of the tremendous extent and resources of Canada should only be mining five per cent of its deposits of iron ore. Can it be expected that we shall make a success of the development of this country if we do not use its great natural resources to the best advantage? Then there are vast areas of agricultural land which cannot be developed without labour, and how are we to get that labour unless we adopt a progressive immigration policy? True we are building up a great military machine to take care of those people in some of the provinces who are considered disloyal. In the province of Quebec we have no such elements in our population. The people there are willing to work ten hours a day. They are quite satisfied and have no use for travelling labour agitators; such men have no influence upon the people of that province or upon organized labour there. That is why immense capital for investment is flowing into the province of Quebec from Ontario, and from the United States and from other countries. Down there in the province of Quebec the people worship God and honour the King. Labour troubles are non-existent, and strikes are practically nil, but how different is the condition in other countries, for example in the United States, where strikes seem to be almost continuous.
With respect to the development of our railways we need money to link up the existing system, but the Minister of Railways seems afraid to make advances in the railway rates for fear the Canadian Pacific will enjoy the advantage of the increase. The Canadian Pacific got through its operations last year with the closest escape from a deficit, and surely it is a picayune idea that

we should retard the development of our National railways, and expose the country to a loss of many millions of dollars, because of the fear that the Canadian Pacific would benefit from any advance in rates that might be ordered.
The admission of Newfoundland to this Confederation would be a decidedly forward step. There was a possibility of Newfoundland entering Confederation when Sir Mackenzie Bowell was Premier of Canada, but it seemed likely to involve an additional expenditure of $8,000,000-which in those days was regarded as a great sum of money [DOT]-and the project fell through. What has the United' States done in the last fifty years? They have doubled their territory toy diplomacy, toy dollars, and by war. Would the Republic to the south part with any portion of its territory even if it were offered a million times more than it cost to acquire it? Possibly it .might in the case of the Phillipine Islands, but not with respect to another inch of its territory. In Canada unfortunately our people are not of a boasting type. We are losing our young men and our young women. We are not increasing in population at the rate we should in view of the fact that Canada is one of the greatest countries on the face of the earth and in area comprises half a continent. The people are becoming despondent, discouraged, and dissatisfied, and it is about time we became 'boosters for our country. One hon. gentleman raised the question of our doing business with the West Indian Islands. For my part, I think we should trade not only with the Mother Country, but with every other Dominion and Crown Colony in the British Empire in preference to any other part of the world. In order to avoid the rigours of the Canadian climate many of our people go to British Honduras, British Guiana, the Leeward Island's, Barbados, or 'the Bahamas. We could trade with the West Indies with advantage to ourselves, and I believe that trade would greatly develop with the progress of the years. I am of opinion that if we could win the admiration of the people of those islands we could win their trade, and if the West Indies were rnoTe closely united with Canada, both would benefit to a surprising degree. The Government should send to the West Indies to promote trade relations men endowed with boundless enthusiasm. I understand that delegates are coming here from the West Indies about the last of this month. Let us show these delegates that it would be a good thing for them to become more closely acquainted with this great country and its wonderful possibilities. I

hope the time will come when commercial union between Canada and the West Indies will be something more than a dream. I hope that we can win the admiration of the West Indies. I do not believe in war, but as one of the results of the war England has acquired a German colony of nearly as extensive an area as Canada, and, therefore, I think that this country deserves some consideration as well. I believe that a mutual agreement with the Imperial Government and the Crown colony of the great Caribbean sea might bring about a rounding out of this great Dominion. "Procrastination is the thief of time," and to-day when the United States are advocating that Great Britain sell those islands to the United States, it is about time for us to wake up. Even one of the prospective presidential candidates, Mr. McAdoo, has brought that subject before the people of the United States. If those islands were sold by England to liquidate her indebtedness to the United States, where would Canada be?
I am not a believer in sentiment, on the ccnnary, I am a believer in hard and fast business principles; but sometimes sentiment is a prevailing factor, and we should cultivate in our sons and daughters the sentiment that Canada is one of the best located countries on the face of the earth, with natural wealth beyond all comprehension, and so stimulate that patriotic pride which means so much in the development of any country. And with that sentiment properly cultivated, I believe that our future is assured.
If we succeed in bringing the West Indies into this great Confederation, the resultant advantages will be great indeed. Instead of depending on our neighbours to the South for the products of those islands our own mercantile marine will bring them direct to our Atlantic ports, and by means of our great inland waterways we shall be able to reach the markets not only of our own provinces but the markets to the South and be able to compete with the Americans in their home cities of Buffalo, Erie, Cincinnati, Toledo, Detroit, Chicago, Milwaukee and Duluth. But if we continue to proscrastinate I am afraid that this Parliament instead of being praised by our people will be cursed.
I feel assured that the people of the West India Islands would be proud to belong to a nation of such vast resources as we possess. They need our products, and we need theirs, and there would be a constant interchange of traffic. They will never be manufacturing centres, but we are certain to become one of the greatest workshops of the world-although our development along that line has so far been slow. However, I think the dawn of a new day is awaiting us, and I sincerely hope that party politics will stop for a while until the people of Canada come to a realization of what vast possibilities are within their reach.
I claim that every product of a tropical character that we need here can be raised in the West Indies, and that emphasizes the importance of a mutually satisfactory arrangement being reached for their becoming part and parcel of this wonderful Confederation. From cotton down to the smallest tropical fruits would it not be a glorious thought for the householders of this country if they could send their children to get Canadian tropical products at the stores? Under our present trade relations with the United States that country holds Canada in one hand and the islands in the other; she discounts their money 41 per cent, she discounts ours from 10 to 15 per cent, and as a result she gains $30,000,000 in handling the products of the West Indies and selling them to Canada. Is it not ridiculous?
With this condition of affairs, is it not time that we ceased fighting over things that should not excite controversy? Because, as I said in my opening remarks, when two great finance ministers of experience get together in kindly fellowship there is a future for Canada that will make this one of the greatest countries upon this earth.
Our country is so vast that we have lost ourselves. There was a time when we used to hear about patriotism-people were proud of tne fact that they belonged to a country on which the sun never set. Love of country? We hear nothing more of it. We have gone far astray, and, like the lost tribes of Israel, we are wandering aimlessly. But it is time that we drew ourselves together. The people in the northern part of the United States are like ourselves, strong and vigorous, and their country is connected with the West Indies by a shipping service which gives her a predominant advantage. Already the United States owns Porto Eico; she has a protectorate over Cuba; she now has her customs officers in San Domingo.
What I am proposing would be a perfectly safe proceeding. It would not have the uncertainty of reaching out into the Orient;

it is a solid, straightforward business proposition. Our people should visit the West Indies and learn the requirements of their inhabitants instead of spending their money in the United States. Some yeaTs ego in the United States they started the slogan: "Look around your own country"; and since the war they have supplemented that with actually learning that they have a wonderful country. Do Canadians know their own country? I would advise the people of this city if they want a real holiday this summer to go right up into the woods, and they will discover that we have bench lands along the rivers-I am speak-more particularly of the province of Quebec -where millions of people could get their livelihood. I have seen thousands of acres red with wild berries-literally thousands of tons of them, which if they could be gathered would return sufficient to pay the interest on our national debt. We have a wonderful country. Too many think that in Canada there are vast ice-bound regions incapable of production, but those who entertain that view are vastly mistaken. Canada is a country which is capable of producing a strong and vigorous race. Yet we find that hundreds of people have left our country and gone to the United States. Just so soon as Canada does the things it should do; just so soon as this House takes steps towards the progressive development of our country, these persons who have left our shores will return to us. It is a crying shame that such a vast country as Canada should stand where it stands to-day for want of patriotism, for want of love of country, for want of boosting. I do urge the people of Canada; I do urge those who are in authority, to make a move toward the development of this wonderful country, with its possibilities-shall I say for I believe it-of maintaining hundreds of millions of people.
