speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT JAMES MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do-not intend to deal at any length at all with the remarks of the previous speakers on the Opposition side who have taken part in this debate. One of the reasons is that it would take, I fear, a tariff acrobat to deal with them all, for the reason that in the first place the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) this afternoon took 
an absolute free trade stand, though I think he soft-pedalled slightly compared with previous orations. Then the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) took a moderate protectionist stand, and I understand my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Baldwin) to take a protectionist stand. I find myself wondering, after thinking that over, if the Agrarian members of the House decide to accept the invitation of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, which of those three constituencies they would come in through. I thought the criticisms of the Opposition speakers were tempered with mercy. In fact, I thought the criticisms of the hon. member for Stanstead were so tempered with mercy that they were almost a paeon of praise to the Minister of Finance. There is one statement the hon. member for Brome made- and I do not say this in any unkind way -with which I thoroughly agree, and that was his statement that the verses which he quoted were rather of an ordinary type. I do not use the word he used, because he might misconstrue it; I think he said of a low type. I think they were at least of an ordinary type.
So far as the three speakers thus far on the Opposition side are concerned, I found myself agreeing to a great extent with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. I feel after having listened for a long time, during four sessions, in this House to debates on the tariff question that no subject in Canada to-day is of more importance than the tariff question. It is not only a question upon which political parties are dividing, but a question in which everybody in this country is taking an interest. It is a question the solution of which is very important to the best interests of Canada. I am not of the farmers, on the one side, or of the manufacturers on the other. I am of that large body of Canadian citizens who belong to neither class, and it might be interesting to place on Hansard the figures as to how many people there are in each of the different classes. According to the census of 1911 the total number of people employed in the different occupations in Canada was 2,723,000 in round figures, and I shall deal only in round figures for the reason that extended figures are rather dreary reading. Of this number the agricultural employees amounted to 933,000, or 34 per cent; manufacturing employees, 491,000, or 18 per cent. All the rest, 1,294,000, or 48 per cent, were of the working population of this country. That 48 per cent includes building trades,

domestic servants, civil servants, professional men, fisheries and forestry, trade and transportation. That 48 per cent, or nearly one-half of the working population of this country, are in danger of being ground between the upper and nether millstones of free trade and protection and that is my reason for speaking here to-day more or less on behalf of that 48 per cent of which I am a member. Belonging to that class, I feel I can look at the question dispassionately, as I have no direct interest in the matter, the only interest I possess being a desire to get the best policy for the betterment and advancement of Canada. I do not want to be misunderstood as trying to prove that free trade as a theory or as a principle is wrong. In that I believe I can fully agree with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's when he said that in theory he was a free trader, but in practice, as I understood him-certainly he implied that-he did not believe in it. To the free traders of this country I presume that is a little bit like what doctors say occasionally "Though the operation was a success, the patient died." Sometimes, no doubt, the patient would prefer the operation to have been not quite so successful.
It would appear to me that Canada must take into consideration not theories, not principles, but actual conditions and facts as they are, and two of these important facts which must be taken into consideration are these: First, just to the South of us we have that immense American republic, the United States, which has a very high industrial development, and with the industries of which our industries must compete. Even if we had free trade in Canada, it would not necessarily mean that they would have free trade in the United States; in other words, our industries would have to compete in a free trade market with the industries of the United States in a protected market. Secondly, we are to the East of the teeming millions of Asia, with low wages and low living conditions, both wages and living conditions being on a very much lower scale than we believe in. So while we might desire the ideal of free trade, while we might desire to lay aside what some people might call the selfish national policy of tariffs, should we be so altruistic as to desire the progress and prosperity of other nations as much as we desire the progress and prosperity of our own? In addition to that, free traders both in this House and outside have been in the habit of making comparisons with conditions in free trade countries, particularly England. They have been making promises to Canada based, no doubt-in fact, it must be-upon the conditions in free trade England. I feel that a clear statement of the facts and a clear statement of comparisons, not with ' the object in view of disproving the theory of free trade, but of paving the way for a fair consideration of this subject on behalf of Canada, would be apropos here to-day, and that is what I intend to attempt; because after careful thought and consideration it appears to me that the moderate tariff course is the wise course for this country to follow. We should go neither to the extreme of free traders, knocking down all tariff walls, or to the protectionist extreme of placing a Chinese wall around this country which would bar out the goods of all other countries. It is not sufficient today to merely state one's conclusions. It is necessary to offer reasons for the faith that is in one. It has appeared to me that too often those who take the same stand as I do, and I think the vast majority of the members of this House have taken that stand, have taken it, some of us, at least, in an apologetic way. We have allowed free traders to try and prove their theories with theories and their facts with theories, and have not often enough insisted that they prove their theories with facts. I admit that the academic question of the tariff is more easily upheld on the free trade side, but facts are stubborn things, and it is facts I intend to deal with.
In the first place, if free trade- is a panacea for all the ills that nations are heir to, how is it that England which adopted it in 1846 is the only great nation of the world that has adopted it? Italy, Spain, Germany, France, Austria-Hungary, the United States-none of these great nations have considered free trade worth while adopting. Even the overseas Dominions of the Empire, with one small exception, have not considered it worth while to copy the methods oi the Mother Country. Cobden's prophesy that if England adopted free trade, in ten years free trade would be universal, is a long distance from being fulfilled. In England itself there is a large body of protection opinion. The other day I made it my business to look over three shelves of books, in the Library dealing with tariff questions, and of forty distinct works by English writers twelve were in favour of protection. So I think I am correct in saying that there is a large body of opinion in England-and we know there is even amongst politicians in England-favourable



would be regarded here as necessaries of life. And the embargo against Canadian cattle entering the United Kingdom, is thinly disguised as a health measure, but it is as a matter of fact nothing more nor less than a protection for the cattle growers of the United Kingdom. The steamship subsidies which are paid by England for mail carrying are also claimed to be in the shape of a subsidy for the home trade, for the foreign steamship companies claim they have no chance of getting the subsidies even if they tender lowest. In other words, England insists on giving the contracts to her own people even if they are higher than the tenders offered by foreign companies. In 1917-18 the customs and excise in England brought in a revenue of $550,000,000; in 1918-19 the estimated revenue was $740,000,000; and this year, according 'to the speech of Mr. Austin Chamberlain reported in the London Times, the figure is $1,500,000,000. I admit that in that figure there are included in excise some duties which we do not impose here, but if you subtract even a great deal from that, you would have a greater income per capita for customs and excise in the United Kingdom than in Canada. So that England is not entirely free trade.
But in Canada, when any one takes the stand I am taking in favour of a moderate tariff policy, some free trader demands that the position should be carried to its "logical conclusion" and suggestions are made about barriers between one province and another and between one district and another, and between one city and another.
That is a favourite argument of free traders. You find it in all the books on the subject. Even that grand old man ol British politics, Mr. Gladstone, used it in a debate with an American. It would be rather strange if we could not answer that question because the answer is very easy. The answer is that to carry protection to such a conclusion would be to carry it to an illogical conclusion. It would be like saying that if a slice of old English bee: is good for your dinner, you should eat a whole ox; or if a thirtieth of a grain of strychnine or an ounce of brandy is good for a failing heart, why do you not give a pound of strychnine or a keg of brandy?

speechtext: Would the hon. gentle-I man give us a few of the items on the free list, in the United States? It will be very interesting to the House.

speechtext:
Yes, I will be pleased to. I only asked for a certain list of goods and out of the list I received I can give a great many more dutiable items, but I do not wish to clutter up Hansard. Amongst the goods admitted free into the United States are eggs, poultry, boots and shoes, meats, cement, coal, tea, coffee, leather goods, agricultural implements, lumber and films. These are the goods I asked about. I am pointing out that in the United States there are many necessaries of life that aTe dutiable. I am not in any way trying to disagree with anybody and my only object in quoting these figures is to prove that the United States is not a free trade country .
Now, let us look a little further into the question of the foreign commerce of the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom. I think I can say without fear of contradiction that before the war the United States and Germany were rapidly gaining, under a protective tariff, on the foreign commerce of the United Kingdom. I am going to give figures to show that in that assumption I am correct. In the

try in the world; and Mr. Hill said that even the railway wages in Germany were higher than those in Great Britain.
Let us make another comparison, this time in regard to pauperism or abject poverty. In 1914, 761,000 paupers were relieved in England and Wales under the Poor Laws; in 1910-I could not get the same year, but I do not think it makes any material difference-84,000 paupers were relieved in the United States, or one-tenth the number with two and one-half times the population of England and Wales. In 1913 in the United Kingdom $89,000,000 was spent on poor relief; I have no records for Germany since 1885, but J. Ellis Barker, whom I have already quoted, in his "Modern Germany" says that there is much more pauperism in England than in Germany.
It has been suggested that comparison between the United Kingdom and the United States are unfair, because of the larger area, greater population, and immense natural resources of the United States. I admit that there is a good deal of truth in that criticism. But, Sir, if after a fair examination we find that the people of England following sixty years of free trade are not on an equal plane with the people of the United States under protection, then Canada being so much similar to the United States in area, in natural resources,-in minerals, fisheries, lumber and all those things, almost in climate except tropically, might it not be much wiser to copy the methods of the United States- probably that will be an unpopular expression-to consider the methods of the United States rather than those of some European country absolutely unlike Canada. At any rate, free trade exists only in England, therefore comparisons cannot be made with any other free trade country of importance.
Let us take other comparisons, for instance, agriculture. How has it stood the test of free trade in England? All hon. members know that the free traders of England are the manufacturers, and that the piotectionists are the farmers; the reverse of what obtains in Canada. The reason is th 't the farmers have seen agriculture deteriorating so rapidly in England. And I am not going to let it go at that; I am going to give my proofs. England imports most of her foodstuffs. In 1913 she imported 215,000,000 bushels of wheat and grew only 57,000,000 bushels, or only one-fifth of her needs. It might be argued that the size of the United Kingom is the reason for the small amount of acreage there under wheat; but the fact is, Sir, that France, Italy, Ger-

many, Austria, and even Spain greatly surpassed her in wheat production. Taking the wheat production of the world in 1913, I find these figures given-and I am leaving out any Asiatic countries, because it is not important to my argument to consider their production; Russia grew 814,000,000 bushels; the United States, 763,000,000 bushels; France, 319,000,000 bushels; Canada, 232,000,000 bushels; Austria-Hungary, 230,000,000 bushels; Italy, 214,000,000 bushels; Germany, 171,000,000 bushels; Spain, 112,000,000 bushels; United Kingdom, 57,000,000 bushels, or half that of Spain, exactly one third that of Germany, a quarter that of Italy, and about one-sixth that of France. I may say, Sir, that those figures are given from the Blue Books of our Department of Trade and Commerce so they are authoritative. So far as oats and barley are concerned, while the figures are not so strongly against England, they are nearly in the same ratio.
England imports 50 per cent of her foodstuffs, and is almost wholly dependent on the outside world in that respect; but before the war Germany raised 90 per cent of her foods, and France 100,000,000 bushels more wheat than we did in this immense country. Therefore England suffers by comparison in agriculture with practically all the European countries.
What a contrast, Mr. Speaker, in the United States, where under protection since 1861-I say under protection, not because of protection-the agricultural states of the west have grown rich, prosperous and populous, selling 90 per cent of their crops in their home market. The production of the wealth of the farms in the United States-and this statement is from the statistics published by the United States Government-including crops and livestock was in 1880, $2,000,000,000; in 1900, $5,000,000,000; in 1910, $9,000,000,000; in 1918, $21,000,000,000. The value of farm property in the United States, including land, buildings, stock and so on, increased 150 per cent in the twenty years from 1890 to 1910 -from $16,000,000,000 to $41,000,000,000.
It seems to me, Sir, that the extreme farmer might well ponder over those figures before demanding a change in the fiscal policy of this country.
Rather strangely the argument has been advanced that protection is immoral, but anybody who has visited these various countries will not claim, I think, that free trade has had any particularly elevating effect on England; I do not imagine that any one will claim that England is more

moral than for example the countries on this side of the water.
Then, Sir, will a free trade policy develop our natural resources? Undoubtedly we need their development very much. What about our pulp wood, for instance? Under free trade there would be none of these provincial restrictions which exist to-day, and the raw pulp wood would go out to feed the pulp and paper mills of the United States, and our pulp wood resources would soon be exhausted.

speechtext:
Are not those figures to conjure with, Mr. Speaker?
I can go a little further, and although I do not like to- tire the House with figures, I cannot refrain from citing these statistics with regard to tin-plate imports into the United States in 1890 before restrictions were imposed. The importation of tin plates to the United States in 1890 amounted to 680,000,000 pounds, and twenty years later, in 1913, that was reduced to 28,000,000 pounds, due to protective policy. Tin-plate manufacturing in the United States amounted in 1890 to 2,000,000 pounds, and twenty-three years later, in 1913, had increased to
2.000.	000.000 ipounds. From 1880 to 1917 the production of natural gas in the United States increased from $215,000 to $140,000,000; of lead from 100,000 tons to 600,000 tons; of copper from 27,000 tons to 840,000 tons; of cement, from 2,000,000 barrels to 91,000,000 barrels. The production of corn increased from 1,700,000,000 bushels in 1880 to 3,000,000,000 bushels in 1917; of cotton, from 6,000,000 bales to 11,000,000 bales; cotton manufactures from $192,000,000 in 1880 to $701,000,000 in 1914; production of phosphate rock from 200,000 tons to 2,500,000 tons; of zinc, from 23,000 tons to 584,000 tons. The export of manufactured cotton increased from $10,000,000 in 1880 to $136,000,000 in 1917. The production of wheat nearly doubled in the same period, and the national wealth increased from $43,000,000,000 in 1880 to $187,000,000,000 in 1912. These figures may be of use on another occasion.
I might also point out-I am not going to put details of these figures on Hansard- that in the production of coal, iron ore, pig-iron and steel, the United States and Germany in some cases surpassed the United Kingdom, though they started away behind her. For example, in the production of coal the United Kingdom, starting with
186.000.	000 tons in 1890, increased to 270,000,000 tons in 1911, while the United States starting with 148,000,000 tons, increased in the same period to 427,000,000 tons; that is, it started behind, but almost doubled the production in the United Kingdom in 1911. Germany, starting with a lower production than the United Kingdom in 1890, almost reached the same point as England in 1911. In the production of iron ore the United States and Germany surpassed the production of the United Kingdom in 1911, though they started equal in 1890, the United States producing in 1911 three times as much as the United Kingdom, and Germany nearly twice as much. France was about equal in iron ore production to the United Kingdom, although it started behind in 1890. In the

production of pig-iron the United States and Germany surpassed the United Kingdom in 1911, though they started about equal (Germany behind) in 1890, France also gained more rapidly than England in the same period. In the production of steel the United States was producing over three times as much as the United Kingdom in 1911, and Germany twice as much, though they started equally in 1890. France also gained very rapidly. The reason I mention those four materials is that they are the basic elements of commercial progress. In the production .of these four different materials the United States and Germany surpassed the United Kingdom in many instances, and in others were gaining very rapidly.
Then there is this argument: that a moderate tariff brings about a -more diversified national life, because it produces greater opportunities to the youth of our land and prevents their exodus to the United States. There is no class of our people in the Dominion who profit more by that fact than the ambitious sons of the farmers of this country, and even if on occasions internal competition does not cut down the prices of materials quite so low as we might wish, is not a complete national development worth something? Do we wish to be simply producers of food and raw materials, simply hewers of wood and drawers of water to the other nations of the world?
We have immense taxes, due to the war, and it is doubtful if we can raise them by the direct method. History shows that every country after a great war has increased its custom-s to a certain extent.
I have not used the argument that we have to compete with cheap Japanese and Chinese labour, nor the quite logical argument as to the specialization in manufacturing in the United States. In other words, if Canadian manufacturers are forced to compete in an open market with American manufacturers in a protected market, and Canadians cannot specialize so greatly, they will be driven out of business in this country. They wrould no longer manufacture to a population of 8,000,000 or 9,000,000, but would go to the United States and manufacture to a population of 110,000,000. I think I have touched most of the important aspects of the life of a people. I have touched on home and foreign markets, agriculture, transportation rates, general taxes, pauperism, foreign commerce, development of our national resources, a diversified national life, and the general well-being of the people; and I have shown that the

people of England are not on an equal plane in most of them with the people of the United States, and in some of them are not on an equal plane with the people of Germany and France. I do not state that protection is the cause of all this. No one cause can be assigned for the progress, or the reverse, of any nation. Contributing circumstances must be taken into account. But if in sixty years free trade England has not succeeded in improving the condition of her people as much as has the United States in the same period, why should we adopt a free trade policy? Certainly the facts in the situation are against free trade. Then why should Canada embark on such a policy? Is it merely because it is claimed by some to be a panacea for all the ills that nations are heir to? Or is it merely to try out the theories of the hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr. M. Clark) and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster)? Suppose we admit that the conditions of the masses of the people did improve very much in England after 1846; that statement can be made truthfully of every other civilized country. Through invention and science alone much was accomplished. But despite its great population the United States leads the world. Protection in United States began in 1861, when that country had a population of 31,000,000. Now its population is
110,000,000, and in general prosperity, developed natural resources, real wages, social condition of her people, general comfort and opportunities in life, the United States is ahead of any other country. Can a parallel be found in the history of the world? I think that an answer may unhesitatingly and unqualifiedly be made in the negative. United States has two and a half times the population of the United Kingdom, twice the national income and two or three times the accumulated national wealth;-I believe that these figures are too conservative. The argument is sometimes put forward by free traders that the United States would be better off under free trade. But, Sir, that is only a speculation, and a very unlikely speculation. One would be just as fully justified in saying that the United States would have failed miserably under free trade. It is not necessary to say that now with her great amassed wealth and with her developed industries, it might he wise for the United States gradually to adopt free trade. In fact, one might easily conclude so. But her early commercial history may be looked upon, it seems to me, as a perfectly good
model for Canada. Our progress has been slow in comparison; but should we experiment on account of that? Mr. Blaine during the course of a controversy with Mr. Gladstone, made a statement in 1896 which was published in the North American Review and which is in the library of Parliament in book form, in which he said that between 1812 and 1861 the United States tried free trade three times, and the result was recurring panics and depression; but that since 1861 the progress and prosperity of the country had been rapid and continuous. Therefore, Sir, we have the strongest arguments against experiments in the history and commercial conditions of United States which, I repeat, in area, resources and minerals is more like Canada than is any European country. Is it not desirable for us to profit by the example of the early commercial history of the United States?
Let us take all these things into account, and also the fact that forty-eight per cent of the people of this country are neither farmers nor manufacturers, and wish only the adoption of a policy which will be the best for Canada's development. I believe you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that the majority of the people of this country, of whatever political party, favour a moderate tariff policy, neither going to free trade extreme on the one hand nor the too high protectionist extreme on the other, by which too high protectionist extreme a group of men may exploit the people and subject them to overcharges. Of course, that is not to say that the present tariff policy must not be maintained as it is. The Minister of Finance has promised a scientific revision of the tariff, as was promised last year. It is not so difficult to understand that the revision that was promised last year was a little difficult to accomplish. Anyway, the Minister of Finance has promised this revision, and I think the House may certainly expect a revision by next year. I believe that tariff revision is very badly needed, but to say that is far from saying that free .trade would be the proper policy for this country. The members of this House are fairly representative, I think, of the people of this country, and certainly the representatives on either side of the House are not leaning towards the free trade extreme. Neither of the old parties has shown any tendency toward that extreme. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's who is, I think, a pretty fair spokesman for the party opposite, does not show any inclination to take to it at the present

time. If divisions in parties are based alone upon the tariff, then I think the supposed difference between the present Liberal Opposition and the present Unionist party is a very artificial difference. Therefore, as a dispassionate observer I believe that the just and proper course would be co-operation between the moderate people of the three great groups, farmers, manufacturers and labourites, the latter including the forty-eight per cent outside of the farmers and manufacturers. I believe that if these groups work together along moderate tariff lines fixing as low duties as possible on the necessaries of life, on raw materials, and on the instruments of production, the result will be the bringing about of the greatest good to the greatest number and the building up in the Northern half of this continent of a great, prosperous, united, freedom-loving people.

speechtext:
(Translation). Mr. Speaker, allow me, at the very outset of the few remarks I am about to make, to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) upon the clear and precise manner in which he delivered yesterday, what it is agreed to call, in parliamentary language, the Budget Speech. Conscious of the responsibility devolving upon me as one of the mandatories of this country, I wish to express my opinion freely, according to the dictates of my awn conscience, while remaining a loyal subject of the loyal opposition of His Majesty. In the course of a protracted debate which took place last year under similar circumstances, I had heard the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) state that, though he did not intend to prolong the debate, still he thought it was in the interest of the country that the discussion should be continued, as this was a means of finding out the opinions of each of the members representing the different parts of the Dominion. I do not wish to protract this debate either, but I do wish to explain my position, to express my opinion on the Government's policy, as well as on the Liberal platform laid down at the convention which took place in August last, and on the amendment now submitted to the House.
The country has passed through a terrible crisis; the war brought the Government face to face with many new problems, but this land never experienced social unrest in the same degree to which we are witnessing it to-day, in practically no part of the world was there ever seen such a social upheaval as that which has followed

in the wake of the economic disturbance brought about by the war -and which instead of lessening seems to gain in strength as time goes on.
What are the oauses of this social unrest which finds expression in numerous and ever recurrent strikes, in popular movements which, at times, border on sedition, giving rise tot popular clamour of every description and apprising us of the existence in the different classes of society of a ferment which threatens to destroy not alone the social equilibrium of this country but the economic equilibrium as well?
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these causes are both deep-rooted and remote; I hold that the economic system which has been established for years in this country is one of the main causes of this social unrest we are witnessing to-day and about which the hon. Minister of Trade and- Commerce (Sir George Foster) asked us yesterday to remain silent while knuckling down to the task of production. Furthermore I hold that these causes are remote. As I- said a moment- ago the war saw colossal fortunes- piled up in this country; but even before the advent of war certain classes- of our citizens- enjoyed special privileges and that was, I believe, one of the conditions responsible for social unrest. The main cause of the trouble is -found, it appears to me, in the fact that instead of recognizing agriculture as the basic industry of this country we have been too considerate of our manufacturing interests, afforded them too much protection.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat gave us a wonderful description of the situation that- obtains in this country to-day. He gave us some very interesting statistics but he forgot, I fear, to -acquaint the House -and I regret that he does not understand what I -am saying-with one of the chief facts of the case. When the hon. member for Fort William was explaining his attitude and -revealing himself in the colours of a moderate protectionist he forgot, ih his comparisons between Germany, England and United States, to mention the respective populations of these countries.
Mr. Speaker, the United States are almost -a world unto themselves, compared to England; Germany also has a much larger territory than England. The United -States have a poulation of 110,000,000, Germany, 70,000,000 and the population of England, so far as I know, does not reach 50,000,000. I haven't the statistics here -and I make no claim to infallibility, but before

the war I was a close student of the commercial activity of these countries and, as a British subject I was proud of the fact that England, the smallest in respect of population, the smallest, in respect of territory, surpassed, in volume of trade, such countries as the United States and Germany; England's trade was greater than that of the United States despite the fact that the United States had two and ia half times the population and four or five the territorial expanse of England.
In my youth whenever I used to hear public men speaking of free trade and protection. I was rather inclined* to be an unreserved free trader since I was enamoured of big ideas; I considered that protection penalized trade. Having had occasion, later on, to become better acquainted with public affairs, I realize today that the economic system of this country should be grounded on free trade while at the same time granting to every industry the measure of protection necessary for the . fostering of that industry.
I am astonished that the hon. member for Fort William should proclaim himself a moderate protectionist and should then express approval of the Budget brought down by the Finance Minister yesterday when that Budget puts a tax as high as 50 per cent on some articles. I wonder just how stiff a tax would be necessary to convince the hon. member that the tariff was rather high. In his opinion this Budget gives moderate protection. I might tell my hon. friend and colleague that since he changed parties, since he entered the Unionist fold, his views have perhaps undergone a change.
The question of protection and free trade is an old question. As I said before, Mr. Speaker. I have practically grown up in the study of this question. This Canada of ours enjoyed prosperity from 1854 to 1866. At that time we had a reciprocity agreement with the United States, but the United States, dissatisfied with our attitude during the Civil War, withdrew from the agreement. In 1878 Sir John Macdonald inaugurated the National Policy. Our country had j ust entered upon its development; Confederation was in its early stages and the country's industries were just beginning to get a foothold. Elected to office the Liberal party in 1897, made a substantial reduction in the tariff the following year and relieved the people to that extent. With what regret Mr. Speaker, the people of this country recall the days of peace and plenty which blessed Canada under the Liberal Administration, which lasted from 1896 to 1911, fifteen years of peace, of social well-being and of material prosperity without precedent in the annals not only of this, but of any other country.
In 1911 things took a new turn in Canada; the Liberal party, consistent with the doctrine it had always held, sought to give a new impetus to agriculutre, realizing that the greatness and prosperity of this country can only be brought about by the development of agriculture. In a treaty negotiated at Washington by the Finance Minister, the Government of the day made certain concessions, took a step in the direction of free trade. But you are as well aware as I of the turn affairs took in Canada at that time. A powerful association sprung up wielding its influence throughout the country. The voters, it seemed, were not entitled to concern themselves with what the Manufacturers' Association considered its own particular affair. The association waged a war to the death against reciprocity with the result that the former Government went down to defeat and the affairs of the country passed into the hands of a party which, up to that time had espoused the doctrine of protection rather than free trade. What wa's the consequence of this ohange, Mt. Speaker? On reading to-day the speech delivered yesterday by the hon. Minister of Finance, I find the practical confirmation of what I said: the total agricultural production in 1910 (page 2555 of the unrevised debates for the 18t.h May, in the speech of the hon. Minister of Finance) amounted to $663,000,000 in round figures; in 1919 it reached $1,975,000,000, an increase in twelve years of $1,312,000,000, an average gain of $145,000,000 per year. So much for our farm produce. Now let us consult the figures for our manufactured products. In the statistics he gave the House yesterday the Finance Minister did not choose, for his comparison, the same years as in the case of agriculture.
In 1906 our manufactured products were valued at $718,000,000; eleven years later, in 1917, they had attained $3,015,000,000 in value, an increase of $2,297,000,000 in eleven years, a yearly average of $208,000,000. So we find that agricultural products increased, on an average; $145,000,000 in value each year while our manufactured products jumped in value $208,000,000 every twelve months.
I believe the present Government has failed to take sufficient interest in the mainspring of this country's development; that it has been too lavish in its favour to a certain class and too niggardly in this respect

towards agriculture. The building of tremendous fortunes both during the war and even prior to the war, thanks to our high tariff wall, is probably one of the causes of the social unrest I was referring to a moment ago.
I would ask each and every member in this House who enjoys the advantage of being conversant with the language in which I have chosen to express my opinions on this matter, even my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. MoMaster) whom the hon. member for Fort William classed as a free trader, to make the following comparison:	take a farmer in your district
whose holding is valued at $10,000 and who tills his soil with the assistance of his son; after ten years of hard work, when this man has raised his family, what will his investment of $10,000 be worth? The answer is easy; it will still represent $10,000. Take $10,000 to-day and invest it in a factory; in ten years your factory will be worth $100,000. Agriculture has not kept pace with the manufacturing industry of this country.
We hear the complaint, Mr. Speaker, that our country districts are becoming depopulated; but everything has 'been done to draw people to the cities. The farmers are asked to increase production-for, after all, the law of supply and demand is responsible for the high cost of living-the farmers are asked to increase production but in order to do that they must have more help; besides up to these last few.years agriculture was far from being remunerative in 'this country.
In my opening remarks-and I was sincere-I had the pleasure of congratulating the hon. Minister of Finance; last year and up to the present time I had an opportunity of admiring his predecessor. When I first came into the House I listened with pleasure to the Budget Speech delivered by the Hon. Sir Thomas White and each year it was with renewed pleasure that I listened to him when he made his address to the House.
With our prosperity tumbling and millions being thrown away I used to admire the former minister, and I admire the present minister; however, I recall the ancient myth of the Danaides who by their father's order, were condemned to go on forever pouring water into a broken cistern. The present hon. Minister of Finance seems like his predecessor, condemned to constantly fill the public treasury vaults while his colleagues as constantly go on spending in the most thoughtless way. A deficit of $47,000.-
tMr. Gervais.]
000 from our railroads; the building of a merchant marine, the profitable operation of which is open to question; millions spent-right and left; an overburdened Budget. The member of former days will not recognize the Parliament of Canada for 1920; all the more reason for admiring the efforts of the hon. Minister of Finance while he strives to fill up the treasury, a reproduction of the broken cistern of the Danaides.
Mr. Speaker, it was in 1918 that I first came into this House; everything was new to me then. At that time I listened to rather inflamed speeches-we were so to speak on IJtie top of a volcano-hovrever I believe the intentions of my hon. friend's have changed for the better; they have realized I believe, that to promote peace and harmony in this country they should make their appeal to the spirit of good-will, to the spirit of tolerance. The war which was ranging then has come to an end. The post-war problems, however, did not dampen the enthusiasm of the association I alluded to a moment ago; here amongst my papers I discovered a gigantic advertisement that the Manufacturers' Association had published in the Montreal newspaper La Presse on the 17th of March, 1919. In this advertisement the Manufacturers' Association asks: Where are you going to get the revenue? Where are you going to find the $400,000,000 you need? In the pockets of the people of course, by burdening them with further taxes. I do not think -the hon. Minister of Finance found his inspiration in this advertisement of last year; however, the same spirit is predominant in the Cabinet, the same spirit which was evident some years ago and is still evident to-day.
Not content with publishing advertisements broadcast in the newspapers this association appealed to manufacturers to enroll in its membership and showed them the advantages of such action. Fortunately the manufacturers of Berthier county recognize the merits of a free trade policy and I take pleasure in reading to the House the answer sent by one of our Berthier manufacturers to Mr. Howard Smith, chairman of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association :
Berthiep.vii.le, P.Q., April 22nd, 1919. Mr. Howard Smith,
Pres. Canadian Mfg. Assn.,
Montreal, Que.
Dear Sir:-
Referring to your communication regarding a petition to the Government at Ottawa to maintain the present high tariff on raw or finished products now manufactured in Canada, would say that our experience is that we would much prefer a reduction in tariff on our lines.

In fact, if you will remove the tariff on our raw material we are certain we would be in a position to compete with the United States very favorably and if the United States would remove their tariff on our finished product, we could and would go into the United States market to a very great advantage, since we would have lt>0 million more people to sell to.
We are therefore very much in favor of lower tariff on all of our lines finished or for the raw material at least.
In fact I am quite sure you are of my opinion in case we can so exchange with the United States.
Very truly yours,
(Signed) George A. Savoy,
Managing Director.
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, everybody is not in favtiur of a high tariff; I believe the great majority of our people desire a revision downwards. Since, as the statistics quoted by the hon. member for Fort William show, the middle classes comprise the major portion of our population, I feel sure that an increase in import duties will bear most heavily on this class of the community. I am almost through, Mr. Speaker. Let me say that I highly appreciate the nice regard shown us by our friends on the Government side in the course of the last, and of the present, session. I am happy to see that the sentiment which sprang up during the war is fast disappearing. I used to wonder if the members from the province of Quebec, who speak the French tongue, who represent the pioneers of this country, those ancestors of ours, who at one time preserved Canada to the British flag, I used to wonder, I say, whether those citizens had the same rights as are granted to other citizens. I believe that the effervescence stirred up by the war has subsided; I believe that all men of good-will are going to work for the cause of union and forbearance and that the energy of each and every one of our citizens will be pledged to the common task of leading our beloved Canada to the promised land of her glorious future.

Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks this evening I desire in the first place to congratulate the Minister of Finance on the very able way in which he presented his Budget Speech yesterday. I think he is to be highly commended for the frankness with which he placed the country's present position, and particularly the financial situation, before the people. The people for some time have been waiting to know just what the conditions were following this terrible period of five years through which we have just passed. Naturally, with such
large expenditures as the Government had to face during those years, it was to be expected that it would take some time to balance the accounts. I am sure that the situation, now that we know the truth, was not so serious as many of us had expected it would be. I think also that the country is to be congratulated on having a Minister of Finance with courage and boldness enough to bring into effect such a Budget as was introduced yesterday. It must have taken considerable courage to go from the beaten track of years into practically a new sphere of taxation, but the minister and his colleagues were convinced, no doubt, that the time had come when the people of Canada should bear the burden imposed by the war and that we should no longer borrow money for the immense revenue we have to raise. In this connection the minister, I think, has brought down a Budget which in every way will make for economy and production. Those who have studied the situation of this country during the last year have realized that if Canada is to take her place in the export markets of the world, if our people are to be prosperous, if posterity is not to be burdened with an enormous debt for years and years to come, then those of us who are directing or helping to direct the policy of the country should immediately get down to business as other countries are doing. In popular parlance the " come-back " of John Bull & Sons proved something; of a boomerang. It was as if John Bull was saying to the world, with the man who was called upon to deny his published obituary notice, "the report is grossly exaggerated."

Is Canada to be the only free trade country with free trade a misnomer as it is at the present time? Free trade, as we understand it to-day, or as it might be possible under our Farmer and Liberal friends, would be a one-sided trade.
In view of the demands which western farmers are making that our Government make an immediate and substantial allround reduction in the customs tariff, it is only proper that we should consider what our Allies are doing!
The importation of manufactured goods into Great Britain is subject to restrictions which constitute very high protection.
France is not lowering her tariff; on the contrary she is shutting out the goods of other countries by a system of import licenses.
Italy, like Great Britain and France, is restricting imports.
The Premier of South Africa has announced that the tariff of that country, heretofore designed for revenue only, will be increased to protect home industries.
Nothing has been heard to warrant the belief that any lowering of the tariff is even under consideration by Australia, New Zealand, Newfoundland, Japan, Brazil or Portugal.
In the United States the Republican party has now a majority in both the Senate and Congress and it has always supported a high tariff. The National Industrial Conference Board of the United States reported -"That a more highly protective tariff will be advocated .... is practically certain," and twenty-six Bills now before Congress increasing the tariff.
The farmer, or one-sided trader might well be challenged to point to a single country in the world to-day which is proposing to lower its tariff at this critical time. And why is this? Because the above-mentioned

countries are determined to reconstruct their industries on a peace basis, to manufacture for themselves what they need, and to provide employment for their soldiers and war workers.
Is Canada to be the only country in the world to throw down its safeguards? Is she going to ignore the great lesson taught by the war, that a nation must maintain within its own boundaries all the elements of self-protection and self-support? Are we to build a nation within the Empire-a Canadian nation, not a dependent; a nation self-sustaining in days of need as well as plenty. Our policy with our immense natural resources and people of initiative should be national, not class.
Referring for a moment to the latest Budget brought in by the Finance Minister of Australia, the new tariff, it is said for the first time follows the Canadian precedent in having three distinct schedules of duties -British Preferential, Intermediate and General Tariff columns. The British Preferential rates came immediately into operation in so far as goods and products manufactured in the United Kingdom are concerned.
The Finance Minister of Australia states:
While it is admitted that no Parliament can bind the succeeding Parliament to any prospective customs duties, yet the new principle of a ''deferred scale of duties" to become operative at fixed dates (mainly on January 1, 1921, and the same date in 1922) has been introduced into the Tariff Bill. The deferred duty proposals comprise twenty-two items, and their incidence bears chiefly upon iron and steel products, vessels trading in Australian waters, and certain lines of fuse and explosives. The minister explained that the deferred duty principle was to give definite encouragement to investors to establish industries within Australia, and quoted instances of the probable establishment of industrial plants when sufficient protection was to some extent assured.

I might point out a few features as to the Australian tariff. Pig iron'was free until the new tariff came in; to-day the general tariff is forty shillings per ton. Pipes cast and wrought per ton, forty-eight shillings before this tariff came down; the Finance Minister of Australia has raised the duty to eighty shillings. Rails and other items in that category which were thirty-five shillings per ton have been raised to seventy-five shillings, eighty-five shillings and ninety-five shillings. And so on throughout this whole tariff. The Australian Government,-and a more or less Labour Government at that,-have at last realized that if Australia is to be a big industrial country these new industries must be protected, and they have gone at it in a wholesale way. Further than that, the value for duty is to be taken as the fair market value of the goods in the principal markets of the country whence the same were exported in the usual and ordinary commercial acceptation of the term and free on board at the port of export in such country, with a further addition of ten per cent on such market value.
Dealing with free trade as it concerns our transportation problem, transportation was a large issue in the Reciprocity campaign of 1911. It is a bigger issue to-day, because since then Canada has begun the operation of the Canadian National railways, a great transcontinental system. She has already spent hundreds of millions upon these enterprises, and may have to spend many millions more. Her only chance to prevent that investment becoming a dead loss is to keep a steady flow of traffic moving from east to west, and from west to east. If ever it becomes diverted to a north and south direction, her transportation plant might as well be scrapped.
Under reciprocity or free trade that is what would inevitably happen. In fact western farmers are quite frank in the expression of their desire to market their grain in Minneapolis and Chicago, and to buy their requirements in manufactured goods from the Middle and Western States. Their wdiole effort at present is to encourage the buying of United States goods in preference to Canadian. Inferentially, therefore, their whole effort is to make it difficult or impossible to operate our transcontinental railways at a profit. These railways were built with the money of the people of Canada, in order that there might be opened up for settlement a territory whose population are now enjoying marked prosperity. Without the railways there would have been
no West. Without the taxes cheerfully paid year after year by Canadians in the East there would have been no railways. Is the partnership arrangement, that has proven so mutually profitable, now to be terminated simply because of the unwillingness of the West to pay its share of the operating expenses? And must the whole investment be wiped out in consequence?
It is essential that Canadian credit should be maintained at the high standard at which it now is. It may be necessary at some day in the future for public works or for other capital	account	to	borrow money.
When Canada goes to her banker, fortunately the Canadian people at the present time, and asks for a loan they will want to know two things: First, what is she going to do with the money she is asking for, and second, what sources of income has she that will justify the belief that she will be able to repay? Canada can hardly borrow money when she has to admit that she is going to give it away, or is going to use it in meeting interest charges on what she already owes. Her chances of success would be better if she could show that she was going to employ it in useful public works, but even then she would have to be in a position to prove that her revenue would be equal to the task of carrying all existing obligations, plus interest and sinking fund on the new loan she was trying to>
negotiate. Faced with the direct question "What is your estimated revenue for the-year ending March, 1921, or 1922, and from what sources?" how would she answer were she at this juncture to enact any measure of free trade? She could show that under her present tariff, with the addition of the special war tariff and taxes, after meeting all claims for drawbacks, she was able to meet all her obligations for the year. But what guarantee would there be that she could do as well under free trade? At the very time when she absolutely must maintain her credit, is she deliberately to invite refusal, if need be, by adopting fiscal changes that will make it impossible foT her to give any satisfactory assurances as to what her revenues will amount to? If she cannot borrow money for public works, and if, in consequence, there ensues a long period of widespread unemployment, what is the effect going to be on Victory Bonds? With business depressed and people out of work, the bonds will undoubtedly come onto the market in large volume, and that in turn will depreciate their value. Is Canada to be a party to an arrangement that will

double-cross her own people who have come so nobly to her assistance in financing the war? I think sometimes governments find it a difficult lesson to learn that future governmental revenues are based entirely on the present development of the nation's resources, and development can only be attained through the attraction of capital into enterprise by the inducement of satisfactory and reasonable returns on the capital invested.
I think it would be advisable for the Minister of Finance, if he can see his w.ay clear, to impose a more moderate rate of income tax next year. It seems to me that the difficulty of collecting the small tax hardly makes it worth while, and the other tax is so heavy as to be almost exorbitant, and at times defeats its purpose.
I am sorry it has been necessary for me to take up so much time this evening, but I felt that, not having declared myself before, I should take a stand before this Parliament and before the country and my constituents. It seems to me that this is a time when all members of Parliament must shoulder the responsibility which rests upon them. After all the country looks to some extent to its law-makers sitting in this House to lead the way. We have a long journey before us in Canada, but it is a journey on which we can see our way. We have great resources. We have a courageous people. We are not so old but that the courage and the faith of our forefathers still remain in us. We are not so old but that we can remember many of the large developments that have taken place in this country. We have before us always the record of the past five years. Surely in Canada we have nothing to be ashamed of. We can look forward with a great deal of confidence to the mastering of the problems that face us financially, and in nation-building; and I do hope that this debate will be characterized by its high national tone.
After all, there is nothing so important at the present time in this country as that Canada shall stand higher than she has ever stood before. There is no real difference between the two sides of this House. The difference is purely imaginery, because while we have one side talking protection, the other side is talking partial free trade but means protection. This is a time in our history for us to forget to a large extent our party differences. The Government have many problems to face, and it behooves all of us who are in the fortunate position to represent constituencies in this

Parliament at this critical time to maintain the general interest, not the interest of a
class.

speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the farmers of Western Canada wish to market their wheat at Minneapolis and also to purchase their machinery there. If I heard him correctly, he is absolutely wrong in his statement.

subtopic: REDUCTIONS IN THE CANADIAN CUSTOMS TARIFF SINCE THE YEAR 1911
speechtext:
Hon. members should not abuse the privilege which they have of asking a question by rising presumably for that purpose and taking advantage of the opportunity to interject a statement or expression of opinion. By a strict interpretation of the rules of debate these hon. members should be considered as having exhausted their right to speak.
Mr. D'ANJOU (Translation): Mr. Speaker, in addressing the House this evening I have no intention of setting forth a definition of protection or free trade. I merely wish to say that I, personally, am in favour of whatever tariff changes may benefit the country and that I .abide by the resolution passed at the great Liberal convention of August, 1919. Therefore, since the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) contains a miniature likeness of that resolution I shall take pleasure in voting for the amendment. The hoin. member from St. John, N.B. stated, amongst other things, that once upon a time he had been a free trader; he forgot to mention, however, that at one time he had been a Liberal also and that while he had altered his mind he had changed parties too, which explains how our former free trader has become converted to the doctrine of protection. A goodly portion of his speech was devoted to attacks against the farming community. Like many another horn, member on the Government side the hon. gentleman from St. John, N.B. seems to fear the farmers' movement; no doubt he despairs of ever being re-elected to a seat in this House, a lot which will assuredly befall the great majority otf the hon. gentlemen on your right, Mr. Speaker.
I myself am not a farmer; I have no brief for the farmers; the important Farmer party in this House is well able to- take care of its own interests. However, as the representative of a riding which is distinctly agricultural in character, I deem it my duty to challenge the statements of any hon. member who starts, hammer .and tongs, after the farmers of this country.
"The hon. gentleman from St. John, N.B. said that the farmers paid no taxes on their

profits, that their profits were exempt. The hon. member, no doubt, is interested in a few mighty corporations and he is not very keen on sharing his profits with the Government. Of course he is perfectly willing to share all honour with the Government, but he would rather keep his profits to himself. He resembles all those profiteers who, during the war, amassed fortunes with the help of this Government. During the war while our people were bowed down in pain and suffering, while so many Of our boys were shedding their blood on the battlefields of old Europe, these gentlemen -we have several of them in this House- at the head of powerful corporations were taking in millions; at that time, I repeat, blood was flowing in torrents on the fields of Flanders and other battle grounds. So it seems to me the hon. member for St. John, N.B., has no right to complain of the farmers.
During the present session it has been insinuated that the farmers were the worst of war profiteers, that the war had enriched them tremendously. Like every other mere mortal the farmer has suffered from the rise in the cost of commodities; he has had to pay more for labour and for agricultural machinery; consequently he is entitled to dispose of his wares at a little higher price. It was brought out in a recent debate, particularly by my hon. friend, the member for L'Islet (Mr. Fafard) that profiteering is not to be found .amongst the farmers, but amongst the middlemen; it is the middleman who goes from farm to farm buying up all the produce at ridiculously low prices and later sells this same produce in the public markets at a fabulous figure. As the hon. member for l'lslet explained, potatoes bought last fall for between 90 cents and $1.10 a bag were later sold at $5 and $6 a bag. Did that money go into the farmer's pocket? No, it went into the pockets of the middlemen who hoarded this produce in cold storage plants; the middlemen that this Government wants to shield-there you have your profiteers. They are the men who deserve the Government's wrath; not only should they he thrown into prison, they should be hanged. That is the treatment meted out to profiteers in certain countries of Europe.
According to the statement of the Minister of Finance himself the country is confronted with .a pyramid of debt. The people of Canada will be astounded to hear this statement from the lips of the minister. However, there is nothing surprising about
it after all the guilty extravagance indulged in by this Government during the last five years. Truly the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) must feel satisfied; at last his dream has come true; the country is bankrupt; we are down to our last farthing.
On March 31st, 1920, our national debt was $3,014,483,774.12. I repeat, there is no room here for surprise. For my part, during the last and preceding sessions I stated that, although not absolutely opposed to our participation in the war, I decidedly was opposed to this .country taking an unreasonable and irrational part in the hostilities; that is my position still. We see to-day the result of this irrational participation in the war. Whatever may be said, this war was not fought for the defence of civilization and liberty; even now that the League of Nations has become a reality, we can very weill see that the last war, like most others, was .fought for commercial supremacy and world domination.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) declared that the paternal Government of which he is such an ardent supporter had .striven with every means at its disposal to promote agriculture in this country; indeed, he said, the Estimates for the present year give $5,000,000 to agriculture-however the Estimates include $12,000,000 for military purposes. Apparently the member .for Fort William is satisfied with this vote of $12,000,000 for military purposes since he finds $5,000,000 sufficient for agriculture. Well, I vrouild like to see those $12,000,000 added to the $5,000,000 already voted; thus agriculture would have $17,000,000 and the army nothing. The war we have just been through cost us enough in blood and treasure. While the war was perhaps not fought .for the defence of freedom and civilization it was fought for the destruction of Prussian militarism, and I maintain that when, at the cost of untold sacrifices we have succeeded in crushing militarism in Germany, is no time to introduce militarism into this country. I do not know what opinions the hon. member for Fort William may hold. I say that instead of voting $12,000,000 for military purposes the Government should have given the money to agriculture, should have used it, as I have often asked, for the establishment of new experimental farms, for schools of agriculture and not for military schools, for an army of tillers of the soil and not for an army of soldiers. I have not changed my attitude and even if some

hon. member on the Government side should accuse me of disloyalty I would not care one whit; I have the courage of my convictions and no one will deter me from taking my stand openly.
When I asked the hon. minister for an experimental farm in Eimouski county he told me that he could not grant my request because the Government lacked the necessary funds. Under cover of the policy of economy the Government is doing things which are neithei to the advantage o.f the country nor in the country's interests. Among other things I was promised nearly $30,000 foT the completion of the port at Eimouski. This undertaking was in the interest not only of Eimouski county alone, hut of a very important district of the province of Quebec; it would have been equally advantageous to the neighbouring county represented by my hen. friend from Ma-tane (Mr. Pelletier). Well, on the plea of economy, I was refused $16,800, and now the Government is going to spend $12,000 -000, perhaps $20,000,000, to establish military encampments all through the country. I do not countenance this policy; I am in favour of economy, but economy well understood. I have said before in the course of the present session and I repeat here to-day, that the 'Government can never [DOT]spend too much money for the promotion of agriculture; since agriculture is the principal industry Of this country and will help us, more than any other thing, to overcome the difficulties which beset our country to-day.
The spirit of unrest is stalking through this country, unrest caused in great part by the high cost of living; still the Budget reveals no attempt on the part of the Government to (bring relief to the people.
If I am in favour of the amendment presented by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, it is because I am convinced that the adoption of this amendment and the carrying out of the policy therein enunciated would bring about an improvement in (the present situation and the lowering of the cost of living.
Over production is certainly one of the best ways of doing this, for with us as in many other countries, consumption has increased enormously and production has decreased. There should at least be equilibrium between the two, and in order to bring that about, production and over-production should he encouraged by all possible means. You hear much said in blame of the farmers, hut during the war we were

very well pleased to see them bend all their energies towards intensified production, so as to feed not only the Canadian soldier at the front but our people at home. The most rational and most efficient way of encouraging agriculture and over-production is to put the farmer in the way of obtaining more cheaply farming implements among other things, by removing the customs duty from them, and also, as asked for in the amendments, from certain necessaries of life.
But the present Government are not in power for the benefit of the agricultural class any more than of other classes in the country save one. The present -Government are in power for their own advantage and that of their supporters. This -Government have the support of the profiteers, of those who were enriched by the war, of the namby-pamby young fellows who paraded the streets of Ottawa, Montreal and elsewhere during the war on a $10, $12 or $15 a d-ay pay, while the workmen's sons were having their 'backs broken in the trenches of Flanders.
I would like to say a word as to the railway policy. Like all the hon. members who sit on this side of the -House, I have always been, -and am still, opposed to the operating of the railways Iby the Government, and the events have proved that we were right. Before the Government -came to the conclusion of finally adopting this policy, we had the examples of England and the United States, which in trying to apply this policy had met -with monumental failure. Consequently, when the hon. Minister of Eailways (Mr. Eeid) came to tell this House that, after a period of nine months, his administration of the Government railways showed a deficit of $45,000,000, the hon. members on this side of the House were not surprised. For my part, I still hold that such a policy is not calculated to benefit the country, but rather to benefit certain railway magnates, close friends of the Government, and who share their advantages, perhaps, with certain members * of this House who advocated this policy and supported it in Parliament.
I do not intend to occupy much of the time of the House. I would like though to say a few words as to the general course followed by the Government. There is no doubt hut that we are governed somewhat according to the Bussian or Prussian system. Autocracy reigns supreme in this country, and as was so truly observed by the hon. leader of the Opposition in the"

magnificent speech which he delivered the other evening, we have coine to the point of using secret diplomacy. Such is the new ill-use of power which this Government has added to their guilt. They decided, without consulting Parliament, that is, without consulting the Canadian people through their representatives, to send an emissary to Washington; and when everything was done, they came and said to Parliament, "Without your authorization, without consulting you as representatives of the people, we have decided this, and to-day, whether you are willing or not, the thing is done, and has to be abided by." A fine way forsooth of governing a democratic country; a fine way of respecting the rights of the people! I for one have already [DOT] had occasion to protest against such ill-use of power on the part of the Government. I find the Canadian nation a long-suffering people. It seems to me that had such abuse of power taken place in some other country, its government would long have ceased to exist. The Canadian people are good, they are patient, tout their hour shall come before long, and whatever toe the government then sitting on your right, Mr. Speaker, toe they a Liberal, Government- as I am convinced they will be-or be they a Farmers' Government, they will toe a vast improvement upon what we have to-day.
We already knew that the Government was no longer trusted by the people, tout we bad further evidence of the fact the other evening when the vote was taken upon the motion of the hon. member .for Shelburne and Queen's protesting against the appointment of a Canadian representative at Washington.
Then how could this Government have the confidence of the people, seeing the .iniquitous way in which they won the election and the fraudulent methods they used to get into power? No wonder that, from the start, the people had no confidence in them and the Government did not act. in .guch a way as to win their confidence. (There remains only one thing for them to do, i.e., to pack up their trunks and to appear before the electorate. The people are anxious to look upon the congenial faces of these hon. gentlemen opposite when they seek re-election; anxious to stare at. these renegades who sit at your right, Mr. Speaker, and who betrayed them. I am sure 'that the answer of the people will be a condemnation of this Government who usurped the executive power and who committed all the abuses of which an autio-.cratic Government might be guilty. It does
pot matter what Government will be formed a,t that time: either a good Liberal administration having at- its head the eminent and able leader of the Liberal Opposition or a Government composed of our friends the Farmers who have a very distinguished leader in the person of the ex-,Minister of Agriculture (iMr. Crerar). What we, of the Opposition want is that the Government come and ask the people for a new ,mandate. We are sure that the verdict .will be one of reprobation and condemna-,tion, because the people who were deceived .and shocked in their most intimate feelings, want to take their revenge and the ^revenge will be unsparing. I am sure, .there might not remain ten of the present tmembers sitting now at your right, Mr. Speaker. The people will elect representatives not like some hon. members of the present parliament who owe their election to the extorting of soldier votes, but who shall have been chosen freely and sincerely through a better franchise Act than that which the Government wishes to impose upon the House now. I am positive that the people will grant their confidence to hon. members of this side of the House, Mr. Speaker, for they have always worked' hard in the interest of the country and this-they will continue to do until the Government decide to appeal to the people.
